The content of this book is compiled from The Essentials of the Buddha-Dharma and the Letters of Mr. Liu Zhuyuan. The author, Mr. Liu Zhuyuan (Master Changzong), is a sage of modern times, broadly versed in the scriptural canon and deeply learned in doctrine and contemplation; because he withdrew from the world and lived in seclusion, few knew of him. The depth of his practice and the loftiness of his realization may be seen in the following three points: First, the meaning and practice set forth in The Essentials of the Buddha-Dharma and the Letters of Mr. Liu Zhuyuan. Master Yinguang praised him, saying: ‘Liu Zhuyuan’s literary and doctrinal understanding is very profound; seeing the recorded conduct of Mr. Zhang, I am filled with boundless admiration. Since the region of Sichuan has such a worthy, and he is also an advocate, it is truly the good fortune of the people of Sichuan, and likewise the good fortune of the Dharma.’ (From the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, First Letter in Reply to the Layman Xie Huilin) Second, ‘Therefore, in teaching people, he would always have them set everything down and contemplate their own mind. Those who followed this teaching, many attained awakening.’ (
The Essentials of the Buddha-Dharma

) Third, ‘In the summer of 1950, the Master passed away at Baiyun Monastery; that night a white light shot up from the monastery toward the sky, and many saw it from near and afar.’ (Recorded in detail in Awakening to Sentiment, volume 11, issue 8)

In his later years the Master delighted in the joy of Chan and cared not for writing; only a few lecture manuscripts survived, which his disciples passed down by copying them from hand to hand; those who obtained them treasured them as something of inestimable worth. Fortunately, his disciple Mr. Jin Hongshu edited and published them, naming them The Essentials of the Buddha-Dharma, and appended the eighteen letters in which the Master instructed him; only then did this black pearl come to light in the world.

The source text of this book is Mr. Liu Zhuyuan’s The Essentials of the Buddha-Dharma. As the title indicates, this is the essential theory of the Buddha-Dharma and the essential practical cultivation. Though not lengthy in extent, it is vast and profound, advancing ever upward until it enters the stage of the Tathagata; it is the great and perfect Dharma.

blocks.text: A Brief Biography of the Master

inline.s: Mr. Liu Zhuyuan (

), styled Fuli, with the courtesy name Zhuyuan, and also known by the alias Liming, was a native of Zhongjiang County, Sichuan Province. In his youth he studied the Confucian classics and passed the examinations for the xiucai degree; because he excelled for years running in the annual examinations, he was recommended to the court (as a bagong scholar). Later he graduated from the College of Classics in Beijing, excelled in literature, and was thoroughly versed in the Three Rites. He served successively as a professor of literature at Sichuan Higher Normal College, Chengdu University, and Sichuan University, twenty years in all. In the twentieth year of the Republic of China (
) he resigned and entered the mountains to cultivate the Way.

[The bagong] In the Qing dynasty, the provincial education commissioners selected students who excelled in both letters and conduct and recommended them to the Imperial Academy (the highest seat of learning in the land) in the capital; these were called bagong students, abbreviated as bagong. [The Three Rites] is the collective name for the Confucian classics the Rites of Zhou, the Etiquette and Ceremonial, and the Record of Rites.

The Master’s study of Buddhism passed from Confucianism into Buddhism, and in Buddhist studies he was self-taught. In his letters he said: ‘In all my life I have had no master, though I first studied the classics. I used their method to read the books of the two schools of nature and characteristics, and to pursue the learning of the Tiantai and Xianshou schools. Later I entered the Chan school, whose gate is not elaborate, and so amid having no master, I found a master.’

[The two schools of nature and characteristics] are the Dharma-nature school and the Dharma-characteristics school. [Tai and Xian] are the Tiantai school and the Xianshou school (that is, the Avatamsaka or Huayan school).
In the twenty-eighth year of the Guangxu reign (

), the Master was already propagating the Buddha-Dharma in Chengdu; the four assemblies looked up to him, and his affinity for the Dharma was exceedingly flourishing (see the Brief Chronological Table of Chinese Buddhism compiled by Tang Shengdi and others). After the founding of the Republic, while teaching at Chengdu University, he opened a lecture series on Buddhist studies on campus and publicly lectured on Buddhism, and was one of the first professors to bring Buddhist studies into the institutions of higher learning. He also established a Buddhist society in Chengdu and gathered assemblies to expound the scriptures and preach the Dharma. From the end of the Guangxu reign onward, over a span of more than twenty years, he exerted a considerable influence upon people in society; and those who, moved by him, took refuge in Buddhism were very many. The later famous master of Tibetan Buddhism, Neng Hai, while at Chengdu, heard the Master’s lecture and, inspired by it, shaved his head and left home.

In his early years the Master was expert in the Consciousness-Only (Vijnaptimatra) school, and once wrote An Outline of the Study of Consciousness-Only, of tens of thousands of words. He privately admired Yongming Yanshou, and in the twenty-first year of the Republic of China (

) wrote the Great Sectional Analysis of the Record of the Mirror of the Source. In his later years he delighted in the joy of Chan and cared not for authorship; only a few lecture manuscripts survived, copied and passed down by his disciples. In the thirty-seventh year (

), in the third lunar month, he shaved his head at Yanzuo Monastery in Xiaoquan, Deyang County, Sichuan, and received the triple-platform great precepts, his Dharma name being Changzong. Before long, at invitation, he lectured on the Surangama Sutra and transmitted the Pure Land contemplation method. Later he returned to Zhongjiang County, took up residence at Baiyun Monastery, and devoted himself to the study of the precepts. In the thirty-ninth year (

) he passed away, at the age of seventy-eight. Besides what has been recorded above, his works include the Detailed Sectional Analysis of the Record of the Mirror of the Source, about five fascicles, and the Method for Reading the Record of the Mirror of the Source, over ten fascicles. He also compiled the Dharma characteristics of the Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom into the three volumes of the Dharma-Treasury of the Nature School, which, however, were never published.

[Privately admired (sishu)] means to revere and emulate someone privately without having formally become their disciple. [Yongming Yanshou] was the Chan master Yanshou of the Song dynasty, known as the Jue-wisdom (Zhijue) master; because he dwelt at Yongming Monastery on Mount Huiri in Hangzhou, he is called the Chan Master Yongming Yanshou. He was originally the third-generation master of the Fayan (Dharma-eye) school of the Chan tradition, but in Pure Land practice and Buddha-recitation he was also most diligent, making tens of thousands of recitations of the Buddha’s name his daily task; he composed the Four Boiled-Down Judgments, advocating the joint cultivation of Chan and the Pure Land, and he is the sixth patriarch of the Pure Land school. He has handed down the hundred-fascicle Record of the Mirror of the Source, the six-fascicle Collection of All Goodness Returning to the One, the one-fascicle Ode on the Spirit Dwelling in Peace and Bliss, the one-fascicle Verse on the Mind-Only, and others.

The sage Mr. Liu Zhuyuan, in his later years, left home and served as abbot of Baiyun Monastery (located in Zhongjiang County, Sichuan), taking the name Master Baiyun (White Cloud); hence his true transmission is called the ‘Essence of the White Cloud Mind.’ Its guiding principle is: directly contemplate your own mind, and seeing your nature, become a Buddha.

Why contemplate the mind? The Buddha-Dharma is vast, but its root is the mind; the gates of practice are measureless, but the principal one is contemplation. The ancients said: ‘If one does not contemplate the mind, the Dharma has no source.’ Because the Buddha-Dharma all rests upon the pure mind; only turning back to contemplate within and shine inward can one draw forth the Buddha-nature, and then all the gates of samādhi, all the gates of dharani, all the gates of liberation, and all the gates of supernormal power appear at once. Therefore know that the mind is the source of the wondrous Dharma: if one does not contemplate the mind, how can it be drawn forth? Hence contemplation of the mind is the foremost wondrous practice of the Buddha-Dharma, which no other practice can match.
To contemplate and reflect constantly is for prajñā to perfume ignorance.

Once ignorance is broken, the Dharma-body manifests at once (clear the mind and see one’s nature). Directly leaping into the stage of the Tathagata, without passing through the asamkhya kalpas, one attains the Dharma-body.

[Contemplating the mind] means to observe one’s own mind. The mind is the lord of all dharmas, and no thing is ever outside the mind; therefore, to contemplate the mind is to contemplate everything. The Sutra of the Mind-Contemplation of the Great Vehicle says:
‘Among the three realms, the mind is the sovereign; one who can contemplate the mind gains ultimate liberation, and one who cannot forever remains in bondage.’
Again it says:
‘Beholding the marks, one arouses the mind and removes wrong views; one should dwell in the forest retreat and contemplate one’s own mind.’
[Lanruo] is aranya, rendered in Chinese as ‘a place of stillness.’
[Sengqi] is an abbreviation of ‘asamkhya kalpas.’

Moreover, to arouse the bodhi mind is to contemplate the mind of pure self-nature (see in detail the chapter ‘Arousing the Bodhi Mind’). The merit of arousing the bodhi mind is supremely excellent beyond compare; it cannot be described fully, for it pervades all the scriptures and is set forth widely in the Avatamsaka, the Yogacara, the Prajñāpāramitā, and the other treatises. For example: ‘One who arouses the bodhi mind is prophesied by all the Buddhas and receives the protection of all the Buddhas.’ At the first arousal of the mind, the Buddha gives the prophecy; this is clearly stated in all the scriptures, such as the Sutra of the Arousing of the Bodhi Mind, the Sutra of the Mind-Contemplation of the Great Vehicle, and the Sutra of Questions on the Meaning of the Wise; it is most fully set forth in the Avatamsaka Sutra. As for the protection of all the Buddhas, the Lankavatara Sutra says: ‘In all the lands of the ten directions, all the measureless Buddhas extend their hands of light and touch the crown of this person’s head.’ Thus all the Buddhas constantly protect such a practitioner. (See the section ‘The Merit of Arousing the Mind’.)

The characteristic of the ‘White Cloud Mind-Essentials’ is sharp, swift, sudden, and perfect. How great is the fortune of one who reads and practices it! One should advance in both understanding and practice together: to understand is to put into practice, and to practice is to understand. Doing the work of tuning and taming each day, with thoughts clarified, wisdom arises; not departing from self-nature, one is a field of merit. When one contemplates to the point that a single thought does not arise, one accords with prajñā. The Mahavairocana Sutra says: ‘What is bodhi? It is knowing one’s own mind as it really is.’ The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: ‘All Tathagatas, in the causal ground from which they originate, all rely upon the perfect illumination of the pure enlightened mark, forever cutting off ignorance, and only then accomplish the Buddha-Way.’

The Essentials of the Mind Transmission says: ‘Apart from all marks, sentient beings and Buddhas are no different; one who can be without mind is at the ultimate. If a student of the Way does not directly become without mind, though he cultivate through many kalpas he will never accomplish the Way, for he is bound by the works of the three vehicles and cannot gain liberation. Yet there are those who realize this mind quickly or slowly: some, upon hearing the Dharma, become without mind in a single thought; some reach the ten stages of faith, the ten abodes, the ten practices, and the ten dedications before becoming without mind; some reach the ten grounds before becoming without mind. Whether it takes long or short, it is only upon becoming without mind that one settles; there is nothing further to cultivate or realize. In truth there is nothing attained, and this is real and not false. To attain it in a single thought and to attain it upon the ten grounds are exactly equal in function, with no gradation of shallow or deep — it is merely that through the kalpas one has vainly undergone hardship.’

View, practice, and fruit are the three essential elements of the bodhi path. ‘View’ is understanding. First, understanding must be correct. How to realize the ‘view’ — this is ‘practice.’ Having realized the ‘view’ — this is ‘fruit.’ The White Cloud Dharma-gate is to be understood thus, and practiced thus.
Question: Will contemplating the mind cause one to stagnate on the path of practice?

The Editor answers: The essential point of the method of contemplating the mind is, toward thoughts, to ‘know them but not follow them.’ And the most crucial thing is the ‘knowing’ — to keep constantly aware of thoughts; as long as one maintains awareness of thoughts, one will naturally not follow them. Moreover, the power of awareness is constantly increasing; once it has grown strong to a certain degree, one can realize a thought the instant it arises and, realizing it, have it vanish at once. When the practice has fused into a single whole, one turns the light back and shines it inward: ‘Who, in the end, is this one who is aware?’ Practicing thus for a long time, when the melon is ripe the stem falls of itself, and one directly sees the original face. Therefore, grasping the essential point of contemplating the mind, one will not stagnate on the path. If one forgets the awareness, then unless one is in a state of scattering, one falls into dullness and torpor.
Question: Is there any contradiction between contemplating the mind and holding the name and reciting the Buddha?
Answer: Not only is there no contradiction, but the two aid each other. The Essential Anthology of the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, in the section on the
Showing the Method of Practice, says:

‘When one first begins to recite the Buddha, before having personally realized samādhi, who can be free of deluded thoughts? What is valuable is that the mind is constantly aware and illumining, not turning to follow delusions.’

This ‘mind constantly aware and illumining, not turning to follow delusions’ is precisely the contemplation of the mind. With the skill of contemplating the mind, to recite the Buddha is like a tiger that has grown horns; try it yourself and you will know. Moreover, to recite the Buddha and understand the first meaning, and attain the upper-grade rebirth — this is clearly recorded in the Contemplation Sutra.

Question: Then why did Master Yinguang say: ‘Do not use the method of contemplating the mind in recitation; you should use the method of gathering the mind in recitation.’ (From the Letter in Reply to the Layman Yang Weizhang)

Answer: Because the other party (the layman Yang Weizhang) was a beginner in the study, without sufficient foundation, yet used the method of contemplating the mind to recite the Buddha, which caused the fire of the heart to blaze upward. So in this letter, Master Yinguang was addressing the other party’s specific situation, prescribing medicine according to the illness, and not negating the method of contemplating the mind to recite the Buddha. Master Yinguang wrote: “
You, an ordinary being of extremely heavy karmic power,
vainly use
the method of contemplating the mind,
and so have brought this upon yourself
(that is, the ‘fire of the heart blazing upward’ mentioned in the other party’s letter)
.” And he continued to write: “The method of contemplating the mind is the method of contemplation used by the doctrinal schools; for a person who recites the Buddha,
it is not quite suited to their capacity

.” Here, ‘for a person who recites the Buddha, it is not quite suited to their capacity’ is a tactful way of saying that your faculties do not measure up to contemplating the mind while reciting the Buddha, and so the fire of the heart blazed upward. Therefore
Master Yinguang told him:
“Do not use the method of contemplating the mind in recitation; you should use the method of gathering the mind in recitation.”

Contemplating the mind while reciting the Buddha is most wondrous, yet it is not suited to those without sufficient foundation. Because beginner students lack a sufficient foundation, if they contemplate the mind while reciting the Buddha, they will often experience dizziness, headaches, the fire of the heart blazing upward, and such symptoms. Therefore, the book Aware Recitation of the Buddha, when it speaks of ‘being aware of the present thought (contemplating the mind while reciting the Buddha),’ has already laid a solid foundation through the preliminary chapter of training (being aware of movement, being aware of sensation, being aware of breathing, being aware of the present moment, being aware of the mind-thoughts) and through ‘being aware of the Buddha-name.’ In the Record of Groping for the Image of the Buddha-Recitation Samādhi, Master Yinguang instructs:
“As for the method,
one must

at the time of reciting, with each recitation turn back and contemplate, concentrating on a single realm, not allowing the mind to race outward, thought after thought watching over the source of the mind, mind after mind in accord with the Buddha-body.”
Is this not contemplating the mind while reciting the Buddha? Therefore, for a person who recites the Buddha to adopt the method of contemplating the mind, one must first have a certain foundation.

Contemplating the mind while reciting the Buddha is the very essence of holding the name and reciting the Buddha. Since ancient times, many ancestral masters and great worthies have attained single-minded and undisturbed concentration through contemplating the mind while reciting the Buddha.
As for the supreme importance of contemplating the mind, Master Yinguang, describing how Śākyamuni Buddha attained the Way, wrote: ‘At the age of nine-

teen, at midnight on the eighth day of the second month, he rode the horse Kanthaka, leapt over the city walls and departed, went straight into the deep mountains, and cultivated the transcendent Way. Again, wishing to show that those of the externalist paths were all not the right Dharma, he wandered for another five years, visiting all the ascetic sages. Later he
sat alone contemplating the mind,
eating but one

sesame and one grain of wheat a day, practicing austerities for six years; and at dawn on the eighth day of the twelfth month, when the morning star arose, he looked up and was suddenly, greatly enlightened. He exclaimed: ‘How wondrous, how wondrous! All sentient beings are endowed with the wisdom and virtue-marks of the Tathagata. Only because of deluded thoughts and clinging can they not realize it. If they were free of deluded thoughts, then all-knowledge, natural knowledge, and unobstructed knowledge would appear at once.’
(A Lecture at the Chaoyang Buddhist Society
No. 1)
Question: What is the relationship between contemplating the mind and practicing the Pure Land?

Answer: For the one who contemplates the mind, the mind is the Pure Land; to contemplate it is precisely faith, vow, and practice, and one is reborn in the Pure Land. The mind is the Tathagata-nature, the Buddha-nature, which is itself the land; therefore, arousing the bodhi mind is the supreme and true Buddha-recitation Dharma-gate. To arouse the bodhi mind is to be mindful of the Dharma-body Buddha. To be mindful of the Dharma-body Buddha is to recite the Buddha by means of reality, the so-called one-vehicle Buddha-recitation, which is the most supreme of the Pure Land school.

[Arousing the bodhi mind] The full name is to arouse the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, abbreviated as arousing the mind. The bodhi mind is the mind of pure self-nature. This mind of pure self-nature is equal in sentient beings and Buddhas, possessed by all, neither increasing nor decreasing. ‘Arouse’ means to initiate, to develop. To arouse the bodhi mind is to initiate and develop the mind of pure self-nature. The first stirring is merely the initiating; seeing one’s nature is called the developing. Yet without contemplation one cannot initiate it, and without contemplation one cannot develop it. Therefore, to arouse the bodhi mind is to contemplate this mind of pure self-nature. The Mahavairocana Sutra says: ‘What is bodhi? It is knowing one’s own mind as it really is.’ [Reciting the Buddha by means of reality]
This is to recite the Buddha by means of the dharmas that are ultimately empty and without any existence.

In the Buddha-Treasury Sutra, the Buddha says: ‘Sariputra, what is called being mindful of the Buddha? To see that there is nothing that exists — this is called being mindful of the Buddha. Sariputra, the Buddhas are measureless, inconceivable, incalculable; for this reason, to see that nothing exists is called being mindful of the Buddha. The reality is without discrimination; the Buddhas are without discrimination. Therefore it is said: to be mindful without discrimination is to be mindful of the Buddha. Again, to see the reality of all dharmas is called seeing the Buddha. What is called the reality of all dharmas? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty, and nothing exists.
Thus by the dharmas that are ultimately empty and that do not exist, one is mindful of the Buddha.

Again, in such dharmas, even a small thought cannot be obtained — this is called being mindful of the Buddha. Sariputra, this Dharma of mindfulness of the Buddha cuts off the path of speech, transcends all thoughts, and cannot be grasped by thought — this is called being mindful of the Buddha. Sariputra, all thoughts have the mark of still extinction. To accord with this Dharma is called practicing the mindfulness of the Buddha. One cannot be mindful of the Buddha by form; why? To be mindful of form is to grasp at a mark, and to relish the flavor is to be consciousness. Having no form, no color, no condition, no nature — this is called being mindful of the Buddha. Therefore know: without discrimination, without grasping, without rejecting — this is truly being mindful of the Buddha.’ ‘Mindfulness of the Buddha is called the destruction of all the considerations of good and evil; without considerations, without reflection, still and without thought — this is called being mindful of the Buddha. Why? One should not recall the Buddhas by considerations and reflections; without considerations and without reflection is called pure mindfulness of the Buddha. In this mindfulness there is not even the subtle mind, thought, and karmic activity — how much the less the actions of body and speech!’ ‘All these dharmas are empty, having no real nature; one cannot be mindful of a single mark, that which is spoken of as markless — this is called true mindfulness of the Buddha. That is, no birth, no extinction, no mark, no effort.’ [Considerations and reflections (jueguan)] In the newer translations this is ‘vitarka-vicara’ (initial and sustained application), and in the older translations it is ‘jueguan.’ Coarse thought is called ‘jue’ (initial) and fine thought is called ‘guan’ (sustained); both can disturb the concentrated mind. [Being mindful of the Dharma-body Buddha is precisely reciting the Buddha by means of reality, the so-called one-vehicle Buddha-recitation, which is the most supreme of the Pure Land school] Master Lianchi, in his Commentary on the Amitābha Sutra, says: ‘Know that the Pure Land is mind-only; there is no external realm beyond it.’ ‘In accord with principle, self-nature returns to the original body — this is the meaning of vowing to be born in that land.’

blocks.text: Chapter One. The Outline of Studying Buddhism

inline.s: The outline of studying Buddhism: First, for what purpose? To clarify the mind and see the nature. Second, on what principle? On the principle of the two emptinesses. Third, what practice? To cultivate the practice of prajñā. Fourth, to what dharma to awaken? To awaken to the dharmas that arise through conditions.

blocks.text: 1. For What Purpose: To Clarify the Mind and See the Nature

inline.s: In recent times people’s minds are much given to the Buddha-Dharma: some keep a family shrine to the Buddha, some make pilgrimages to the mountains and burn incense, some diligently practice giving, some cultivate offerings, some receive the three refuges, some observe the five precepts, some recite the scriptures and the Buddha-name, some hold mantras and practice the Dharma, some deeply study the doctrinal principles, and some exclusively practice Chan contemplation. Though their ways differ in many respects, in believing the Buddha they are one.

I now wish to ask a question: You, gentlemen, practice thus diligently — for what purpose, in the end? You weary your bodies and exhaust your spirits, spending your energy and days without complaint; what is your aim? They will say: ‘We have heard that the Buddha-Dharma is extraordinary, and so we like it; it has become the fashion in the world, and we follow the crowd.’ I say: This is not an answer to my question.

Again they say: ‘We wish to escape suffering.’ The poor wish to gain wealth; the sick wish to pray for recovery; those in distress hope for success; the fallen long for deliverance. I say: These words are close, but still not the true answer.

Again they say: ‘We wish to remove karmic hindrances. The suffering of this life is all brought about by the evil karma of former lives. Now we will abandon evil and cultivate good, hoping that the karmic hindrances may be removed and we avoid the retribution of suffering.’ I say: These words seem right, but they are still not complete.

Again they say: ‘We wish to cut off afflictions. Human beings create karma because of afflictions. Now we will extinguish the afflictions, so that the bitter fruit no longer arises.’ I say: These words seem right, but they are still not complete.

They startle and say: ‘To cut off afflictions, to remove karmic hindrances, to leave suffering and attain bliss — this is the orthodox aim of the Buddha-Dharma; how is it still not complete? Giving, observing precepts, worship and offerings, reciting the scriptures and the Buddha-name, holding mantras and practicing contemplation — these are the orthodox practices of the Buddha-Dharma; how are they still not complete? With these we will save ourselves and save others; how could there still be any regret?’

I say: Be a little calm and do not be impatient; I will speak it for you. Generally, in discussing principles one must trace them to their root; in doing things one must ask their reason. What you have spoken of does have meaning within the Buddha-Dharma, but it is the branches and leaves, the minor details. If one practices in this direction, though one’s resolve be good, one wastes one’s energy. The scripture says: ‘Without knowing the real Dharma, it is not called giving. Without knowing the real Dharma, it is not called offering.’ I now take this as an example and add a few more words: Without knowing the real Dharma, it is not called observing the precepts. Without knowing the real Dharma, it is not called worship. Without knowing the real Dharma, it is not called reciting the scriptures. Without knowing the real Dharma, it is not called being mindful of the Buddha. Without knowing the real Dharma, it is not called holding mantras. Without knowing the real Dharma, it is not called practicing contemplation. You have not spoken of the real place, and so I do not approve. The scripture says: ‘If the causal ground is not true, the fruit is twisted and crooked.’ Again it says: ‘If one wishes to cultivate the great practice, one must know the dharma-practice of the causal ground.’ People of the world, dull and confused, do not seek this, and so they labor in vain to no benefit. Now for you all I will make clear the real, and you will gain twice the result with half the effort.

The real Dharma is our own mind. Because this mind has the nature of awareness, it is called the Buddha-nature. Because it is the root of all dharmas, it is called the Dharma-body. Because it never changes, it is called true thusness. Because its nature is not false, it is called reality. Because it knows everything, it is called bodhi. (Bodhi is right wisdom, and therefore it knows everything.) Because it is still and unmoving, it is called nirvāṇa. The nature of all dharmas is called the Dharma-nature. All these various names are but different names for our true mind. All people originally possess it, and each is perfectly complete in it; it is close within the mind, needing no distant search. To become a Buddha or a patriarch is this one mind, which the Chan school calls ‘clarifying the mind and seeing the nature.’ The mind is the nature (mind and nature are one; this comes from the Avatamsaka Sutra)

; the so-called real Dharma is this mind. We all have this mind, yet do not know it ourselves, and suffer through long kalpas — is this not pitiable? Studying Buddhism is nothing other than clarifying the mind and seeing the nature. If one clarifies the mind and sees the nature, then afflictions are cut off by themselves without waiting to be cut, karmic hindrances are removed by themselves without waiting to be removed, all sufferings are extinguished by themselves without waiting to be extinguished, the three jewels are offered to without need of speaking of offering — one has already offered to the three jewels of one’s own mind; one gives without giving a single coin and yet the giving surpasses the seven jewels; one holds no mantra and yet spontaneously attains the seal and the mantric power; one recites no scripture and yet the twelve divisions of the scriptures are all penetrated. If one sets to work from the root, the fruit is great and the merit lofty thus; you gentlemen, how can you not take it up?

The ancients said: Sentient beings exist through karma; karma exists through delusion; delusion exists through consciousness; consciousness exists through the mind; and the mind is the final, ultimate place. If one does not penetrate this one key point, the consciousness persists, afflictions are cut off only to arise again, karmic hindrances are dispelled only to spring up again, and the bitter fruit is never removed. It is like felling a tree: if you cut off only its branches and leaves, it grows again the next year — when will there be an end? If you cut off its root and stalk, it will never sprout again. Therefore, when the Buddha said that without knowing the real Dharma it is not called giving or offering, the intent was to spur the people of the world to know that the real place lies in our own mind. (This meaning comes from the Avatamsaka Sutra and the Prajñāpāramitā sutras; the passages are very extensive and one may study them.) Otherwise, one cultivates the cause without the fruit. Why? Because the fruit lies in the real place. (Note: one must apply effort in the real place before the fruit can come about.) Otherwise (note: if not so), the scripture says the mind is the source of evil and the body is the gathering place of offenses. (Note: this mind is the consciousness-mind, distinct from the true mind above.) If one has not understood where the real place is, how can one cut off afflictions, remove karmic hindrances, and escape the sea of suffering? As for what purpose one studies — it is to seek to clarify the mind and see the nature.

blocks.text: 2. On What Principle: On the Principle of the Two Emptinesses

inline.s: We already know that the Buddha-nature is our own true mind. But what, in the end, is the substance and mark of the true mind? It is said: the true mind has no nature of its own; its substance is empty, and so it is called true emptiness; its mark is like empty space. Empty space has two meanings: first, like empty space, it does not waver; second, like empty space, it fills all lands. The master Yongming says: ‘The true mind’s own substance cannot be expressed in words; it is clear as the boundless empty space, bright as the round and luminous pure mirror, beyond both praise and blame, hard to fathom in principle.’ People of the world do not know that the true mind is vast and round and luminous, and so they turn in samsara through long kalpas, suffering without end. Now, to understand one’s own true mind: first, do not take this body, a temporary union of the four great elements, as real; second, do not take the mind that is the shadow of the conditions of the six sense-objects, nor the mountains, rivers, and great earth, as real. In the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, the Buddha says: ‘All sentient beings, since the beginningless past, have had all manner of inverted views, like a confused person who shifts his directions in the four quarters; they falsely take the four great elements as the mark of their own body, and the shadows of the conditions of the six sense-objects as the mark of their own mind. It is like one whose eyes are diseased, seeing flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good man! There are in truth no flowers in the sky; the sick one grasps them falsely, and because of this false grasping, not only does he delude himself about the nature of this empty space, but he also loses the true place where the real flowers are born. Because of this false existence, they turn in the round of birth and death — this is called ignorance.’

[The four great elements] are the great earth element, the great water element, the great fire element, and the great wind element. Earth has the nature of hardness, water of wetness, fire of warmth, and wind of motion. All the material forms of the world possess these four natures of solidity, wetness, warmth, and motion, and so are called ‘great.’ [The shadow of the conditions of the six sense-objects] means the various thoughts produced when the six sense-organs condition upon the six sense-objects; and because these thoughts are all illusory and unreal, they are called the shadow of the conditions of the six sense-objects — the illusion of the conditions of the six sense-objects.

In entering the gateway of the Buddha-Dharma there are two essential principles: first, that sentient beings are empty; second, that all dharmas are empty. If sentient beings are not empty, this is called the attachment to a self; if all dharmas are not empty, this is called the attachment to dharmas.

What is the attachment to a self? It is the belief that I can have sovereignty and control. This sovereignty is but consciousness; there is no real self. If I could truly control, who would be willing to enter the hells or willingly become an animal or a hungry ghost? Therefore know that there is no self in the body; it is entirely the discriminations and attachments of consciousness. Consciousness is the very root of birth and death, and should be cut off urgently, not tolerated. Therefore the Mahayana bodhisattva first cultivates the contemplation of non-self, to realize the emptiness of the person.

What is the attachment to dharmas? Dharmas — the inner five sense-organs (the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body) and the outer five sense-objects (form, sound, smell, taste, and touch), all formed by the four great elements (earth, water, fire, wind) — are called material dharmas; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are called mental dharmas. The nature of both the material and the mental dharmas is empty. Sentient beings, not knowing this, take them as really existing, give rise to delusion and create karma, and so birth and death never cease. Therefore the Buddha-Dharma teaches people to cultivate the emptiness of dharmas. The emptiness of dharmas is to empty the dharmas of the six sense-organs, the six sense-objects, and the six consciousnesses. To realize that all dharmas have no self-nature, and that their substance is originally empty, is called realizing the emptiness of dharmas.

People of the world are all veiled by the attachment to a self and the attachment to dharmas, and so they do not know their own true mind. In the Mahayana Dharma-gate, if one wishes to awaken to the mind, one must first believe and enter the principle of the emptiness of the person and the emptiness of dharmas. The meaning of the Dharma spoken in the thousand scriptures and ten thousand treatises is nothing other than these two emptinesses. If one can believe and enter, then awakening to the mind has a certain time, and one becomes a Buddha in an instant. If one does not believe in these two emptinesses but merely seeks blessings and rewards, one is a newcomer beyond the gate and can never gain the benefit of the Buddha-Dharma.

How do we know that there is no self? If I could truly control, then at the moment of death I could take my wife and property along with me; why can I not? If there were a blissful paradise in heaven, all who do evil could be reborn there; why can they not? Since I can do neither, where is my sovereignty? Moreover, in a single person’s body the six sense-organs all operate together; could there be six selves? If one takes the six sense-organs as the self, the organs of the dead person still remain — why can they no longer act? Therefore know that there is no self. The scripture says: ‘All sentient beings exist because of attachment to a self; if one departs from this attachment, then there is no place of birth.’

How do we know that dharmas do not exist? The sense-organs, the body, and the world of objects, within the shared karma and common nature of the human realm, are seen as real; but in the other five destinies, each sees things differently. Thus we can see that in the six destinies (gods, humans, asuras, animals, hungry ghosts, and hells) each transforms its own realm of the six sense-objects, all produced by karmic consciousness — how could there be any fixed dharma? Therefore know that all the activities and undertakings of human life are impelled by the wind of karma and produced by the consciousness-mind, like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow — empty and unreal. The scripture says: ‘Not knowing that all dharmas are empty, they forever undergo the suffering of birth and death.’ If one can awaken and enter into the two emptinesses, then one realizes the patience of non-production of dharmas and attains anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Thus it is said: in studying the Dharma, one studies only the principle of the two emptinesses.

[Shared karma] means the common karmic cause. [Common nature] refers to the common characteristics of sentient beings. [The patience of non-production of dharmas] is abbreviated as the patience of non-production: having realized that all dharmas are but illusions, originally unborn and so also unceasing (neither arising nor ceasing), one abides in this principle without wavering. ‘Patience’ means abiding, that is, the mind resting in the principle without being moved. The Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom

Volume Fifty says: ‘As for the patience of non-production of dharmas: within the real mark of the dharmas that neither arise nor cease, believing, receiving, penetrating, without obstruction and without retreat — this is called the patience of non-production.’

blocks.text: 3. What Practice: To Cultivate the Practice of Prajñā

inline.s: The essentials of the Buddha-Dharma do not go beyond doctrine, practice, and fruit. The doctrine is the aggregates, the sense-fields, the elements, the truths, and dependent origination, as set forth in the foregoing on the one mind and the two emptinesses. The fruit is the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique dharmas, and so forth. One who knows the doctrine and wishes to attain the fruit cannot accomplish it without putting forth practice; now we should discuss practice.

[The aggregates, the sense-fields, and the elements] In the older translations these are called the skandhas, the entrances, and the realms (yin, ru, jie). ‘Aggregates’ (skandhas) are the five aggregates, also called the five heaps: form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness — the body and mind of sentient beings. ‘Sense-fields’ (ayatanas) are the twelve sense-fields, also called the twelve entrances: the places where the six sense-organs meet the six sense-objects. ‘Elements’ (dhatus) are the eighteen elements, namely the six sense-organs meeting the six sense-objects and producing the six consciousnesses; three sixes together making eighteen, called the eighteen elements. These five aggregates, twelve sense-fields, and eighteen elements are commonly called the ‘three sets.’ [The truths (shidi)] are the principles that are real and not false. The principle of the false and vain matters of the world is called ‘the conventional truth’; the principle of the tranquility of nirvāṇa is called ‘the ultimate truth.’ [Dependent origination] means that all dharmas arise from the coming together of conditions. When conditions meet, they arise; when conditions scatter, they cease; though there seems to be existence, the illusory marks are not real; what exists is not truly existent, for their very substance is empty.

[The eighteen unique dharmas] The eighteen unique dharmas are limited to the eighteen kinds of meritorious dharmas possessed only by the Buddha; because they are limited to the Buddha and are not shared with the three vehicles, they are called the ‘unique dharmas.’ First, no lapse of the body: since the Buddha, from immeasurable kalpas past, has always used precepts, concentration, and wisdom, and compassion and kindness, to cultivate his body, and because his merit is complete and all afflictions are exhausted, this is called ‘no lapse of the body.’ Second, no lapse of speech: the Buddha is endowed with immeasurable wisdom and eloquence, and whatever issues from the Buddha’s golden mouth is word after word, phrase after phrase, in accord with true principle — this is called ‘no lapse of speech.’ Third, no lapse of mindfulness: the Buddha possesses the supreme, profound and wondrous meditative concentration, the mind not scattered, ever in samādhi, dwelling nowhere with regard to all dharmas — this is called ‘no lapse of mindfulness.’ Fourth, no differing thoughts: the Buddha delivers sentient beings equally, with a mind without discrimination — this is called ‘no differing thoughts.’ Fifth, no unsettled mind: the Buddha, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, is never apart from the profound samādhi — this is called ‘no unsettled mind.’ Sixth, no knowing-and-then-abandoning: the Buddha, in preaching the Dharma and delivering beings, knows nothing he does not speak of, and speaks nothing he does not exhaust; there is no dharma he knows and then abandons — this is called ‘no knowing-and-then-abandoning.’ Seventh, desire never diminishes: the Buddha, out of pity for sentient beings, desires to deliver them, and his mind knows no satiety — this is called ‘desire never diminishing.’ Eighth, diligence never diminishes: the Buddha takes the saving of sentient beings as his own task, and so constantly delivers all beings without rest — this is called ‘diligence never diminishing.’ Ninth, mindfulness never diminishes: toward the Dharma of the Buddhas of the three times and all wisdom, he is correspondingly complete, without regression — this is called ‘mindfulness never diminishing.’ Tenth, wisdom never diminishes: the Buddha possesses all wisdom, measureless, boundless, inexhaustible — this is called ‘wisdom never diminishing.’ Eleventh, liberation never diminishes: the Buddha is far from all attachments and possesses two kinds of liberation — the first is conditioned liberation (the liberation that corresponds to undefiled wisdom) and the second is unconditioned liberation (when all afflictions are entirely exhausted without remainder) — this is called ‘liberation never diminishing.’ Twelfth, the knowledge-and-vision of liberation never diminishes: within all liberations the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are clear, and his discrimination of them is unobstructed — this is called ‘the knowledge-and-vision of liberation never diminishing.’ Thirteenth, all bodily actions follow wisdom: whatever the Buddha’s body does is guided by wisdom, so all is filled with wisdom — this is called ‘all bodily actions following wisdom.’ Fourteenth, all verbal actions follow wisdom: whatever the Buddha speaks is guided by wisdom, so all is filled with wisdom — this is called ‘all verbal actions following wisdom.’ Fifteenth, all mental actions follow wisdom: whatever the Buddha’s mind thinks is preceded by wisdom, so all is filled with wisdom — this is called ‘all mental actions following wisdom.’ Sixteenth, wisdom knows the past without obstruction: the Buddha, by wisdom, illuminates all the dharmas of the past and knows them all entirely without obstruction — this is called ‘wisdom knowing the past without obstruction.’ Seventeenth, wisdom knows the future without obstruction: the Buddha, by wisdom, illuminates all of the future and knows it entirely without obstruction — this is called ‘wisdom knowing the future without obstruction.’ Eighteenth, wisdom knows the present without obstruction: the Buddha, by wisdom, illuminates all of the present and knows it entirely without obstruction — this is called ‘wisdom knowing the present without obstruction.’
Conduct has countless aspects, but the Six Perfections are their sum. The sutras speak freely, sometimes teaching one practice:
the arousing of bodhicitta

. Or they teach two practices, called wisdom and expedient means. Or three practices: precepts, concentration, and wisdom. Or four practices, called the four abodes: first wisdom, second precepts, third giving, fourth concentration. Or five practices: giving, keeping the precepts, patience, diligence, and calm-abiding with insight. Or six practices, called the Six Perfections. The Six Perfections are giving, keeping the precepts, patience, diligence, meditation, and prajñā. Though the gates of practice are many, the Six Perfections embrace them all without exception.

The meaning of these Six Perfections has countless gates. Here I briefly speak of three: first, the characteristics of the Six Perfections; second, what the Six Perfections counteract; third, how the Six Perfections lead into principle.

What are their characteristics? All practices flow from bodhicitta; united, they are bodhicitta; divided, they are the Six Perfections. A mind without attachment is giving; a mind without regard to keeping or breaking is keeping the precepts; not offending a single being is patience; thought after thought unbroken is diligence; a mind that does not flow is meditation; knowing all dharmas to be empty is prajñā.

What do they counteract? They counteract the six realms, so as to escape the cycle of the three worlds. The perfection of giving is established to counteract the realm of hungry ghosts; the perfection of precepts to counteract the hell realm; the perfection of patience to counteract the animal realm; the perfection of diligence to counteract the asura realm; the perfection of meditation to counteract humans and the six desire heavens; the perfection of prajñā to counteract the heavens of form and formlessness.

How do they lead into principle? By following the Dharma-nature. The substance of the Dharma-nature is free of miserly greed, so the perfection of giving is established. The Dharma-nature is free of the five desires, so the perfection of precepts is established. The Dharma-nature is free of anger and vexation, so the perfection of patience is established. The Dharma-nature is free of indolence, so the perfection of diligence is established. The Dharma-nature is ever still, so the perfection of meditation is established. The Dharma-nature is free of ignorance, so the perfection of prajñā is established.

The Dharma of these Six Perfections takes prajñā as its master. The sutra says: “The five perfections are like the blind, and prajñā is like the eye.” Giving without prajñā only gains the splendor of one lifetime, and later must repay the remaining karmic debt. Keeping precepts without prajñā, one is temporarily reborn in the upper desire realm and yet falls again into the mud (hell). Patience without prajñā yields an upright and handsome form, but does not realize the patient endurance of cessation. Diligence without prajñā wastes effort in the work of arising and ceasing, and does not reach the sea of true constancy. Meditation without prajñā merely practices the meditations of the form realm and does not enter the vajra-samādhi. All good without prajñā becomes only a conditioned cause, and does not accord with the unconditioned fruit.

According to the Yogacara, the bodhisattva's practice has four kinds: first, the practice of the Six Perfections; second, the practice of the factors of the path; third, the practice of the four means of gathering; fourth, the practice of spiritual powers. In sum, all take prajñā as master. Though the Buddha-Dharma is divided into the Great Vehicle, the Lesser Vehicle, the One Vehicle, and the Three Vehicles, the Four Noble Truths already embrace them all. The cause and effect of the world are the two truths of suffering and its accumulation; the cause and effect of transcendence are the two truths of cessation and the path. Cessation is the Buddha-fruit, and the path is the bodhisattva's practice. Prajñā is the substance of the path-truth, and therefore prajñā is the essential practice.

[The practice of the factors of the path] is the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right exertions, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path — altogether thirty-seven items, the important provisions for cultivating the Way. [The four means of gathering] are the means of gathering through giving, through kind speech, through beneficial conduct, and through shared activities. [The Four Noble Truths] are the four noble truths: the truth of suffering, the truth of its accumulation, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path. First, the truth of suffering explains the truth that life is full of suffering. Suffering has the characteristic of oppression. Life has the three sufferings, the eight sufferings, and measureless sufferings; suffering is the true reality of life. Second, “accumulation” means attracting and creating; it is the truth that explains how the suffering of life arises. The suffering of life comes from craving and attachment, which create karma, and then one experiences suffering and the cycle of rebirth. Third, the truth of cessation explains the truth of extinguishing all suffering. When all the accumulation (craving) of suffering is forever cut off without remainder, without defilement and without attachment, one no longer experiences suffering and rebirth — this is the truth of cessation. Fourth, the truth of the path explains how to forever cut off the accumulation (craving) of suffering, that is, the way of extinguishing suffering — the eightfold noble path. Among the four noble truths, accumulation is the cause and suffering is the fruit; the path is the cause and cessation is the fruit. [The practice of prajñā] The Diamond Sutra says: “All forms are false and unreal.” It also says: “Do not grasp at marks, and be unmoved in thusness.” It also says: “Being free of all marks, that is called all Buddhas.” The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “To know illusion is to be free of it, without needing expedient means; to be free of illusion is enlightenment, without any gradualism.”

blocks.text: 4. What Is Awakened: Awakening to Dependent Origination

inline.s: Whether studying the teachings or meditating in Chan, all seek great and thorough enlightenment. The state of thorough awakening is the patient acceptance that dharmas are unarisen. The student single-mindedly seeks awakening — what dharma is it, in the end, that is awakened? I reply: awakening to dharmas that arise from conditions. What are dharmas arising from conditions? They are dharmas produced by causes and conditions. All dharmas arise when conditions gather and cease when conditions disperse; not existing yet seeming to exist, their illusory forms are unreal; what exists is not existing, and in substance they are emptiness.
[The true characteristic of dharmas] The true state of all dharmas. The Buddha Treasury Sutra

Chapter on Reciting the Buddha's Name, the Buddha says: “What is called the true characteristic of dharmas? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty, without anything existing.” The Diamond Sutra says: “All forms are false and unreal.”

The reply: since the marks of dependent origination are already false and unreal, how can awakening to marks be the summit of achievement? The reply: if one's seeing of the nature is not true, one cannot understand the marks; if one's seeing of the nature is true, then one can clearly see that the vast array of all phenomena are all produced by causes and conditions upon one's own nature, which is called wondrous existence. Therefore the essential point of studying the Dharma is to understand that dependent origination is empty of self-nature. If one sees the nature of conditions, one is free from the bonds of conditions. (The nature of conditions means the nature of dependent origination, which is the Buddha-nature. The twelve links of dependent origination are the marks of the cycle of rebirth; the Buddha-nature is the nature of that cycle, and seeing the Buddha-nature instantly cuts off the cycle. The bonds of conditions are the bonds of the cycle of the twelve links of dependent origination.) Therefore, realizing the nature is to understand dependent origination, and to understand dependent origination is to realize the true nature — these are one matter.

Students of the Great Vehicle are taught to contemplate dependent origination from the very outset, in order to prepare the proper cause for future awakening. What does this mean? The Buddha-Dharma takes emptiness as its master, and its teaching of emptiness takes causes and conditions as its tenet; causes and conditions are the meaning of dependent origination (“dependent arising” means dependent origination). Ordinary people do not believe it, followers of non-Buddhist paths do not know it, and the Lesser Vehicle's provisional teachings, though they know of it, do not know it thoroughly; only the great bodhisattvas who study the Buddha Vehicle must focus on it the most. Why? Because when the Buddha speaks of the mind-ground, he speaks of the two emptinesses. Without the meaning of dependent origination, the two emptinesses cannot be established.

The discriminating mind of people creates good and evil karma, and so there is rising and sinking, but the true mind is originally unmoving. The discriminating mind is a burden, and one suffers the cycle of rebirth in vain. One should know that delusion, karma, and suffering are all produced by causes and conditions; dependent origination is empty of self-nature, and so it is called the emptiness of persons. The sense-faculties and sense-objects are likewise produced by causes and conditions; faculties and objects have no self-nature, all is empty, and so it is called the emptiness of dharmas. Without the meaning of dependent origination, persons and dharmas would both be real, and the true mind would not manifest. With the meaning of dependent origination, persons and dharmas are both empty, the true mind manifests, and one attains the fundamental dharma-body, which is the Buddha-fruit. The dharma-body is like empty space, so it is called true emptiness. Within the body of true emptiness, all the lands as numerous as dust in the ten directions are all manifest. Hence the Nirvāṇa Sutra says: “The Buddha-nature is the emptiness of the ultimate truth; the emptiness of the ultimate truth is itself wisdom.” And the Sandhinirmocana Sutra says: “If one does not understand the dharmas without marks, the defiled dharmas with marks cannot be cut off; and because the defiled dharmas with marks are not cut off, one destroys the realization of the subtle pure dharmas with marks.” If one can awaken to dependent origination, one realizes the patient acceptance that dharmas are unarisen, which is great and thorough enlightenment. Students of the Great Vehicle should practice thus — strive on, strive on!

[Emptiness] In describing the existence of things, besides “existence” and “nonexistence,” there is another situation, that of illusory appearance — like things in a dream, having form but no real substance, not truly existing — and the concept “emptiness” is used to describe it. The Vimalakirti Sutra

Chapter on the Disciples, the third, says: “All dharmas are ultimately without anything existing; this is the meaning of emptiness.” In this sentence, “all dharmas” speaks of the existence of marks, and “ultimately without anything existing” speaks of real nonexistence; this situation of having marks yet being really nonexistent (illusion) is called emptiness.

blocks.text: 1. What Is Meant by Arousing the Mind

inline.s: To arouse bodhicitta, whose full form is “to arouse the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi,” is also called simply “arousing the mind.” Bodhicitta is the pure mind of self-nature. This pure mind of self-nature is equal in sentient beings and Buddhas, possessed by everyone, neither increasing nor decreasing. “Arousing” means to initiate and to develop. To arouse bodhicitta is to initiate and develop this pure mind of self-nature. The initial mind is only the initiating; seeing the nature is called the developing. Yet without contemplation one cannot initiate it, and without contemplation one cannot develop it. Therefore, to arouse bodhicitta is to contemplate this pure mind of self-nature. The Mahavairocana Sutra says: “What is bodhi? It is to know one's own mind as it truly is.”
[Bodhi] is translated into Chinese as “awakening.”
Question: What is meant by the pure mind of self-nature?

Answer: The pure mind of self-nature is our true mind. Because this mind has the nature of awakening, it is called the Buddha-nature. Because it is the root of all dharmas, it is called the dharma-body. Because it never changes, it is called thusness. Because its nature is not false, it is called the true characteristic. Because it knows all things, it is called bodhi. Because it is still and unmoving, it is called nirvāṇa. Because it is the nature of all dharmas, it is called the Dharma-nature. All these various names are different names for our true mind. Everyone originally possesses it, everyone is fully endowed with it; it is near, within the mind, and there is no need to seek it far away. To become a Buddha or a patriarch is this one mind; false thoughts rely on it to form the three worlds, and it is the basis of the world's establishment and the source of life's dependent origination. Sentient beings, not knowing this, from time without beginning have never contemplated it, and in vain create the cycle of rebirth, sinking in birth and death.
Question: Why contemplate the pure mind of self-nature?

Answer: As said above, to arouse bodhicitta is to initiate and develop the pure mind of self-nature. Yet without contemplation one cannot initiate it, and without contemplation one cannot develop it. Therefore, to arouse bodhicitta is to contemplate this pure mind of self-nature. The Buddha-Dharma teaches people to turn back and contemplate within, which is to enter the Buddha-nature, to enter the dharma-body, to enter thusness, to enter the true characteristic, to enter nirvāṇa, to enter the Dharma-nature, and to enter the Dharma-realm. It instantly cuts off the cycle of rebirth and quickly escapes birth and death. Therefore the root of the Buddha-Dharma is the mind, and the root of the practice is contemplation. The Sutra of the Mind-Ground of the Great Vehicle says: “Within the three worlds, the mind is master; one who can contemplate the mind is ultimately liberated, and one who cannot is forever in bondage.” The Nirvāṇa Sutra says: “To be able to contemplate the nature of the mind is called the highest concentration.”
Question: To arouse bodhicitta is to arouse the mind of compassion and vows; why is it said to be contemplating the pure mind of self-nature?

Answer: Arousing bodhicitta has two kinds: first, the mundane; and second, the ultimate. To arouse the mind of compassion and vows is a conditioned dharma, called the mundane. To contemplate the pure mind of self-nature is an unconditioned dharma, called the ultimate. The mundane cannot encompass the ultimate, but the ultimate can encompass the mundane.
Question: Great compassion and great vows are essential practices of the Buddha-Dharma; why are they set aside here?

I reply: It is not that they are set aside. For one who has not seen the nature, compassion and vows are very narrow; only upon seeing the nature can they become vast; therefore seeing the nature is most urgent. What is called compassion and vows is but seeking the Buddha-way above and transforming sentient beings below. Now, to seek to see the nature is originally in order to become a Buddha and benefit sentient beings, which is itself great compassion and great vows — why need one arouse them again?
Question: Does this kind of arousing the mind have other names?

Answer: Yes. When contemplating, not dwelling on external objects, it is called the practice of no-thought. When the one mind is unmoving, it is called the practice of not-moving. When the mind has no object of support, it is called the practice of no-marks. When the mind does not abide in objects, it is called the practice of no-abiding. When one contemplates with prajñā (not giving rise to a discriminating mind while contemplating), it is called the practice of prajñā. In short, to constantly cultivate this practice is to be free of discrimination, free of subject and object, which is to be free of mind, thought, and consciousness; once mind, thought, and consciousness are free, the true mind naturally manifests. Such is the function of arousing the mind — thus, and thus.

[Subject and object] The active dharma is called “subject,” and the passive dharma is called “object.” For example, in the six faculties confronting the six objects, the six faculties are the active perceiving and the six objects are the perceived. Here “subject and object” refers to the contemplator and the contemplated. [Mind, thought, and consciousness] “Mind” refers to the eighth consciousness (alaya-vijnana), “thought” refers to the seventh consciousness (manas), and “consciousness” refers to the remaining six consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental consciousness).
Question: What does “contemplating apart from mind, thought, and consciousness” mean?

Answer: “Contemplating apart from mind, thought, and consciousness” means that the key to Chan contemplation is to be free of mind, thought, and consciousness; once the subtle thoughts come to rest, self-nature reveals itself in its original state, which is to see the mind and realize the nature.

To attain seeing the mind and realizing the nature, there are three steps: first, the coarse thoughts come to rest (ten thousand thoughts return to one); second, the fine thoughts come to rest (the one thought returns to nothing); third, the subtle thoughts come to rest (both subject and object vanish, and faculties and objects are entirely released). When the subtle thoughts come to rest, self-nature is restored from the state of habitual nature to the state of original nature; at this time one thoroughly sees the original nature, which is what is commonly called seeing the mind and realizing the nature. Therefore “contemplating apart from mind, thought, and consciousness” means that Chan contemplation should pass, through non-discrimination and freedom from subject and object, to the point where “both subject and object vanish and faculties and objects are entirely released,” in order to thoroughly see the original nature.

[Coarse thoughts, fine thoughts, and subtle thoughts] Mind-thoughts have three kinds: coarse thoughts, fine thoughts, and subtle thoughts. For example, for one who recites the Buddha's name, delusive thoughts are coarse thoughts, and the thought of reciting the Buddha's name is a fine thought. Usually, when both coarse and fine thoughts are stilled, it is called no-thought; this is the no-thought generally spoken of. Further, if subtle thoughts also cease, this is the ultimate no-thought. [Subtle thoughts] The subtle arising and ceasing flow of the discriminating mind is the characteristic of the alaya-vijnana.
Question: What is the original nature?

Answer: Self-nature has these two states, delusion and awakening. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says: “When self-nature is deluded, that is a sentient being; when self-nature is awakened, that is a Buddha.” Self-nature awakened is the original state of self-nature, called the original nature. To see the nature is to see the original nature. When self-nature gives rise to thoughts and moves, it is in the state of delusion, called the habitual nature; this is the deep-rooted habitual state that self-nature has formed from time without beginning, by producing thoughts and relying on objects (the seeds of ignorance, which by long standing have become a nature). The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says: “Self-nature contains all dharmas; this is called the store consciousness. If it gives rise to thinking, that is the transforming consciousness.” In this passage the Sixth Patriarch gives an extremely important instruction on self-nature: when self-nature is deluded (gives rise to thinking), it transforms from the state of original nature into the state of habitual nature. And practice is to restore self-nature from the state of habitual nature to the state of original nature, and so one goes from being a sentient being to becoming a Buddha.
Question: Why arouse bodhicitta?

Answer: In order to see the mind and realize the nature. Hence it is said: one who arouses the mind arouses the mind that seeks to see the nature. To study Buddhism without seeking to see the nature is to be a follower of non-Buddhist paths; only one who resolves to see the nature is a child of the Buddha. If one sees the mind and realizes the nature, afflictions are cut off of themselves without being cut off; karmic obstructions are removed of themselves without being removed; all sufferings are extinguished of themselves without being extinguished; and though one does not speak of making offerings to the Three Jewels, one has already made offerings to the Three Jewels of one's own mind; though one gives not a single coin, one's giving surpasses the seven treasures; though one does not recite mantras, one obtains the seal of the mantras; though one does not recite the sutras, the twelve divisions of scripture are all penetrated. Because one proceeds from the root, the fruit is thus great and the merit thus high.
Question: How is it that contemplating the mind attains seeing the nature?

Answer: The ancients said: “If one does not contemplate the mind, the Dharma has no source.” Because the Buddha-Dharma all rests on the pure mind; only by turning back and contemplating within can one draw forth the Buddha-nature, and then all the gates of samādhi, all the gates of dharani, all the gates of liberation, and all the gates of spiritual power manifest at once. Therefore know that the mind is the source of the wondrous Dharma; if one does not contemplate the mind, how can it be drawn forth? Thus contemplating the mind is the foremost wondrous practice of the Buddha-Dharma, which no other practice can match. Hence the Avatamsaka Sutra says: “At the first arousing of the mind one attains right enlightenment.” This means that one's own mind is the Buddha; seeing one's own true Buddha, one attains right enlightenment. The Treatise on the Arousing of Bodhicitta says: “If a person seeks the Buddha's wisdom and penetrates bodhicitta, this body born of parents will quickly attain the stage of great enlightenment.” The people of today wish to become Buddhas, yet they race their minds outward seeking — alas! Without ever arousing the mind, they cultivate sundry contemplations and practices, gaining only the fruit of rebirth in the heavens, and cannot escape the cycle of rebirth.
Question: What is the relationship between arousing bodhicitta and the other contemplative practices?

Answer: Arousing bodhicitta is the general characteristic; the other contemplative practices are the particular characteristics. The particular must rely on the general, and the general can encompass the particular. The Nirvāṇa Sutra says: “Though one believes the particular characteristics, if one does not believe the characteristic of the one undifferentiated body (that is, bodhicitta), it is called incomplete faith. Because faith is incomplete, all the precepts are also incomplete, and all extensive learning is also incomplete.” The ancients said: “Without bodhicitta, even the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts are not accomplished, because one does not know the root of the Buddha-Dharma.” Such is its importance. The people of today learn a bellyful of Buddha-Dharma, yet are utterly confused here — why?

blocks.text: 3. The Merit of Arousing the Mind

inline.s: The merit of arousing the mind cannot be fully spoken of; it pervades the many sutras, and is extensively set forth in the Avatamsaka, the Yogacara, and the Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom. Here I cite a few items below:
1. The Benefits of Taking Birth

Having aroused this mind, one obtains four benefits: (1) The seed is supreme, because bodhicitta is the seed. (2) The mother that gives birth is supreme, because prajñā-paramita is the mother that gives birth. (3) The womb is supreme, because the bliss of great meditation is the womb. (4) The wet-nurse is supreme, because great compassion nourishing is the wet-nurse.
2. The Merit of Leaving Home

A layman cannot obtain the merit of leaving home; but if a layman arouses the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, it is equal to leaving home, and he too can obtain this merit. The Vimalakirti Sutra says: “Do you arouse the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi; this is to leave home, and this is to be fully endowed.” (The passage reads: “Then Vimalakirti said to the sons of the elders: You should together leave home within the true Dharma. Why? Because a Buddha's appearance in the world is hard to encounter! The sons of the elders said: Layman, we have heard the Buddha say that without the parents' permission one cannot leave home. Vimalakirti said: Indeed! Do you arouse the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi; this is to leave home, and this is to be fully endowed.”)
[Not permitted] Not allowed.
3. Being Fully Endowed with the Buddha-Dharma

The Vimalakirti Sutra says: “To arouse the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, everything is fully endowed.” The Vibhasa Treatise says: “This Dharma-gate is the mother of the Buddhas, the father of the Buddhas, the eye of the Buddhas, the mother of the patient acceptance that dharmas are unarisen, the mother of great compassion and great mercy; constantly cultivate it, and the merit is measureless and boundless.” The Great Prajñā Sutra says: “It is like shooting an arrow at an object — sometimes it hits, sometimes it misses; but shooting an arrow at the ground, there is none that does not hit.” One who arouses the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi and becomes a Buddha is like shooting an arrow at the ground — there is none that does not succeed.
4. Entering the Eons and Transcending the Eons

Worldly people often resent that becoming a Buddha takes three great asamkhya eons, and that the time is too far. They do not know that those who cultivate sundry contemplative practices are still outside the three great asamkhya eons. Today, having aroused the mind, one who has not entered the eons enters them, and one who has already entered them can transcend them.
5. The Buddhas' Prediction and the Buddhas' Blessing

At the first arousing of the mind, the Buddhas give their prediction; this is clearly stated in many sutras, such as the Sutra of the Birth of Bodhi, the Sutra of the Mind-Ground of the Great Vehicle, the Sutra of the Questions of the Youth, and most extensively in the Avatamsaka Sutra. As for the Buddhas' blessing, the Lankavatara Sutra says: “In all the lands of the ten directions, all the immeasurable Buddhas extend their hands of light and stroke the crown of this person's head.” Thus the Buddhas constantly bless such a practitioner.
6. Being Able to Transform the Female Body
In the canon there is the Sutra of Transforming the Female Body. When the Buddha spoke of bodhicitta, eight hundred laywomen were transformed into male bodies.
7. Rebirth in the Highest Grade

Worldly people recite the Buddha's name without knowing to arouse the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi; even if they attain rebirth, they only attain the middle or lower grades. If, while reciting the Buddha's name, they also arouse the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, then they may hope for rebirth in the highest grade. The Contemplation Sutra says: not knowing the ultimate truth, one cannot attain rebirth in the highest grade. The ultimate truth is bodhicitta. There are many other sutras; I will not cite them all here.
8. Being Free of Disasters and Calamities

The Vibhasa Treatise says: “Calamity, fire, officialdom, thieves, enmity, poison, dragons, wild beasts, and massed illness — that they should afflict this person is without any likelihood. For this person is constantly guarded, thought of, and praised by the eight classes of devas and nagas and by all the Buddhas.” This treatise briefly lists nine kinds of disasters and calamities: first, the calamity of eons; second, the calamity of fire; third, official troubles; fourth, the calamity of thieves; fifth, enmity; sixth, poison and harm; seventh, the calamity of dragons; eighth, vicious beasts; ninth, illness. In fact, all disasters are entirely eliminated. The full account is as in the Avatamsaka and the Yogacara-bhumi Treatise.
9. The Essential Path to Buddhahood

The Bhadrakalpa Sutra says: “The Tathagata Star King, formerly a cowherd, first aroused bodhicitta before the Tathagata Sound-Giving. The Tathagata Name-Accomplished, formerly a weaver, first aroused bodhicitta before the Tathagata Lightning-Light. The Tathagata Bright-Flame, formerly a city-guardian, first aroused bodhicitta before the Tathagata Boundless-Light. The Tathagata Hard-to-Vanquish, formerly a woodcutter, first aroused bodhicitta before the Tathagata Firm-Stepping. The Tathagata Merit-Banner, formerly a water-drawer, first aroused bodhicitta before the Tathagata Wondrous-Name. The Tathagata Power-Army, formerly a physician, first aroused bodhicitta before the Tathagata Great-Parable.” This passage illustrates the following three points: First, lowly origins: cowherds, weavers, and such are not from high families, so arousing bodhicitta is not restricted by one's position or family. Second, attaining the fruit: these six all attained the fruit of the Tathagata, showing that arousing bodhicitta is not in vain. Third, the essential path: they attained the Buddha-fruit not by the merit of other contemplative practices but by the merit of arousing bodhicitta; therefore arousing bodhicitta is the essential path to Buddhahood.
Question: Arousing bodhicitta is certainly about quickly becoming a Buddha; if one does not succeed in this life, is there any fruit?

I reply: There is. From the arousing of bodhicitta up to the attainment of Buddhahood, the intermediate births are called in the Yogacara treatises “the successively superior births,” meaning that in life after life the benefits double and increase. The Sutra of the Birth of Bodhi says: if one seeks riches and honor, or to become a king of the heavens, one can obtain it as one wishes. How can one say there is no fruit? Moreover, if one truly arouses bodhicitta, from the stage of the ten faiths onward one becomes thirteen kinds of Dharma-teachers, that is, thirteen kinds of kings among humans and gods. This meaning is seen in the Sutra of the Benevolent King and the Sutra of the Garland of Jewels. The first item above, “the benefits of taking birth,” sums up its fruit, which the treatises call obtaining the four holy wheels.
Question: How does one arouse bodhicitta?

Answer: The Sutra of Manjusri's Questions says: “Not arousing is the arousing of bodhicitta.” What does “not arousing” mean? It means not arousing any mind that seeks benefit, or any mind of compassion and vows that has conditions. For when one arouses the mind, one must set aside all external conditions and be free of thoughts, pure and clean. To give rise to thoughts and set the mind moving is to go against the substance of the Dharma, hence “not arousing.” Then why is it also called “arousing”? Because when thought after thought is all still, and self-nature is perfectly fused, pervading without limit — that is arousing the mind. Wisdom functions within, not without, and so “not arousing” is “arousing.” The Flower-Hand Sutra says: “Contemplate this mind; thought after thought it arises and ceases, illusory and without anything existing, yet it obtains great fruit-reward.” Layman Pang said: “Only see the place of arising and ceasing; this is thusness.” Savor these words well.

There are three further essential points: First, when arousing the mind, one should know there is no agent that arouses — this destroys attachment to self. Second, there is no realm in which it is aroused. Third, there is no expedient means by which it is aroused. These two destroy attachment to dharmas. In sum, the aim is ultimately emptiness, nothing existing, nothing attained.

Moreover, when arousing the mind, if any wondrous states or even small spiritual powers appear, one should immediately abandon them, because this is a dharma without marks. All sundry practices and all sundry contemplations must not be mixed in with this cultivation.

blocks.text: 5. The Ritual of Arousing the Mind

inline.s: The ritual of arousing bodhicitta:

The Treatise on the Manifestation of the Noble Teachings says: “Standing respectfully before the wise one, rouse the exalted intention and make this vow: I, disciple So-and-so, from today onward, arouse the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Because I wish to benefit all sentient beings, whatever I cultivate, the Six Perfections and so forth, are all for the sake of realizing anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
