I now walk the same path as the great bodhisattva-mahasattvas; may the venerable one vouch for it.” Saying this three times accords with the ritual.

In the Letters of Mr. Liu Zhuyuan it says: You cultivate no-thought, yet your discriminating mind is great; how can you accord with prajñā? I think of how earnestly you seek the Dharma; now I should teach you to arouse the ultimate bodhicitta (urging the arousal of the true mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi):
A. Four matters to examine beforehand. (Not for use while in sitting meditation; one should know them beforehand.)
One, for what purpose? (If it is for the sake of gaining benefit, the cause is not upright; one should seek to see the mind and realize the nature.)
Two, wash away old views. (One should wash away old views and old hearing until thoroughly clean.)
Three, with what mind? (One should be free of the mind of perception, that is, free of mind, thought, and consciousness, and not employ the mind.)
Four, what practice? (Not mixing in the marks of dharmas, solely the one method of contemplating the mind and guarding the mind unmoving.)
B. The method of proper practice. (This method is based on the four lines transmitted by Master Bodhidharma. Those with true faith may all study it; those without faith should not.)
One, harmonize all external conditions to rest. (Cast away the affairs of faculties and objects until thoroughly clean.)
Two, within, the mind has no panting. (“Panting” means movement; it says the mind does not move.)
Three, the mind is like a wall. (It says discrimination does not arise, and one is free of subject and object.)
Four, one may enter the Way. (This line is the fruit; the effort is only in the three lines above.)

Every day seated in full lotus, contemplate the mind according to the three lines. If a mind-thought arises, neither suppress it nor follow it; one should contemplate that delusive thoughts have no self-nature, and that their substance is empty, and the mind will naturally become still. When delusive thoughts cease, the spring of the mind is empty and still, prajñā accords, and the true nature first manifests. This method is the practice of no-thought, the practice of no-abiding, the practice of not-moving, which is the samādhi of thusness; it breathes through the same nostril as the Treatise on the Awakening of Faith, and instantly realizes in a single thought. (During contemplation one should not let states appear; this is most important. The number of sittings and their length may be as one pleases.)
C. The ceremony of receiving the Dharma.

One must bathe, then bow to the Buddha and say: “Disciple So-and-so, today from such-and-such a worthy one, I study arousing bodhicitta; I believe and rejoice, and will practice it my whole life, vowing never to forget.” Saying this three times, do three prostrations. Afterwards, simply practice, and no further declaration is needed. From then on, one may not be negligent for a single day.
[From then on, one may not be negligent for a single day.] Most important! Most important!

Recitation may be reduced; the Diamond Sutra may be recited — who says all sutras must be recited every day? Now, merely by arousing bodhicitta one directly enters the realm of the sages; why be greedy for more?

blocks.text: 6. The Three Essentials of Arousing the Mind

inline.s: Surveying the bodhisattva-pitaka, about three-tenths of it speaks of the meaning of arousing the mind. In the chapters and commentaries of the great masters it is explained in detail item by item, and the categories of meaning are especially many. Here I briefly speak thus. Finally there are three essential points: First, one must believe that one's own mind is the Buddha; second, one must have a good spiritual friend to teach; third, one must be willing to diligently contemplate the mind. Possessing these three essentials, there is no one who does not become a Buddha. Even a moment's cultivation plants the Buddha-seed. Its supreme merit cannot be compared with the ordinary recitation of sutras, reciting the Buddha's name, reciting mantras, and other contemplative practices.

Ordinarily one should often think over the principle of mind-only, that one's own mind is the Buddha, the meaning of the two emptinesses, and that all dharmas have no self-nature, as a preparation. Nurturing and self-examination are especially not to be neglected. One should know that worldly affairs are like dreams and illusions, and life is like the morning dew; in a moment it is all impermanent, and everything is in vain. If one can stir up the thought of indifference and the thought of renunciation, one most easily accords. To cultivate with a single thought for ten thousand years — that is it.
The Ratnakuta Sutra verse says
Were one to build stupas, as many as the sands of the Ganges,
Yet it would not compare with a single moment of thinking on this matter.
Though one pass through all future eons, visiting all Buddha-lands,
Without seeking this wondrous Dharma, one can never attain bodhi.
[Thinking on this matter] Contemplating the nature of the mind (contemplating the mind). The original note says: “‘Thinking’ means contemplation, and ‘this matter’ means the nature of the mind.”
The Avatamsaka Sutra verse says:
A child of the Buddha, having first aroused such a wondrous jewel-mind,
Then transcends the stage of the ordinary man and enters where the Buddha walks,
Born in the Tathagata's family, his lineage without flaw,
Equal with the Buddha, he will surely attain supreme enlightenment.

The above is roughly the meaning the Master often taught. If one can give rise to a single thought of faith, a moment's cultivation already has measureless merit; how much more so diligent and focused cultivation, whose recompense is beyond thought. May all who study, and who are fortunate enough to hear this, each treasure it and encourage themselves.
Question: I suspect that the method of arousing the mind is too high, suited to the highest faculties and not to the middling and low.
[Servant] A humble term for “I.”

Answer: It is not high. If one does not arouse the mind, one is not genuine. The Avatamsaka says: it is like taking medicine — if the medicine does not match the illness, one may keep changing it; only the single flavor of water cannot be changed. Water is a metaphor for bodhicitta. The later masters speak of the method of reciting the Buddha's name and do not speak of arousing the mind — first, because the ignorant do not know it, and second, because their method is not complete. The three Pure Land sutras — the Larger Amitābha (referring to the Sutra of Immeasurable Life Spoken by the Buddha) and the Contemplation Sutra (the Sutra of the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life Spoken by the Buddha) — both have passages on arousing the mind; it is wrong to say that the Smaller Amitābha (referring to the Amitābha Sutra Spoken by the Buddha) has none. This sutra (the Amitābha Sutra Spoken by the Buddha) has the words “non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-sambodhi”; if one had not first aroused the mind, with respect to what would one speak of non-retrogression? This meaning has never been explained by anyone; think it over and it becomes clear by itself.
Question: I suspect that one who recites the Buddha's name while also cultivating the arousal of the mind will be mixed and impure.

Answer: It is not mixed. Does not reciting the Buddha's name seek single-minded concentration? (For one who has never contemplated the mind, how can he know single-minded concentration?) The one method of arousing the mind directly enters the state of single mind; how can it be said to be mixed? Moreover, when we recite the Buddha's name from morning to night, can our three karmas of body, speech, and mind be never apart from the Buddha? In dealing with affairs and meeting people, can we be never apart from the Buddha for even an instant? If one says, not yet — we are apart from the Buddha for much of the time. Then in this separation one does not complain of the mixture, yet in a single arousal of the mind one alone complains of the mixture — is that acceptable? For a student of the Dharma to refuse to arouse the mind, I fear there is no such principle.
[How could this be called mixed practice?] How can it be called mixed practice? The word e (
wū
) de means “how could it be.”
Question: I suspect that people of superior capacity are few.

Answer: They are very many. I say that among ten thousand people, nine thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine are of superior capacity, and those of the very lowest capacity are no more than one. One asks: Why is it that none of them succeed? I answer: It is because they do not believe — not because their faculties are spoiled. Consider the six kinds of people cited in the Sutra of the Auspicious Kalpa: before they had aroused the mind, who could have determined that they were of superior capacity? The Diamond Sutra says: “Sentient beings, sentient beings — the Tathagata teaches that they are not sentient beings; therefore they are called sentient beings.” Among the Confucian scholars of principle, none will say that there are no good people in the world. Among the perfect-and-sudden schools of Buddhism, none will say that sentient beings are of inferior faculties (it is because they have not yet been polished; once polished, they become vessels). Someone may ask: Why does the Chan school so often say that the highest of superior capacities are required? I answer: These are words of warning, meant to spur one on and upward. When the Chan school speaks, all its words are living phrases. To grasp them as literal fact is biased construction — that is a dead phrase; how could that be understanding the words!

[The six kinds of people cited in the Sutra of the Auspicious Kalpa] Those who attained Buddhahood, as cited in the Sutra of the Auspicious Kalpa, include a cowherd, a weaver, a city guard, a woodcutter, a water-drawer, and a physician. The sutra says: “The Tathagata Star King was formerly a cowherd, and first aroused the bodhi mind in the presence of the Tathagata Sound Gift. The Tathagata Renown was formerly a weaver, and first aroused the bodhi mind in the presence of the Tathagata Lightning Light. The Tathagata Bright Flame was formerly a city guard, and first aroused the bodhi mind in the presence of the Tathagata Boundless Light. The Tathagata Victory was formerly a woodcutter, and first aroused the bodhi mind in the presence of the Tathagata Steadfast Step. The Tathagata Merit Banner was formerly a water-drawer, and first aroused the bodhi mind in the presence of the Tathagata Wondrous Renown. The Tathagata Power of the Army was formerly a physician, and first aroused the bodhi mind in the presence of the Tathagata Great Likeness.”
Question: Why is it that understanding the one mind surpasses vowing to be born in the West by ten thousand times?

Answer: This meaning is the highest teaching of the Pure Land school, and it is also common talk in the Pure Land school; it is plainly present in the sutras. The Larger Amitābha Sutra (the Sutra of Immeasurable Life) speaks of rebirth in three grades, all of them grounded in arousing the bodhi mind. It also says that one who does not understand the four wisdoms is born only in the borderland city of doubt. The Contemplation Sutra says, “All Buddhas, the Tathagatas, are the dharmakāya, and enter into the minds and thoughts of all sentient beings,” and further, “This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha” — how could it not take the understanding of the one mind as its root?
Cultivated in this way, one may hope within this life to attain the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas.

The three words of the ordinary path — faith, vow, and practice — are of course not to be rejected, yet if no weight is given to the bodhi mind, then even if one is born in the West, one can hardly hope for the highest of the highest grade. Why? Because the one mind has not been understood. The one mind is hard to believe in, and to understand it is harder still. If one can understand it, one enters the stage of no further learning. Yet the meaning of the Mahayana should begin from this point, and only then is it arousing the mind. Simply believe that all dharmas are within the mind, that all Buddhas and sentient beings are also within the mind, and that the Pure Land and the defiled land are also within the mind; then recite the Buddha’s name with all your strength, and after a year or half a year of effort, ask again — do not rely on talk. In ordinary Buddha-recitation, if this matter is not understood, then even though one attains rebirth, it is still the lowest grade. I am teaching you the ultimate truth, beginning from the understanding of mind; naturally it is ten thousand times higher, for I am urging one of rather good faculties with the teaching of definitive meaning, grounded in arousing the bodhi mind. The books on arousing the mind in the scholastic tradition are broad in text and wide in meaning, and hard to grasp at once. I instruct you with a simple method: understand the one mind alone, and all meanings are included; that is truly arousing the mind. If the one mind is not understood, then even though one vows to be reborn in the West, one still lingers in the borderland city of doubt. This is of course better than worldly dharmas, but it is in the end not the original intent with which our Buddha draws in sentient beings. This is why I urge you to read the Platform Sutra: that book never speaks of arousing the mind, yet every sentence points straight at the human mind, and every word is ultimate definitive meaning. You may calmly take it up; that book will make it clear without remainder. Why ask further about the ultimate truth? To understand the one mind is the true ultimate truth. The ultimate truth is the one mind. Called Buddha-nature, called true suchness, called dharmakāya, called dharmadhatu — all are other names for the true mind, and all are our own mind. Buddhas and sentient beings are equal, without a second. If you still do not understand, then recite the Buddha’s name honestly, and a day of clarity will come. But to chase after words alone leaves no hope. The reason I urge you always to read the Platform Sutra is that this very book may open your bodhi mind.

[The four wisdoms] The wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done, the wisdom of wondrous observation, the wisdom of equality in nature, and the wisdom of the great perfect mirror. The wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done is that attained by converting the afflicted first five consciousnesses; it is the Buddha’s wisdom in accomplishing all that is to be done for the universal benefit of sentient beings. The wisdom of wondrous observation is that attained by converting the afflicted sixth consciousness; it is the Buddha’s wisdom in observing all dharmas and the faculties of all sentient beings, prescribing medicine according to the illness and turning the ordinary into the sage. The wisdom of equality in nature is that attained by converting the afflicted seventh consciousness; it is the Buddha’s wisdom in penetrating the principle of non-self and equality, and in bringing forth toward all sentient beings the unconditioned great compassion. The wisdom of the great perfect mirror is that attained by converting the afflicted eighth consciousness; it is the Buddha’s wisdom in illuminating all phenomenal appearances and principles without the least obscurity — a wisdom pure and perfectly luminous, seeing through within and without, like a great perfect mirror reflecting all things. [Understanding the one mind] Realizing the one mind. The one mind is our own mind. Everyone possesses it by nature, each one is complete in it; it is near, within the mind, and need not be sought afar. To become a Buddha or a patriarch is this one mind; the Chan school calls it illuminating the mind and seeing the nature — mind is the nature (mind and nature are one; this comes from the Avatamsaka Sutra). [The stage of no further learning] At this stage the afflictions of view and thought are exhausted and the truth is ultimate; there is no dharma left to learn, and so it is called no further learning — for example, the fourth fruit of the sravakas, the arhat.
Question: Letting go is the hardest thing of all. By what method should one counter it?

Answer: You should know that when you cannot let go, recite the Buddha’s name with a single mind, and you will be able to let go. The Pure Land school’s parable of the pearl clearing muddy water is exactly this. If the mind scatters and runs, oppose it with the Buddha’s name, and in time it will of itself grow still. In learning any dharma, who does not use bitter effort? If one could let go without effort, why would there be any need to learn? As for your daily recitation schedule, you may set it yourself. In my view, whenever one takes up a task, one should give it one’s whole strength — as in Buddha-recitation: then one keeps the thought fixed on it all day long, without pause. If you set fixed hours, your rest periods will be many indeed, and how could the day of success ever come? Recite with effort, recite without interval — press on, press on. Besides Buddha-recitation, the various mantras you uphold, since you have already studied them, need not be abandoned. Only know that the mind is the root, and every dharma-gate enters the ultimate truth. The Buddha-Dharma is the speech of one family: if you simply penetrate the mind school and recite the Buddha’s name diligently, the merit is inconceivable. As for those who gain no result, it is that they are unwilling to practice long, they hold that there are dharmas outside the mind, and they practice by fits and starts.

[The parable of the pearl clearing muddy water] The Threefold Recitation of Zhongfeng says: “In the Western Heaven there is a jewel called the clear pearl. It is said that when this pearl is cast into muddy water, then for every inch it enters, an inch of the muddy water becomes clear. As the pearl sinks from an inch to a foot and all the way to the bottom, the muddy water grows clear and still along with it. You should know that the clear pearl is a parable for the pure thought of Buddha-recitation, and the muddy water a parable for the confused and scattered deluded mind.”
Question: How does one benefit sentient beings?

Answer: That you have the mind to benefit others is, as the Buddha said, “to save others before oneself is saved” — how could it be wrong? Yet you may not realize that the sutras say again and again: “If one is oneself in bonds and wishes to loose the bonds of another, that is impossible.” And again: “If one does not practice oneself and wishes another to practice, that is in the end impossible.” If you truly wish to benefit others, you should be diligent without weariness until you have some attainment. To be a father and mother to the six realms and a teacher to gods and humans is a matter within your own portion. What benefit is there in publishing in newspapers or passing things from mouth to ear?
Question: The dharma-gates are immeasurable. How should one study and practice them?

Answer: In learning any dharma, what matters is a resolute mind (not wavering until success), a long-enduring mind (doing it always, without interruption), and an uninterrupted mind (as when a hen broods on her eggs — once the warmth breaks off, there is no life in them). With these three minds, nothing fails. Now, the Buddha has all manner of dharmas to cure all manner of minds among sentient beings. Therefore the sutra says: the expedient means are many. Must one try every gate before one can succeed? What matters is to trust one gate, and enter its depths — there lies the matter. The vow in the four universal vows, “the dharma-gates are immeasurable, I vow to learn them,” is spoken vertically, not horizontally; do not mistake it. Vertically means: master one dharma, then learn another kind, and afterward there will be immeasurable dharma-gates. It does not mean advancing on all at once. If you advance on all at once, not one dharma can be accomplished — what benefit is there in that? Though the dharma-gates are immeasurable, one must penetrate deeply through one gate; there lies the matter. Therefore the great masters of old, in teaching people, always said: you must have a point of entry. Once there is a point of entry, the wisdom of emptiness shines bright, and through all the ten thousand transformations you take this as your base. Otherwise you remain an outsider at the gate your whole life. You are a fine vessel; I hope you will set your mind on one dharma alone, spend your months and years on it, and bring it through to openness. Do not run after many at once, and do not change your mind at every new sight. To count grains of sand in the sea, to speak of food that does not fill you — these you should firmly renounce.
Question: Is arousing the bodhi mind the same as arousing the mind that seeks the Way?

Answer: To explain arousing the mind as the mind of the Way is far too vague. Let me give you a definition: to arouse the bodhi mind is to arouse the mind that sees the nature. This is a word that pierces to the bone and marrow, a truly exact explanation. Only when there is no object to be conditioned upon can one see the nature — what is called no gate as the dharma-gate. You cultivate no-thought and do not know this: is that not to drive south while your destination lies north? The ancient worthies said: “If one does not contemplate the mind, dharmas have no place to come from.” That is to say, pure conditions cannot arise. So know that contemplating the mind or not is truly the hinge of life and death in learning the dharma. To study Buddhism without arousing the mind gains only human and heavenly causes and results. If one can arouse this ultimate mind, then one receives the Buddhas’ prediction, and can enter the kalpas and transcend the kalpas.

blocks.text: Chapter 3 The Essential Point Lies in Contemplating the Mind

inline.s: The ancient worthies said:
“If one does not contemplate the mind, dharmas have no place to come from.”

For the Buddha-Dharma is all upon the pure mind; only by turning the light around and illuminating within can the Buddha-nature be drawn forth, and then all gates of samādhi, all gates of dharani, all gates of liberation, and all gates of spiritual power appear at once. So know that the mind is where the wondrous dharma comes from; if one does not contemplate the mind, how can it be drawn out? Therefore contemplating the mind is the first wondrous practice of the Buddha-Dharma; no other practice can match it.
[The gate of dharani] The Sanskrit dharani
is translated into Chinese as
“total retention.”
Because

the bodhisattva, by the dharma of total retention, follows the speech and sounds of all sentient beings, opens and guides them to right faith, causes them to extinguish all evil thoughts and to practice all good dharmas — this is the bodhisattva’s gate of dharani.
In the Mahayana Sutra of Mind Ground Contemplation, the Buddha says:
“This dharma
(mind contemplation)

is called the most excellent and secret mind-ground dharma-gate of the Tathagatas of the ten directions; this dharma is called the sudden-enlightenment dharma-gate by which all ordinary beings enter the Tathagata’s ground; this dharma is called the true and right road by which all bodhisattvas proceed to great bodhi
the true and right road

, this dharma is called the subtle jewel palace in which the Buddhas of the three times enjoy the bliss of the dharma for themselves; this dharma is called the inexhaustible treasury of all that benefits sentient beings.
Good man,
within the three realms, the mind is sovereign. One who can contemplate the mind attains ultimate liberation; one who cannot remains forever in bondage.”
The Nirvāṇa Sutra says:
“To be able to contemplate the nature of the mind is called supreme concentration.”
Daoxin, the Fourth Patriarch of the Chan school, says:

“The hundred thousand dharma-gates all return to the square inch; the wonderful virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges all lie in the source of the mind. All gates of precepts, gates of concentration, and gates of wisdom, with their spiritual transformations, are complete in themselves and do not depart from your mind.”
The Fifth Patriarch Hongren says:
“Not to know one’s own mind — to learn the dharma is of no benefit.”
The Sixth Patriarch Huineng says:

“Good friends! Unawakened, the Buddha is a sentient being; at the moment of a single thought of awakening, a sentient being is the Buddha. So know that all dharmas are wholly within one’s own mind — why not, from within the mind, suddenly see the true-suchness of one’s own nature? The Sutra of Bodhisattva Precepts says: ‘My original self-nature is pure; if one knows one’s own mind and sees the nature, all attain the Buddha Way.’ The Vimalakirti Sutra says: ‘At that moment one is suddenly opened, and returns to one’s original mind.’ Good friends! In the presence of Master Ren I heard it once and was at once awakened, suddenly seeing the true-suchness of my own nature. Therefore I cause this teaching to flow abroad, so that those who learn the Way may suddenly awaken to bodhi. Each of you contemplate your own mind and see your own nature.”
Therefore the root of the Buddha-Dharma is the mind, and the root of practice is contemplation.
To observe and illuminate constantly is prajñā perfuming ignorance.
Once ignorance is broken, the dharmakāya appears at once. One leaps straight into the Tathagata’s ground, and without passing through kalpas beyond number attains the dharma body.
The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
“All Tathagatas, from their original ground of causation, rely on the perfect illumination of the pure enlightened mark, forever cut off ignorance, and only then accomplish the Buddha Way.”

Moreover, arousing the bodhi mind is precisely contemplating the pure mind of one’s own nature (see “Arousing the Bodhi Mind” in the previous chapter). The merit of arousing the bodhi mind is incomparably excellent, and cannot be fully told. For example:
“One who arouses the bodhi mind receives the Buddhas’ prediction and the Buddhas’ sustaining power.”

When one first arouses the mind, the Buddha bestows the prediction — the sutras state this plainly, as in the Sutra of the Arising of Bodhi, the Mahayana Sutra of Mind Ground Contemplation, and the Sutra of the Meaning of Thought, and most extensively in the Avatamsaka Sutra. As for the Buddhas’ sustaining power, the Lankavatara Sutra says:
“In all lands of the ten directions, all the immeasurable Buddhas all extend hands of light and stroke the crown of that person’s head.”
Thus do the Buddhas constantly sustain such practitioners. (See the section on “The Merit of Arousing the Mind” in the previous chapter.)

Our Buddha taught the dharma for forty-nine years, in somewhat more than three hundred assemblies; the meanings of the teachings differ in a thousand ways, yet their homecoming is not two. To cover it in one phrase: the one mind alone (the one mind is the true mind). If the one mind is not understood, then there are outer objects, and from these one gives rise to confusion and creates karma, turning in the wheel of rebirth without end. If one truly understands the one mind, then the three insights, the six spiritual powers, the ten powers, and the four fearlessnesses come without being sought. Therefore it is said: of all dharmas, the mind is foremost. Whoever learns the dharma yet drifts along with objects, not taking mind contemplation as the root, is an outsider.

[The three insights] The insight of past lives, the heavenly eye, and the extinction of outflows. The insight of past lives is the clear knowledge of all the past lives of oneself or others; the heavenly eye is the clear knowledge of all future lives of oneself or others; the extinction of outflows is the cutting off of all afflictions by sagely wisdom. [The six spiritual powers] The spiritual powers attained by the sages of the three vehicles are six in all: the heavenly eye, the heavenly ear, the knowledge of others’ minds, the knowledge of past lives, the power of unimpeded travel, and the extinction of outflows. [The ten powers] The ten powers possessed by the Tathagata. First, the power of knowing what is possible and impossible, that is, the power to know the reasonableness and unreasonableness of all things; second, the power of knowing the karmic retribution of the three times, that is, the power to know the karmic causes and results of all sentient beings throughout the three times; third, the power of knowing all meditations, liberations, and samādhis, that is, the power to know all meditative concentrations, liberations, and samādhis; fourth, the power of knowing the superiority and inferiority of the faculties, that is, the power to know whether sentient beings’ faculties are superior or inferior and whether the fruits they attain are great or small; fifth, the power of knowing all manner of understanding, that is, the power to know universally the different understandings of all sentient beings; sixth, the power of knowing all manner of realms, that is, the power to know universally the different realms of all sentient beings; seventh, the power of knowing the path to every destination, that is, the power to know the causes and results of the paths practiced by all sentient beings; eighth, the power of the unobstructed heavenly eye, that is, the power to see with the heavenly eye the birth and death of sentient beings and the conditions of their good and evil karma without obstruction; ninth, the power of knowing past lives and the state without outflows, that is, the power to know sentient beings’ past lives and to know nirvāṇa without outflows; tenth, the power of forever cutting off habitual tendencies, that is, the power to know truly that the residual traces of all deluded afflictions are forever cut off and no longer arise. [The four fearlessnesses] First, the fearlessness of all wisdom: in the midst of the great assembly the Buddha declares plainly, “I am one of all wisdom,” with no fear in his mind. Second, the fearlessness of the extinction of outflows: in the midst of the great assembly the Buddha declares plainly, “I have cut off all afflictions,” with no fear in his mind. Third, the fearlessness of teaching the dharmas that obstruct the Way: in the midst of the great assembly the Buddha teaches the various obstructive dharmas of confusion and karma, with no fear in his mind. Fourth, the fearlessness of teaching the way that ends suffering: in the midst of the great assembly the Buddha teaches the right way of precepts, concentration, and wisdom that ends all suffering, with no fear in his mind.
Bodhidharma’s Treatise on Breaking Form says:
“Question: If there are people who aspire to the Buddha Way, what dharma should they practice to be most economical and essential? Answer:
Only the one dharma of contemplating the mind embraces all dharmas; it is the most economical and essential.

Question: How can one dharma embrace all dharmas? Answer: The mind is the root of all dharmas; all dharmas are born only from the mind. If one understands the mind, then all dharmas are complete — as with a great tree: all its branches and twigs, flowers and fruits, depend entirely upon the root. The one who plants the tree keeps the root, and only then does it begin to produce; the one who fells the tree removes the root, and it must surely die. If one understands the mind and cultivates the Way, then little effort brings easy success; if one does not understand the mind and cultivates, then effort is spent without benefit. So know that all good and evil come from one’s own mind. To seek elsewhere, outside the mind, is in the end nowhere to be found.”

First, one must rest the mind and still the thoughts: all six sense-objects and ten thousand conditions must be laid down altogether; good matters and bad matters alike are not pondered; past and future are not thought of at all. One looks directly at the thoughts of the present moment, coming and going in confusion, arising and ceasing without pause; do not cling to them, do not follow after them, do not cut them off. Simply watch quietly and closely. When a deluded thought arises, at one look it is gone no one knows where; soon it arises again, and one watches in the same way; if no thought arises, one simply watches.

When this has grown thoroughly familiar over a long time, and one sees the state in which not a single thought arises, one is then in accord with prajñā. (At this time it is contemplation without thought, and thoughtlessness with contemplation.) The
Treatise on Arousing the Bodhi Mind says:
“If a deluded mind arises
(if a deluded thought arises)
, know it and do not follow it; when the delusion
has ceased
(when the deluded thought has ceased)
, the source of the mind is empty and still, the ten thousand virtues are complete, and its wondrous function is inexhaustible.”

So wondrous is the nature of the mind. That we are ordinarily not in accord with it is because we are shrouded by deluded thoughts; this is the deluded mind. Upon what does ignorance depend? It arises depending on true suchness. To contemplate the deluded mind is to contemplate the mind of true suchness; to contemplate the nature of the mind is to contemplate the deluded mind. Why? Because true suchness is the substance of thought, and thought is the function of true suchness. When one contemplates and attains stability, this is the samādhi of true suchness, the king of samādhis, and so it is called supreme concentration.

[Know it and do not follow it] Watch this thought without judging it, and do not let it continue (do not give rise to thought upon thought). The key to “knowing it and not following it” is to work at the “knowing”: watch as a cat guards a mouse hole, and know the moment a thought arises. Once you can “know the moment a thought arises,” “not following it” becomes easy. [The source of the mind] The mind is the source of all dharmas, and so it is called the source of the mind. [The ten thousand virtues are complete] The ten thousand virtues are all present. Si means “then,” as in: with preparation, then one may be without care.
The key to mind contemplation:

Whatever thought arises, know it and do not follow it. Neither delighting nor loathing, neither grasping nor rejecting, not setting out to correct it, only clarifying the mind and observing closely. This is prajñā perfuming ignorance, and the transformation from the ordinary to the sage will come about of itself.
If one does not know, there is no wisdom; if one follows, there is no concentration. To know and not follow is the balanced holding of concentration and wisdom.
The first task of mind contemplation:
to know and not follow, and so to purify and remove the flowing stream of one’s own deluded thinking.

Question: In the Mahayana method of calm abiding and insight, the contemplation for the practice of no-thought is: “When a single thought arises, observe it at once; at the very moment of observing, the previous thought has already ceased and the next thought has not yet arisen, so the present is without thought.” This method is contemplation of thoughtlessness. What does the master think of it?

Answer: This differs somewhat from my own view. What I rely on is the verse of the sutra: “You should observe this mind: thought after thought, it ever arises and ceases, like an illusion, possessing nothing; and yet one attains the great fruit.” This is truly arousing the bodhi mind; this is the practice of no-thought, no-abiding, and no-mark. (Editor’s note: The former method focuses on observing the blank gap of thoughtlessness, and calls it the practice of no-thought. The latter method focuses on observing that thoughts have no self-nature, and knowing without following — being thoughtless amid thoughts — and calls that the practice of no-thought. The difference between the two methods is subtle, and yet it is the crucial point. The latter method is superior to the former.)
Question: In mind contemplation, should one thoroughly investigate where deluded thoughts arise?

Answer: “Thoroughly investigate where deluded thoughts arise” — these words are quite wrong! For thorough investigation requires the use of the intellect. This method of mind contemplation transcends mind, intellect, and consciousness; how could there be any reason to use consciousness? Just look directly, and that is enough; there is no need to investigate thoroughly. The ancient worthies said: when the light of the mind shines through, the remaining flaws vanish of themselves. How simple and essential! What need is there for pondering?
Question: Why is it said that “just look directly, and that is enough”?

Editor’s answer: This is a method of contemplation that transcends mind, intellect, and consciousness. One need only observe with concentration, and no delusion will arise (“when the light of the mind shines through, the remaining flaws vanish of themselves”); moreover, the power of awareness grows swiftly, and of itself will bloom and bear fruit.

Question: On what sutra is this method of mind contemplation based? You often cite the Sutra of Mind Ground Contemplation. Is it perhaps based on that sutra? Yet what that sutra teaches is the contemplation of the moon disc — why, then, do you not have us contemplate the moon, but instead have us contemplate the mind? This doubt is not yet cleared; I beg you to instruct me.
Answer:

1. As to the sutra relied upon. Every practice of contemplation must rely on the meaning of a sutra. The method I give you relies on the Lankavatara Sutra, not on the Sutra of Mind Ground Contemplation. The Sutra of Mind Ground Contemplation speaks of the method of mind contemplation most fully, and I cite it as evidence. In truth this Tathagata Chan takes the Lankavatara as its basis, and so Bodhidharma transmitted the mind with it. The Tang translation of the Lankavatara Sutra (that is, the Mahayana Sutra of Entering Lanka) says in fascicle three: “Mahamati Bodhisattva Mahasattva again addressed the Buddha: ‘World-Honored One! I pray you to speak of the marks of the practice of realizing the sagely wisdom, and of the marks of the practice of the one vehicle, so that I and all bodhisattvas, mahasattvas, having gained this skill in means, may not be enlightened by the help of another in the Buddha-Dharma.’ The Buddha said: ‘Listen well; I will speak for you.’ Mahamati said: ‘So be it.’ The Buddha said: ‘Mahamati! The bodhisattva mahasattva, relying on the holy teachings, is without discrimination. Dwelling alone in quiet retreat, he observes self-awakening, not enlightened by the help of another, free of the views of discrimination, advancing higher and higher, and enters the Tathagata’s ground. Such practice is called the marks of the practice of self-realized sagely wisdom. What are the marks of the practice of the one vehicle? It is the realization and knowledge of the way of the one vehicle. What is it to know the way of the one vehicle? It is to dwell in accordance with reality, free of the discrimination of the grasped and the grasper. Mahamati! This way of the one vehicle, save for the Tathagata alone, is not to be attained by outsiders, the two vehicles, Brahma kings, or the like.’ This sutra is the governing principle, and no doubt should arise; if one cites the Lankavatara, its testimonies are very many. But its sentences are profound and expansive, and not easy to understand. Therefore I take the Contemplating the Mind chapter as evidence, for this is the common meaning of the Vaipulya teachings.

[Vaipulya] Fang means “broad” and deng means “equal”: in the third period the Buddha broadly taught the four teachings of the Tripitaka, the common, the distinct, and the perfect, benefiting equally the sharp and the dull faculties, and so it is called “Vaipulya.” [The four teachings] That is, the four teachings of the method of conversion: the Tripitaka teaching, the common teaching, the distinct teaching, and the perfect teaching. These four teachings — Tripitaka, common, distinct, and perfect — are the dharma-gates for teaching and converting sentient beings, and so they are called the “method of conversion.” The Tripitaka teaching is the three baskets of sutra, vinaya, and abhidharma, whose divisions are clearly distinguished; it teaches the four noble truths of arising and ceasing by cause and condition, and is directly for the sravakas and pratyekabuddhas, indirectly converting bodhisattvas. The common teaching teaches the four true truths of emptiness and non-arising, and is studied in common by the three vehicles, though the bodhisattva is the true recipient and the two vehicles the secondary recipients. The distinct teaching is that which speaks especially to bodhisattvas of the immeasurable dharmas of the Mahayana, and does not extend to the two vehicles. The perfect teaching is that which speaks to bodhisattvas of the sharpest faculties of the middle way and true mark, in which phenomenon and principle are perfectly interfused. [The four noble truths] The truth of suffering, the truth of the origin of suffering, the truth of the cessation of suffering, and the truth of the path. First, the “truth of suffering” sets forth the truth that human life is full of suffering. Suffering has the mark of oppression. Human life has three sufferings, eight sufferings, and immeasurable sufferings; suffering is the reality of actual human life. Second, the “truth of the origin” — ji means “to bring about” or “to cause” — sets forth the truth of how the suffering of human life comes about. The suffering of human life comes from creating karma through craving, and so one suffers and turns in rebirth. Third, the “truth of cessation” sets forth the truth of stilling all suffering. When all the origin of suffering (craving) is forever cut off without remainder, with no defilement and no attachment, one no longer suffers or turns in rebirth — this is the truth of cessation. Fourth, the “truth of the path” sets forth how to forever cut off the origin of suffering (craving), that is, the way to end suffering — the noble eightfold path. Among the four noble truths, origin is the cause and suffering the result; path is the cause and cessation the result.

[The five periods of the Buddha’s teaching] After the Buddha attained the Way, in the first three weeks he taught the Avatamsaka Sutra, saving the great bodhisattvas: this is the Avatamsaka period. Next, at Deer Park and other places, over twelve years he taught the Small Vehicle Agama sutras, saving the sravakas and pratyekabuddhas: this is the Agama period. After the Agama period, over eight years he taught the Vimalakirti, Srimala, Golden Light, and other great Mahayana sutras, broadly treating the four teachings and benefiting all faculties equally: this is the Vaipulya period. Thereafter, over twenty-two years, he taught the various Prajñā sutras, emphasizing the meaning that all dharmas are empty: this is the Prajñā period. In the last eight years he taught the Wondrous Dharma Lotus Sutra, gathering the three vehicles into the one Buddha vehicle. After the Lotus Sutra, as the Buddha was about to enter nirvāṇa, in the sala grove at Kusinagara, in a single day and night, he taught the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra, revealing the meaning of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, and making plain that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature, and that even icchantikas shall attain Buddhahood: this is the Lotus-Nirvāṇa period. There is a verse that sets out the course of the five periods: Avatamsaka first, three weeks; Agama twelve, Vaipulya eight; twenty-two years of Prajñā discourse; Lotus and Nirvāṇa together eight years more.

2. As to why the contemplation of the moon disc is not given. This dharma-gate is straightforward and sets aside expedient means, while the moon-disc contemplation employs expedient means: that is the first difference. This dharma-gate is a markless dharma, while the moon-disc contemplation has marks: that is the second difference. This dharma-gate transcends mind, intellect, and consciousness, while the moon-disc contemplation makes exclusive use of the sixth consciousness: that is the third difference. This dharma-gate is free of the grasped and the grasper, while in the moon-disc contemplation grasper and grasped are plainly present, exactly the opposite: that is the fourth difference. This dharma-gate enters directly into the ocean of the nature of true suchness, while the moon-disc contemplation, when first practiced, enters the solitary image object: that is the fifth difference. With these five differences, they are as far apart as heaven and earth. They must not be practiced together. The establishment of the moon-disc contemplation in the Sutra of Mind Ground Contemplation is for another class of faculties, and must not be spoken of in the same breath.

[The solitary image object] The images that float up depending on the thoughts of the sixth consciousness (the mental consciousness); they have no substance, and are merely illusions — for example, the object of flowers in the sky or of a hare’s horns.
Question: How does one illuminate the mind and see the nature?

Answer: Bodhidharma’s three phrases (“Outwardly put to rest all conditions; inwardly, no panting of the mind; make the mind like a wall”) cover everything. The Sixth Patriarch’s “not thinking of good, not thinking of evil” is precisely “outwardly putting to rest all conditions.” “At that very moment” is precisely “inwardly, no panting of the mind.” The words differ; how could there be two meanings? To reach “at that very moment” is simply to remain unmoved in one flavor, going on that way for a single thought or ten thousand years — what further dharma is there? “Which one is the original face of the Layman Ming?” is a question, and it is customarily called setting the trigger to work. (In the scholastic tradition this is called the ordinary trigger. The Buddha-Dharma takes the mind as the trigger, and so it is said: “When a single thought turns the trigger, one is the same as one who has attained from the beginning.”) The Chan school says: ordinary people have their mysterious gate tightly shut, and the lock of consciousness is hard to open. The trigger is the mysterious gate; one who is skilled casts a single phrase at it, strikes it into motion, and that person is at once awakened. Yet what matters most in this case is the three words “at that very moment” (that is, when one does not think of good or evil); this is the secret of the Chan school. If one who has aroused the mind can dwell in the mind in this way, then awakening is not far off. The patriarchs say: “‘At that very moment’ is called the time before the Buddha was born.” It is also called “dwelling at the summit, precious beyond compare.” Only when one can dwell in the mind in this way for several hours each day does one accord with the dharma. The conditions for the trigger to work will come of themselves; there is no need for someone to guide one. The patriarchs say: “If one can simply be ‘at that very moment,’ one need not worry about not awakening thoroughly.” This belongs to the secret essentials of the mind dharma, and may be practiced with strength.

[Not thinking of good, not thinking of evil] The Sixth Patriarch says: “If you wish to know the essentials of the mind, then do not think of anything good or evil at all, and you will naturally enter the substance of the pure mind, still and ever quiescent, its wondrous function as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.” [At that very moment] The Sixth Patriarch says: “Not thinking of good, not thinking of evil, at that very moment — which one is the original face of the Layman Ming?” (See
A Detailed Explanation of the Sixth Patriarch’s Platform Sutra
Question: One who has seen the nature is liberated and at ease, having already left the round of rebirth; but I do not know where, when this illusory body is cast off, such a one is reborn.

Answer: In any of the Pure Lands of the ten directions, one may be reborn according to one’s vow. If one vows to be born in the West, one will certainly attain the highest of the highest grades. If one is not born in a Pure Land, then among humans and gods one may lodge as one wishes, and it is equal to the Pure Land.
Question: For one who has not seen the nature, how should the mind be applied at the time of death, so as to escape the round of rebirth and attain liberation? I pray you to instruct me.

Answer: For one who has not seen the nature, at the approach of death, if he dwells peacefully in the bodhi mind, he will naturally attain liberation. (Chan Master Huangbo says: “Simply forget the mind, and become one with the dharmadhatu, and you will attain ease.” Note by Shu.)

Editor’s answer: When the method is correct, one will not stagnate on the path of practice. The passage above says, “if no thought arises, one simply watches” — the three words “simply watches” are the key: this is stillness and yet illumination. To be still without illuminating is to stagnate on the path of practice. Therefore, when a deluded thought arises, know it and do not follow it; when the deluded thought has ceased, keep watching as before — this is illumination, this is awareness. The correct method of mind contemplation is: illumination and yet stillness, stillness and yet illumination. The wonder of mind contemplation lies precisely in this: it is an unceasing awareness, perfuming ignorance with prajñā, until at last it becomes the great awakening. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “All Tathagatas, from their original ground of causation, rely on the perfect illumination of the pure enlightened mark, forever cut off ignorance, and only then accomplish the Buddha Way.”
Question: When I concentrate on contemplating the mind, I am without thought; how am I to do the work of “knowing it and not following it”?

Editor’s answer: When ordinary people have a deluded thought arise, they immediately sink into the delusion, and only after a while, or even quite a long while, do they realize they have been lost in deluded thinking. Your power of awareness is already fairly strong, so you are able to be without deluded thought when you concentrate on contemplating the mind; but as time goes on there will be slips, and at such moments deluded thoughts steal in through the gap. To do the work of “knowing it and not following it” is, the moment a deluded thought arises, to become aware of it at once and to be master of oneself, not turning with the deluded thought. If you go on in this way, as the days deepen the practice, then when your power of awareness is not only concentrated and continuous but also lasting, you will be able to dwell for long periods in the state of stillness and yet illumination, illumination and yet stillness, and further attain oneness in movement and stillness — this is the prelude to illuminating the mind and seeing the nature.

In general, the essential points of mind contemplation are: when there is a thought, contemplate the thought (know it and do not follow it); when there is no thought, contemplate emptiness (stillness and yet illumination). The Sixth Patriarch says: “If you wish to know the essentials of the mind, then do not think of anything good or evil at all, and you will naturally enter the substance of the pure mind, still and ever quiescent, its wondrous function as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.” (The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch.)
Question: When contemplating the mind, my head easily grows dizzy. What should I do?

Editor’s answer: This is caused by insufficient power of awareness. The foundation of mind contemplation is to have sufficient power of awareness. For this, first practice according to the preliminary section of The Chan of Awareness (awareness of movement, awareness of feeling, awareness of breathing, awareness of the present moment, and awareness of thoughts), so as to cultivate sufficient power of awareness, and then come back to contemplate the mind. In addition, at the beginning, the number of times you contemplate the mind each day should be greater, while the duration of each session should be shorter; seek practical effect.
Question: How does one accomplish “if a deluded mind arises, know it and do not follow it”?

Editor’s answer: How to accomplish “if a deluded mind arises, know it and do not follow it” — this is the key to the work of mind contemplation, and therefore there have always been many discussions of it. For example: the moment a thought arises, cry out at it; when a thought arises, give a stern awakening at once; if a deluded thought arises, ask it (ask the thought) where it comes from; and so on. Another example: observe the thoughts of the mind closely; if a deluded thought arises, simply watch it, and see how it will develop — if you really watch it in this way, the deluded thought will cease; if it arises again, watch it again in this way, and the deluded thought will cease; continue in this way until there is no thinking and no thought. The Sutra of the Buddha Treasury says: “The unsurpassed perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas is entirely without thinking and without thought.”

“Knowing it and not following it” is the result of a powerful awareness. Therefore one should contemplate the mind often and keep awareness turning without pause, so as to cultivate a powerful awareness. As for how to cultivate awareness, in
The Chan of Awareness
Awareness in Buddha-Recitation
and
Inquiring into Buddha-Recitation
the preliminary sections all discuss it in detail.

Here I shall introduce one more way of contemplating the mind: contemplating the mind in presence, that is, contemplating the mind while abiding in presence. By "presence" I mean abiding in awareness of this very moment, with no thought and no conceptualizing. When you are present, you have already stepped free of delusive thinking. So to contemplate the mind while in presence works exceedingly well.

When contemplating the mind in presence, if a delusive thought arises, it is because awareness has been lost; then with a sharp, clear wakefulness draw awareness back, and the delusive thought subsides. Remember: when a delusive thought arises, this is karma binding the mind; to be aware of it and be free of it, this is the mind turning karma around. Continue in this way, and when your practice deepens you will be able to remain for long periods in the state of no-thought, and if a delusive thought occasionally arises it will drift away and vanish; further, you will be able to remain long in the state of no-thought and know clearly that it is no-thought—what is called still yet illumining, illumining yet still.

To be aware of the present moment means to be aware of whatever can be known right here and now. For example: gazing steadily at a tree with no thought and no conceptualizing; listening to sounds from outside the window with no thought and no conceptualizing; being aware of your movements with no thought and no conceptualizing; sensing the presence of what is around you with no thought and no conceptualizing; even being aware of this very moment with no thought and no conceptualizing—all of these are abiding in presence. To use this method of contemplating the mind in presence, you must first train the skill of presence. Practice often both on and off the cushion, until you can enter the state of presence at any time and in any place, even if it does not last very long.
Question: How should one train the skill of presence?
Answer: When you study
Awareness of Buddha-Recitation

, the chapter "Awareness of the Present Moment" in the preliminary section speaks specifically of presence. Moreover, the chapters in that section on "Awareness of Movement," "Awareness of Feeling," "Awareness of the Breath," and "Awareness of Thoughts" are each a single aspect of the skill of presence. Now that you know what presence is, simply put these techniques to use together, then extend, deepen, and consolidate them.
Question: When one contemplates the mind while in presence, which is primary and which is secondary?

Answer: At the beginning, let presence be primary and contemplation of the mind secondary; in this way it is easy to sustain. Once your practice is deep, contemplation of the mind should become primary, and it too should be sustained, with the strength and depth of contemplation gradually increased. Sometimes this situation arises: it is hard to carry on with contemplation of the mind as primary. Then let presence be primary and contemplation secondary, holding the last line of defense so that no delusive thought arises. When conditions improve, return to contemplation of the mind as primary and presence as secondary.
Question: In contemplating the mind in presence, should the eyes be open or closed?
Answer: Either is fine. The essential point of contemplating the mind in presence is this: not to let a single thought slip past, to see through every thought.
[Not to let it slip past] Not to be deceived by it. [To see through it] Not to be shrouded by it, not to follow its coaxing, not to take it as something real.

Question: Generally speaking, I do not give rise to a single thought, but when certain matters come up I lose control, even becoming emotional, and afterwards I cannot be calm for a long time. What should I do?

Answer: In practice, if you can discover a problem, you will find a way to solve it; once the problem is solved, you have taken a great step forward on the bodhi path. So it is very important to discover problems in time. As for the problem you raise, there is a wonderful method: observe your thoughts, feelings, emotions, and reactions—your liking and disliking, your grasping and rejecting.
The
Vegetable Roots Discourse
says:
The ancients said:
Bamboo shadows sweep the steps, yet the dust does not stir; the moon's disk pierces the pool, yet the water keeps no trace.
Our Confucians said:
However swift the stream, the scene stays still; however thick the falling blossoms, the mind stays free.
If one always holds to this intent in responding to affairs and meeting people, how free the body and mind will be.

One should practice this often in daily life, doing it in different settings; once it becomes familiar, it will be ready to hand the moment something arises. Practiced over and over in this way, you will reach the state in which the mind is like a wall, and the ten thousand dharmas find no entry. Patriarch Bodhidharma said:
"Cut off all outward conditions, within have no panting, let the mind be like a wall; then one may enter the Way."
Question: How can old karma be dissolved?
Answer: On this, Master Hanshan gave the following instruction:

"The ancients taught people: 'Dissolve old karma as it comes; never create new calamity.' For beings heavy with karma, the Buddha opened the single gate of repentance, which is the most effective means of escape from suffering. The verse says: 'All offenses are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can dispel them. If one wishes to repent, sit upright and contemplate the true mark.' This is the main practice; all else is auxiliary.

"The self-nature of sentient beings is equal to the Buddha's; it is originally undefiled, and has no marks of birth or death, coming or going. But because of the initial non-awakening, one is confused about one's own nature, and this is called ignorance. Because of ignorance, all kinds of delusive thoughts arise, all kinds of inversion, creating all kinds of karma, and falsely grasping the suffering of birth and death within the three realms. All this is ignorance: not understanding one's own mind, one turns with delusive thought. It is like a person fast asleep who has evil dreams—all kinds of scenes, all kinds of terror, unbearable sufferings. When he wakes, he seeks for the things in the dream and cannot find them at all. Thus sentient beings fall into the dream of ignorance, turn with delusive inversion, create all kinds of karma, and bring suffering upon themselves. Seen with waking eyes, how could any of those inverted states be found?"

"Even now, within the dream of ignorance, how can old karma be dissolved? One must use the light of wisdom to shine through and shatter ignorance, and truly believe that one's own mind is originally pure, not driven by delusive inversion; then karmas have no cause, for delusive thought is the cause of all karma. Why is this so? From beginningless time one has been confused about one's own mind, and life after life has created all kinds of karma with the delusive mind. Karmic habits accumulate within the eighth consciousness, irrigated by the water of ignorance, causing these evil seeds to sprout as karmic shoots; this is the root of offense, and from it all evil karma arises."

"Now if you wish to dissolve old karma, you must first bring forth the great light of wisdom to shatter ignorance, and not allow delusive thoughts to sprout and quietly grow. If at the very place where a delusive thought arises you cut it off with a single thought, then the long-accumulated root of karma is dissolved on the spot. As it is said: 'Do not fear the arising of a thought; fear only that awareness comes too late.' If awareness and illumination are even slightly late, you will be turned about by it. If in daily life, at the place where thoughts arise, you become aware of each thought and dissolve each thought, this is what is meant by 'all offenses are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can dispel them.' For the darkness of ignorance can be broken only by wisdom; this is what is meant by 'wisdom can dispel them.' If day and night without cease you diligently observe, never letting a thought pass, and at the very place where delusive thought arises you investigate it to the end until there is no mark of arising at all, looking and looking, in the end it cannot be found. When this becomes thoroughly familiar over a long time, your own mind will be pure and without anything; a mind without anything is the true mark. If one constantly contemplates this mind, what delusive thought could remain and what karma could lodge there?"
(For the annotations, see the article
Dissolving Old Karma
in full)

blocks.text: 3. What Kind of Mind Is Contemplated

inline.s: The Treatise on the Generation of the Bodhi Mind says: "When a delusive mind arises, know it and do not follow it; when the delusive subsides, the source of mind is empty and still, and all virtues are complete, with inexhaustible wondrous function." Such is the wonder of the mind-nature. That we do not accord with it in ordinary times is because we are covered by delusive thoughts; this is the mind of ignorance. On what does ignorance depend? It arises depending on suchness. To contemplate the mind of ignorance is to contemplate the mind of suchness; to contemplate the mind-nature is to contemplate the mind of ignorance. Why so? Because suchness is the essence of thought, and thought is the function of suchness. When contemplation brings one to samādhi, this is the samādhi of suchness, king of all samādhis, and so it is called the supreme concentration.

What kind of mind is contemplated? The answer: the mind of ignorance. Why not contemplate the true mind? Because the true mind, since beginningless time, has been perfumed and obscured by ignorance and cannot manifest. Where does this ignorance abide? It abides upon the true mind, like glue stuck to lacquer, unable to be freed; hence it is called ignorance of the ground of abiding. This ignorance is the root of birth and death; if a single portion of it is not exhausted, birth and death continue forever; hence it is called fundamental ignorance. One who studies the Dharma and seeks the truth should begin right here at this ignorance of the ground of abiding. Why? To cut a tree without severing its root, or to cauterize a disease without finding the point, brings not the slightest benefit. Therefore the followers of the Two Vehicles and the bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings cut off the four abidings of ignorance but do not know the ignorance of the ground of abiding; they can escape fragmentary birth and death, but in the end they still undergo transformational birth and death. The followers of the One Vehicle begin from contemplating the mind, in order to break the ignorance of the ground of abiding and forever end birth and death; this is what is called drawing blood from the throat—the wondrous secret of attaining Buddhahood, the truest and most real. Elder Li said: "Fundamental ignorance is precisely the fundamental unmoved wisdom." Yongjia said: "The true nature of ignorance is the Buddha-nature." The Tiantai school says: "The essence of ignorance is precisely illumination, precisely the true mark, precisely the Dharma-nature." The scriptures contain countless citations, all pointing to precisely this.

At first, contemplate the mind of arising and ceasing, neither grasping nor attaching, neither following nor cutting off; or else simply rest the thoughts and forget considerations—the two methods are one. (The Essentials of the Transmission of Mind says: "Rest the thoughts and forget considerations, and the Buddha appears of himself.") Constantly contemplate and illumine: this is prajñā perfuming ignorance. Once ignorance is broken, the dharma-body instantly appears. One leaps straight into the Tathagata's ground, and without passing through kalpas of ascetic practice one attains the dharma-body; hence this is called the perfect and sudden teaching.

Choose a quiet place and sit in the full lotus position. (First place the left toes over the right thigh, then the right toes over the left thigh, so that the soles of both feet turn upward on the two thighs. The hands likewise: the right over the left, resting palm-up on the crossed legs. This is the full lotus, called the auspicious sitting posture. Or one may use the half lotus, with the right foot over the left; this is also acceptable. There is also the posture for subduing demons: first place the right toes over the left thigh, then the left toes over the right thigh, with the hands left over right; the Chan school has largely transmitted this posture, but each person may choose for himself. For the elderly, sitting upright is also acceptable.) Let the body be upright, unmoving and unshaking. Form the samādhi mudra with the hands. (Both hands palm up, the right resting on the left, the tips of the two thumbs touching, placed below the navel upon the crossed legs. This is called the samādhi-of-the-Dharma-realm mudra; it can dispel all wild and delusive thinking.) Close the eyes and cut off light, close the mouth and let the teeth meet, place the tongue against the upper palate, let the nose be aligned with the navel. The spine should be straight as a brush. Let the two shoulders be level, neither leaning nor tilting; sit in this way.

Those busy with affairs must sit at least once every day, for at least half an hour each time. If one can sit two or three times, for one or two hours each time, that is excellent. The more and the longer, the better. When sitting, loosen your clothing and belt and be calm and unhurried; do not sit in a draft, and do not sit on a full stomach. After sitting, move the body slowly, open the mouth and eyes gradually, rub the hands warm, and massage the face, abdomen, waist, legs, and feet; rest a while, then rise from the seat.
Question: Because of physical limitations I cannot sit in the lotus position. What should I do?

Answer: You may sit cross-legged loosely (with the legs simply crossed), or sit upright on a chair or stool; the posture should be one in which the back is straight (but the chest not thrust out too much) and which can be held steadily and for a long time.
Question: When contemplating the mind, must one form the mudra?
Answer: One may contemplate the mind without forming the mudra.
Question: When contemplation of the mind is finished, to whom should the merit be dedicated?

Answer: Contemplating the mind is itself dedication to suchness and the ultimate reality; since the Buddha of others and one's own Buddha are one and the same substance, what further doubt is there? If you are newly entering the Dharma gate, dedicating to the Buddha of others is also acceptable.

Contemplating the mind requires unbroken continuity; it must not be forgotten. The ancients said: "When the single thought is absent (the single thought of contemplation being absent), one is no different from a dead man." The essential secret of contemplating the mind is this: to be able to contemplate at all times and in all places, to be contemplating at all times and in all places—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, never apart from the present thought, always being the master. When your practice reaches this stage, its wonder is deep, vast, and boundless; as one who drinks water knows for himself whether it is cold or warm.
Question: How should one practice while in activity?

Answer: Just as in stillness. Before one is skilled in contemplating the mind, there is a distinction between movement and stillness. Once one is skilled, movement and stillness are no different. The Chan school says: "Among a thousand and ten thousand people, be as if there were not a single person; amid the turmoil of ten thousand affairs, be as if there were not a single affair." From this we know that movement and stillness are one. Beginners have not yet attained concentration, so the patriarchs taught people to keep and carry—meaning that in responding to affairs and meeting people one should always keep and carry this method of contemplating the mind. You need not worry; with long practice you will understand of yourself. Let me cite a passage from the Lankavatara Sutra for your use. The sutra says: "Contemplate all dharmas as having no self-nature. They are like clouds in the sky, like a wheel of fire, like a city of the gandharvas, like a dream, like a flame, like the moon in the water, like things seen in a dream—not apart from one's own mind. Because of beginningless false views, one takes them as external. Having contemplated thus, one cuts off the conditions of discrimination and is also free of the names and meanings grasped by the delusive mind. One knows that body and things, together with the place where one dwells, are all states of the storehouse consciousness. There is no grasper or grasped, and no arising, abiding, or ceasing. Thinking thus, one dwells in it constantly without letting it go." Savor this passage in your heart, and deep faith will arise. That you are unable to do so has two causes: first, the teachings are not yet familiar; second, the power of concentration is not yet developed. In short, walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, one must never be apart from contemplating the mind.

Question: I have already reached single-mindedness in Buddha-recitation, and now I am studying The Heart Essentials of Baiyun in order to understand the mind and see the nature. But I cannot sustain contemplation of the mind, and it is still harder to be never apart from it while walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. What should I do?

Answer: It can be done in two steps. First, accomplish this: while walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, let Buddha-recitation be uninterrupted and undistracted. Then, raise a single phrase of the Buddha's name and contemplate the mind for a while; raise a single phrase of the Buddha's name and contemplate the mind for a while—gradually making the transition to contemplating the mind entirely, so that walking, standing, sitting, and lying down are never apart from contemplation of the mind.

blocks.text: Chapter Four: The Essential Tenets of the One Vehicle

inline.s: [One Vehicle] The only teaching that can bring people to Buddhahood. "Vehicle" means a carriage; it is a metaphor for the Buddha's teaching, which can carry people across to the farther shore of nirvāṇa, and so it is called a "vehicle." The Lotus Sutra

Chapter Two, "Expedient Means," says: "In the buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the Dharma of the One Vehicle; there is no second and no third, except as the Buddha's expedient teaching." It also says: "Only this one matter is true; the other two are not real." The Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra says: "The perfect and sudden teaching is the One Buddha Vehicle." [No second and no third, except as the Buddha's expedient teaching] There is no Two Vehicles and no Three Vehicles. The Two Vehicles and the Three Vehicles are the Buddha's expedient teaching. [Two Vehicles] the vehicle of the shravakas and the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas. [Three Vehicles] the vehicle of the shravakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, and the vehicle of the bodhisattvas. The shravaka vehicle is also called the small vehicle, the pratyekabuddha vehicle the middle vehicle, and the bodhisattva vehicle the great vehicle.
[Noble wisdom] The wisdom that directly illumines the ultimate truth and is far removed from false discrimination is called noble wisdom.

[The Buddha said: Mahamati! The bodhisattva-mahasattvas, relying on the noble teachings, are without discrimination. Dwelling alone in quiet seclusion, they observe self-awakening; not awakened by another, free of the views of discrimination, they advance upward step by step and enter the Tathagata's ground. Such practice is called the marks of the practice of self-realization of noble wisdom.]
(Lankavatara Sutra)
[Marks of practice] The appearances of what is done by body and mind.
In this passage the Buddha answers concerning the marks of the practice of self-realization of noble wisdom; it is the root of the sudden teaching. I shall now explain it sentence by sentence:

[Sudden teaching] The teaching that "points directly at the source, without passing through stages, seeing the nature and attaining Buddhahood." Its purport is: sudden awakening to one's own nature, originally pure, originally complete, one's own nature being the Buddha.
Relying on the noble teachings"

—relying on the teaching transmitted from Buddha to Buddha of old. Its point of entry is precisely the meaning of Patriarch Bodhidharma's three lines: "Cut off all outward conditions, within have no panting, let the mind be like a wall." (This verse has four lines in all; the fourth line, "then one may enter the Way," is the fruit, and the practice lies only in the first three lines.) "Relying" means to guard this method closely, not permitting the slightest deviation, in the hope of thorough awakening.
[Cutting off all outward conditions]
"Outward" means to stop all clinging to conditions. [Within have no panting] "Within" means the single mind is unmoved. [The mind like a wall] No arising of discrimination.
Without discrimination"

—this sentence is the true track of practice, most important! Most important! What is the discriminating mind? It is the sixth consciousness. When faculties and objects meet, the mind arises, or one recollects past and future. Now if one wishes to enter the Dharma, one should first stop this mind and not give rise to discrimination
I shall now explain it in three parts:
1. When first entering contemplation, first set down all matters of faculties and objects, past and future—this is "
cutting off all outward conditions

." The teaching schools call it cultivating cessation; the Chan school calls it resting the mind and ceasing considerations. Once delusive thought subsides, the mind becomes still; when the mind is still, prajñā is born. The ancients compared it to "a pearl emitting light that shines back upon the pearl itself." The pearl is the mind of nirvāṇa (nirvāṇa being stillness); the light is wisdom (wisdom being prajñā). "The light is born from the pearl" means that prajñā is born from the mind of nirvāṇa. "Shining back upon the pearl itself" means that the light of prajñā shines back upon the dharma-body. The Treatise on the Manifest Teaching says: "Nirvāṇa is unborn, yet it can give rise to prajñā." Hence resting conditions is the most important point of entry.
2. Once outward conditions have been stilled, prajñā gradually arises. At this point one should let the single mind be unmoved, and so it is said, "
within have no panting
" (panting means moving). This unmoving state is precisely no-thought, no-abiding, and no-mark. Although there are four aspects (unmoving, no-thought, no-abiding, no-mark), their practice is one.
The mind like a wall

." This sentence describes the mark of being without discrimination and unmoved; it is the most crucial point of all, being the practice of detachment from consciousness. What the Chan school calls "like a great dead man, forever cut off from remaining thoughts," and again "revived after extinction, you cannot be deceived"—this is precisely that state. Treasure it! Treasure it! The withered tree puts forth blossoms; herein it lies.

Patriarch Bodhidharma's three lines ("Cut off all outward conditions, within have no panting, let the mind be like a wall") encompass everything. The Sixth Patriarch's "not thinking of good, not thinking of evil" is precisely "cutting off all outward conditions." "Just at such a time" is precisely "within have no panting." The words differ; how could there be two meanings? When one reaches "just at such a time," there is simply unmoved singleness; practice it as one thought lasting ten thousand years—what other dharma is there? "Which is the original face of the Venerable Ming?" is a question, and it is called triggering the mechanism. (In the Buddhadharma the mind is the mechanism; hence it is said: one thought turns the mechanism, and one is immediately equal to the original attainment.) The Chan school says: for ordinary people the mysterious gate is tightly shut and the lock of consciousness is hard to open. The mechanism is the mysterious gate; one who excels casts a single phrase at it, striking the mechanism into motion, and the other immediately awakens. But the most important part of this public case is the three words "at such a time" (that is, when not thinking of good or evil); this is the secret of the Chan school. If those who have aroused the aspiration can abide in the mind in this way, awakening is not far off. The patriarch said: "'At such a time' is called the time before the Buddha was born, and is also called dwelling at the summit; it is incomparably precious." If one can abide in the mind thus for several hours a day, that is only just in accordance with the Dharma. The causes and conditions for triggering the mechanism will come of themselves; there is no need for anyone to guide you. The patriarch said: "If only you can be at such a time, you need not worry that you will not awaken thoroughly." This belongs to the secret essentials of the mind method; you may put it into practice with all your strength.
Dwelling alone in quiet seclusion"

—this sentence has two meanings. First, "dwelling alone" means that one person practices exclusively, without taking companions; the Avatamsaka Sutra says, "One alone arouses the aspiration, not seeking companions," which is this. From this we can know the error of the recent practice of forming groups to sit intensive retreats of seven days. Second, "quiet seclusion" means choosing a pure and quiet place, far from clamor. "Dwelling alone" is spoken with regard to people; "quiet seclusion" with regard to place.
Observing self-awakening"
