—if this sentence is explained literally, there is an observing mind and an alerting mind, and the mind's threads are in confusion—what sort of practice would that be? I say it is not so, and explain it in three parts: 1. explaining "observe"; 2. explaining "discern"; 3. explaining "self-awakening."

1. Explaining "observe." To observe means to contemplate the mind. What kind of mind is contemplated? The mind of ignorance. Why not contemplate the true mind? Because the true mind, since beginningless time, has been perfumed and obscured by ignorance and cannot manifest. Where does this ignorance abide? It abides upon the true mind, like glue stuck to lacquer, unable to be freed; hence it is called ignorance of the ground of abiding. This ignorance is the root of birth and death; if a single portion of it is not exhausted, birth and death continue forever; hence it is called fundamental ignorance. One who studies the Dharma and seeks the truth should begin right here at this ignorance of the ground of abiding. Why? To cut a tree without severing its root, or to cauterize a disease without finding the point, brings not the slightest benefit. Therefore the followers of the Two Vehicles and the bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings cut off the four abidings of ignorance but do not know the ignorance of the ground of abiding; they can escape fragmentary birth and death, but in the end still undergo transformational birth and death. (There are two kinds of rebirth: first, the twelve links of causation within the three realms, undergoing fragmentary birth and death; second, the twelve links of causation outside the three realms, undergoing transformational birth and death.) The followers of the One Vehicle begin from contemplating the mind, in order to break the ignorance of the ground of abiding and forever end birth and death; this is what is called drawing blood from the throat—the wondrous secret of attaining Buddhahood, the truest and most real. Elder Li said: "Fundamental ignorance is precisely the fundamental unmoved wisdom." Yongjia said: "The true nature of ignorance is the Buddha-nature." The Tiantai school says: "The essence of ignorance is precisely illumination, precisely the true mark, precisely the Dharma-nature." The scriptures contain countless citations, all pointing to precisely this.

At first, contemplate the mind of arising and ceasing, neither grasping nor attaching, neither following nor cutting off; or else simply rest the mind and cease considerations—the two methods are one. Constantly contemplate and illumine: this is prajñā perfuming ignorance. Once ignorance is broken, the dharma-body instantly appears. One leaps straight into the Tathagata's ground, and without passing through kalpas of ascetic practice one attains the dharma-body; hence this is called the perfect and sudden teaching.

2. Explaining "discern." To discern means to supervise. When contemplating the mind there are two kinds of supervision: the first is right mindfulness, the second is right knowing. Right mindfulness means single-mindedly guarding the object of contemplation, not permitting a second thought to arise. The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching says: "Focus it on one place, and there is nothing that cannot be accomplished." The Sutra of the Adamantine Samādhi says: "Focus it on one place, and all conditions are cut off." To focus on one place is right mindfulness. The ancients said: "If one does not guard the mind and yet attains Buddhahood, such a thing is impossible." Right knowing is as the Awakening of Faith says: "If the mind scatters, gather it back and abide in right mindfulness." If one does not gather it back, ignorance increases. This supervisory office has these two powers. In the Chan gate there is a simile: "The one who sits in meditation is like an official, and outside the gate stand two guards; these two guards are named Right Mindfulness and Right Knowing." This may be called a good simile.

3. Explaining "self-awakening." Self-awakening means that this supervisory office constantly causes right mindfulness to guard the mind and right knowing to gather the mind, not permitting indulgence.
Not awakened by another"

not awakened by another means that when one reaches great, thorough awakening, all dharmas naturally manifest from the mind and are not bestowed by another. This is what is meant by the wisdom without a teacher, the natural wisdom; it is the unarisen dharma-patience.
Free of the views of discrimination"
this sentence is explained in two parts: 1. freedom from discrimination; 2. freedom from views.

First, explaining freedom from discrimination. This discriminating mind differs from that mentioned above: the former was the ordinary person's clinging to outward objects, while this is the practitioner's clinging to the object of contemplation. Otherwise it would be repetition. How does one cling to the object of contemplation? This is a markless dharma, and marks are not permitted. If a surpassing state appears, or an image of a Buddha or bodhisattva appears, or the sound of teaching is heard, these are all demonic states and should be strictly rejected. If one grasps them, the discriminating mind has arisen and one enters the demon's net; hence it is said, be free of discrimination.

Next, explaining freedom from views. "Views" means the various views, which obstruct people so that they cannot see the Way. The various views are sometimes spoken of as the five views (the view of the body, the extreme view, the evil view, the view of grasping views, and the view of grasping precepts and prohibitions), and sometimes as the sixty-two views. To give rise to views means that in contemplation a state appears, and one thinks it inferior or superior, or in accord with a certain sutra, or corresponding to a certain samādhi, and takes it as a noble state; this is precisely a view, and one will surely enter the demon's net. The Sutra of the Buddha's Treasury says: "Arousing the bodhi mind is simply a matter of freedom. Freedom from what? First, freedom from desire; second, freedom from views." "Desire is ignorance; views are recollection." The Huayan Treatise says: "Where views are present, one is ordinary; when feeling is gone, one is Buddha." The Fourth Patriarch said: "No need to seek the truth; only cease views." The fault of views may be called extremely grave, and so one must be free of them.

[Sixty-two views] These are the evil views of non-Buddhists, which take the five aggregates as the object of views and take form-dharmas and mind-dharmas as their root. The sixty-two views are: taking the five aggregates of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as object, one gives rise to views of permanence, impermanence, both permanence and impermanence, and neither permanence nor impermanence—four times five makes twenty views; taking the five aggregates as object, one gives rise to views of having an end, having no end, having both an end and no end, and having neither an end nor no end—these twenty views, added to the above, make forty views; taking the five aggregates as object, one gives rise to views of having coming and going, having no coming and going, having both coming and going and no coming and going, and having neither coming and going nor no coming and going—these twenty views, added to the above, make sixty views; to these sixty views are added the two root views of form and mind, making sixty-two views in all.
Advancing upward step by step"

advancing upward step by step means that when contemplation of the mind reaches this stage, one should apply greater diligence, practice without interruption, and grow in secret, beyond all measure. "Upward step by step" means, for instance, that from the stage of faith one advances to the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten dedications, and the ten grounds. Rising higher at every step is called advancing upward step by step.
Enter the Tathagata's ground"

the Tathagata's ground is the fruit of great, thorough awakening. When contemplation becomes thoroughly skilled, one enters without being conscious of entering; hence this Dharma gate is called Tathagata Chan.
Such practice is called the marks of the practice of self-realization of noble wisdom"

the marks of the practice of self-realization of noble wisdom means the marks of practicing the noble wisdom inwardly realized by oneself. "Self-realization of noble wisdom" was translated in the Song as "self-awakened noble wisdom." To realize is to see. Awakening is realization, realization is seeing; the two names are not different. This is precisely
fundamental wisdom

, which has many names in the sutras and treatises; the Avatamsaka calls it universal radiant wisdom, which is the function of the nature's own stillness and illumination. The Avatamsaka says: "Knowing all dharmas as the self-nature of mind, one accomplishes the body of wisdom, not awakened by another." This is speaking of this meaning. When this wisdom is accomplished, one becomes a Buddha. The Lankavatara says: "The Tathagata takes wisdom as body, for wisdom is the substance." It also says: "The Buddha is neither a person nor aggregates, but only undefiled wisdom." This wisdom is the practitioner's enjoyment-body Buddha.

[Undefiled] "Defilement" is another name for affliction, meaning leakage. Afflictions such as greed and hatred leak and flow out day and night through the six sense gates of eye, ear, and so on, without cease; this is called defilement. "Undefiled" means without affliction. [Undefiled wisdom] is the pure wisdom free of affliction and defilement. Cutting off delusion and realizing the truth is the function of this wisdom.

blocks.text: 2. The Marks of the Practice of the One Vehicle

inline.s: [What are called the marks of the practice of the One Vehicle? They mean attaining the realization and knowledge of the One Vehicle Way. What is called knowing the One Vehicle Way? It means being free of the discrimination of grasper and grasped, and abiding as it truly is. Mahamati! This One Vehicle Way, except for the Tathagata, cannot be attained by non-Buddhists, the Two Vehicles, Brahma kings, and others.]
(Lankavatara Sutra)

In this passage the Buddha answers concerning the marks of the contemplative practice of the followers of the One Vehicle. Since Mahamati thought the practice here might differ from the preceding chapter, the Buddha answered with
freedom from discrimination
, which is still the same in meaning as the preceding chapter. I shall now explain it briefly.
What are
"the marks of the practice of the One Vehicle"

? "Marks of practice" means the marks of the mind abiding without abiding. "The marks of the practice of the One Vehicle" means the marks of settling the mind in the practice of the One Vehicle Dharma.
Free of the discrimination of grasper and grasped"
—the grasper is the seeing aspect, the grasped is the perceived aspect; when grasper and grasped are distinctly present, that is discrimination, and one should be free of it.

[Four aspects] The four functions of the substance of consciousness. 1. The perceived aspect: "perceived" means mark and appearance, that is, the images of outward objects reflected in the mind-consciousness. 2. The seeing aspect: "seeing" means seeing and illumining; by the seeing aspect one sees and illumines it and knows it. 3. The self-realizing aspect: here the mind-consciousness's own substance verifies whether the seeing of the "seeing aspect" is erroneous or not; this function of verification is called the "self-realizing aspect." 4. The aspect of realizing the self-realization: after the self-realizing aspect has verified, it again verifies whether its result is erroneous or not; this act of verifying again is called the "aspect of realizing the self-realization." "Four aspects" means four parts. Although four aspects are spoken of, in fact they are still one substance: the self-realizing aspect and the aspect of realizing the self-realization are the substance of consciousness, while the perceived aspect and the seeing aspect are the functions of consciousness.
Abiding as it truly is"

—if taken as a noun, "as" means suchness, "truly" means the true mark, and the phrase means abiding in suchness and the true mark. If taken as a verb, "as" is the "as" of "thus"; one abides according to the true mark. "Abiding according to the true mark" means not abiding in faculties, objects, or consciousness, but abiding in the principle of suchness. This meaning is of the greatest importance, and I should cite scripture to establish it. The Sutra of the Adamantine Samādhi says: "The principle of suchness is complete with all dharmas. Good man, abiding in the principle of suchness (that is, abiding as it truly is), one crosses the sea of the three sufferings (that is, the sufferings of the three realms)." It also says: "If one abides in the great ocean (a simile for the Buddha-fruit), one encompasses all streams (a simile for the Three Vehicles); if one abides in the single flavor (a simile for the one Dharma of guarding the mind), one contains all flavors (a simile for faith, abiding, practice, dedication, and the grounds)." The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra says: "Suppose a person bathes in the great ocean; know that this person has already used the waters of all rivers, springs, and pools. The bodhisattva-mahasattva is likewise: having cultivated this adamantine samādhi, know that he has already cultivated all other samādhis." To contemplate the mind and enter the principle is to cultivate the adamantine samādhi; when this samādhi is accomplished, all samādhis are without exception complete—hence it is perfect and sudden.

[True mark] This is the true mark of all dharmas. The so-called "true mark" is the real situation; "the true mark of all dharmas" is the real situation of all dharmas. The Sutra of the Buddha's Treasury says: "What is called the true mark of all dharmas? It means that all dharmas are ultimately empty, without anything whatsoever." The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra says: "All dharmas are like illusory marks; the Tathagata, amid them, by the power of expedient means, is undefiled and unattached. Why? Such is the nature of the Buddhadharma." The Lotus Sutra says: "The bodhisattva-mahasattva contemplates all dharmas as empty, as the true mark, neither inverted, nor moved, nor retreating, nor turning." [Such is the nature of things] Naturally so. [Faith, abiding, practice, dedication, grounds] That is, among the fifty-two stages, the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, ten dedications, and ten grounds. [Fifty-two stages] The stages a bodhisattva passes through from ordinary being to Buddhahood, fifty-two in all: the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, ten dedications, ten grounds, equal awakening, and wonderful awakening.

Also the Sutra of the Adamantine Samādhi says: "The bodhisattva Great Strength said: What is meant by preserving the three and guarding the one, and entering Tathagata Chan? The Buddha said: Preserving the three means preserving the three emancipations. Guarding the one means guarding the one mind of suchness. Entering Tathagata Chan means contemplating the mind of suchness in principle; entering such a ground is entering the ultimate reality." The ultimate reality is the dharma-body of suchness. "Preserving the three emancipations" means not realizing the three emancipations. Guarding the one mind of suchness is Tathagata Chan. The words of the sutra are this clear, yet people in the world do not know it. How sad!

[The three liberations] The full name is “the three gates of liberation”: first, liberation through emptiness; second, liberation through the markless; third, liberation through wishlessness. These are three kinds of samādhi.

The Avatamsaka Sutra says: “At the first arousing of the mind one attains right enlightenment, accomplishes the body of wisdom, and is not awakened by another.” This is precisely that state. The Diamond Sutra says: “One should give rise to the mind without abiding anywhere.” To abide nowhere is precisely the “abiding in accordance with reality” of this sutra; and the arising of that mind is precisely the self-realization of noble wisdom manifesting before one.

This sutra (the Lankavatara Sutra) says in verse: “Abandoning all of these (all the various meditations listed above are to be abandoned), and dwelling where no object is conditioned, such a one can enter the true and actual mark of thusness.” To dwell where no object is conditioned is to abide in accordance with reality. To enter the true mark is the Tathagata Chan. The Nirvāṇa Sutra says: “All sentient beings are originally complete in the wisdom-nature free of outflows.” Cultivated thus, there is no one who does not realize it. Why then do people not believe, and willingly sink down into the three realms? An ancient worthy said: “Wonderfully find the gate, and becoming a Buddha is not apart from the present thought. Lose its purport, and cultivating the cause only wears one out through many lives.” Think on this! Think on this!
The Avatamsaka Sutra says in verse:
If one would know the Buddha’s realm, let the mind be pure as space;
Far from false thinking and all grasping, let it rest in unobstructed place.
If one would gain the Tathagata’s wisdom, from all false discrimination turn away;
Seeing being and non-being both as equal, one soon becomes the world’s guide and stay.

blocks.text: Appendix One: Postscript to Essentials of the Buddha-Dharma

inline.s: The Buddha-Dharma is vast and great, and its root lies in the mind. The gates of practice are immeasurable, and their essence lies in contemplation.
“Directly contemplate your own mind; see the nature and become a Buddha”
— this is the essential purport of Essentials of the Buddha-Dharma as taught by my teacher, Mr. Liu of Zhongjiang.

Mr. Liu was thoroughly versed in the scriptural canon and deeply studied doctrine and contemplation. He dwelt in seclusion in the deep mountains, abiding in simplicity and stillness. He was already seventy-three years old, yet his spirit was hale and he taught without weariness; whenever the neighboring towns invited him, he lectured without cease. He often said: To study Buddhism without seeking to see the nature is to be an outside path attached to Buddhism; to aspire to see the nature — that alone is to be a son of the Buddha. If one would seek to see the nature, one must contemplate the mind. To contemplate or not to contemplate is truly the critical juncture of life and death for one who studies the Dharma. The people of the Three Vehicles contemplate the mind, but not deeply and not thoroughly; only the people of the One Vehicle suddenly see the original nature and suddenly become Tathagatas. Therefore, in teaching people, he would always have them set everything down and contemplate their own mind. Those who followed this teaching, many attained awakening.

I, Hongshu, heard the Way late in life; through the introduction of Mr. Zhang Xinruo I was at last permitted to be counted among his disciples. Over fourteen years I received every kind of instruction and guidance, led on step by step, earnestly and warmly. He once taught me: In studying the Mahayana, take the understanding of the one mind as the root. If one truly understands the one mind, then the three insights, the six spiritual powers, the ten powers, and the four fearlessnesses come without being sought. Therefore it is said: of all dharmas, the mind is foremost. The spiritual powers are complete in everyone; gain the mother, and the child comes of itself. He also said: The Larger Amitābha Sutra speaks of rebirth in three grades, all of them grounded in arousing the bodhi mind. One who does not understand the four wisdoms is born only in the borderland city of doubt. The Contemplation Sutra says: “This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha.” All of these take the understanding of the one mind as their root. The one mind is hard to believe in (the one mind is one’s own true mind), and to understand it is harder still (one understands only on seeing the nature); if one can understand it, one enters the stage of no further learning. He also said: Cultivating contemplation and holding the name — the two methods are equal. One who cultivates contemplation sees clearly; one who holds the name understands only when he reaches one mind undisturbed. These are all the true and definitive meaning of the Buddha-Dharma, and everyone who studies Buddhism ought to know them.

But I, Hongshu, am dull by nature. Though I received the method of the Pure Land contemplation, I never came to practice it exclusively; and meeting with the chaos of the times, I had no leisure to dwell in peace, so that to this day I have accomplished nothing — my shame is great. Lately, because my strength has failed and my nature inclines to what is simple, I again asked him to grant me an essential method for my practice; and then he taught me “to arouse the ultimate bodhi mind.” He told me: To arouse the mind is to arouse the mind that sees the nature, that is, to contemplate the pure mind of one’s own nature. The Avatamsaka says: “At the first arousing of the mind one attains right enlightenment.” The Nirvāṇa Sutra says: “To be able to contemplate the nature of the mind is called the highest concentration.” Both speak of this. Even the samādhi of thusness of the Treatise on the Awakening of Faith, the recitation of the Buddha by means of reality of the Pure Land school, and the Tathagata Chan of Master Bodhidharma — different names, the same reality — are all contemplation of the mind. Then I knew that the two gates of Chan and Pure Land were originally one dharma. Soon after, he sent me three lecture records; what he transmitted is all there, and in greater detail. Reading them over, my admiration was endless. I then carefully arranged and edited them and submitted them to him for approval, entitling them Essentials of the Buddha-Dharma. I raised funds to have it printed for the benefit of students.

In my humble view this book is concise in word and refined in meaning, pointing to the One Vehicle. It reveals the principle of the two emptinesses and the entry into dependent origination. It arouses the bodhi mind and penetrates to the original nature. It clarifies the profound meaning of the Lankavatara and lays bare the root of the sudden teaching. Measuring out the essentials of the sages who went before, it is a shortcut to becoming a Buddha. It is what is meant by “accomplishing the body of wisdom, not awakened by another,” and it lets out every profound purport of the scriptural canon without remainder. If a student can practice according to it, then in time, becoming thoroughly familiar, he will suddenly awaken, clarify the mind and see the nature, and in a single thought realize it at once. How could the greatness of his merit, wisdom, and good conditions ever be compared with the ordinary recitation of sutras, recitation of the Buddha’s name, holding of mantras, and cultivation of contemplation? Why? Because the merit of the mind-nature is immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable. This method of contemplating the mind is the Tathagata Chan; it speaks only of seeing the nature and does not speak of meditation and liberation, and no other dharma can approach it. Therefore the Avatamsaka says: “Though one pass through all future eons, visiting all Buddha-lands, without seeking this wondrous Dharma, one can never attain bodhi.” What is this wondrous Dharma? It is the contemplation of the mind. The Mahayana Sutra of Mind Ground Contemplation says: “This dharma is harder to meet than the udumbara flower; all the world should thirst and long for it. The Buddhas of the ten directions who attain great enlightenment — not one has accomplished it apart from this dharma.” This verse cries aloud from the Buddha’s own golden mouth; what doubt can remain? It also says: “All sentient beings who hear this dharma joyfully hasten to bodhi and receive the prediction. All those with the affinity who receive the prediction, cultivating this gate of contemplation, shall become Buddhas.” From this we see that as soon as the mind is aroused the prediction is given, and as soon as the prediction is given one becomes a Buddha — this is a definitive meaning. What does it mean to have the affinity? To hear this dharma is to have the affinity; to arouse the mind at once is to have the affinity. May all who have the affinity under heaven practice according to the Dharma, advance without retreat, and all quickly realize unsurpassed bodhi.
The twelfth day of the eleventh month of the dinghai year, 1947. Disciple Jin Hongshu respectfully writes this postscript.

blocks.text: Appendix Two: Letters of Mr. Liu Zhuyuan

inline.s: Mr. Liu Zhuyuan of Zhongjiang, Sichuan
Respectfully recorded by his disciple Jin Hongshu
In the twenty-third year (AD
), winter, the twenty-eighth day of the eleventh month

To the layman Hongshu: I have just received your kind letter, forwarded to me through Mr. Zhang Xinruo. Such earnest devotion to the Dharma and such keen longing for the Way are rarely met with in this turbid world, and my admiration is beyond words. As for (your servant’s) understanding of the Buddha-Dharma, I know only faith; of attainment I dare not speak at all. Your letter heaps praise upon me, but it is all outside rumor and by no means the truth; reading it only increases my trepidation.

You ask about the Pure Land dharma-gate, wishing to discuss in writing the wondrous contemplation. Now in the cultivation of the Pure Land there have come down two kinds: holding the name and calm abiding and insight. Holding the name covers all capacities; calm abiding and insight must rely upon personal instruction. Calm abiding and insight, though wondrous, are not as safe as holding the name. Since you (a respectful form of address) are entering the Way, you should begin from holding the name; pray postpone your inquiry into calm abiding and insight. For the dharma of meditation requires that one dwell together with the one who transmits it; otherwise a hundred abuses arise — one may turn into a crooked path, or easily fall away. Hence after Master Lianchi only the one method of holding the name was advocated, and the cultivation of contemplation was not favored; the intent was far-reaching and there is no forked road in it. Holding the name looks easy, but in truth it reaches above and below: its depth accords with the depth of doctrine and principle, its breadth with the breadth of the mind aroused, and the height or lowliness of one’s grade of rebirth depends on the urgency or slackness and the familiarity or unfamiliarity of one’s practice. It equals the cultivation of contemplation in effect: if ten thousand practice it, ten thousand are reborn. The method is complete in the three sutras and one treatise, and does not go beyond faith, vow, and practice. It flourishes in the South; why should you doubt and trouble yourself to ask? Master Yinguang of Putuo is an honored elder of the realm who advocates this teaching exclusively. (Your servant) has never met this master face to face, but I have seen his published Collected Writings; though they develop the old sayings, they add many clarifications. I do not know whether you have given them your attention. (Your servant’s) learning and practice are worth nothing; I am ashamed that I cannot satisfy your clear question — ashamed, ashamed. Nevertheless, there is also a most essential meaning I would urge upon you (
xù
, meaning to encourage):

Our Buddha taught the dharma for forty-nine years, in somewhat more than three hundred assemblies; the meanings of the teachings differ in a thousand ways, yet their homecoming is not two. To cover it in one phrase: the one mind alone (the one mind is the true mind). If the one mind is not understood, then there are outer objects, and from these one gives rise to confusion and creates karma, turning in the wheel of rebirth without end. If one truly understands the one mind, then the three insights, the six spiritual powers, the ten powers, and the four fearlessnesses come without being sought. Therefore it is said: of all dharmas, the mind is foremost. (The Buddha-Dharma and the outside paths are divided precisely here.) You believe in the Buddha, and you should believe thus. Otherwise, though you hold the name and cultivate contemplation, it is all outside paths and heavenly demons, not the Buddha-Dharma. Why? Because there are dharmas outside the mind. This is the root meaning of the Dharma.

Next, there are two preliminary practices: first, do not indulge in false thinking; second, endure coldness and indifference. What does it mean not to indulge in false thinking? Toward every object and state, take it all as empty and do not cling to it so as to give rise to thoughts. Birth and reception in the world are all made by false thinking; this is the root of birth and death, and one must not fail to know it. What does it mean to endure coldness and indifference? People in the world create karma all because they cannot endure coldness and indifference. If one wishes to be a sage or worthy who has left the world, yet is no different from worldly folk in greedily chasing the five desires, then not only will one not become a Buddha — Lord Yama is no blind man. People today, as for the Buddha-Dharma, at first suffer from not hearing of it. Once they have heard it, they say again that their affairs are too many and they will not practice. There is no other reason: first, they do not understand the great meaning of the one mind; second, they let their false thinking run on without stopping. Why the false thinking? Just because they cannot endure coldness and indifference. This is a great and deep root of illness. If one first removes these two illnesses, the mind of itself becomes still and pure, wisdom of itself becomes bright, and one has a share in turning toward the Buddha-Dharma.

Your servant is an ignorant man, crouching in a country village; I am moved that you, sir, from several thousand li away, send a letter to ask my opinion. I respectfully answer with what I have learned; I do not know what one of your discernment will make of it. I write this wishing you the joy of Chan; there is more I need not say.
Liu Fuli bows his head.
Winter of the twenty-third year, the twenty-fourth day of the twelfth month.

To my worthy younger brother Danyuan: I have just received your letter, a thousand words poured out, setting forth in full your family background and history, your early years spent in the outside paths, and your awakening in recent years, your taking refuge in the Three Jewels, and your wish to be my disciple and brother in the Dharma. One can picture the sincerity of your resolve and the courage of your direction — rare, rare indeed. Seeking the Dharma in this way, if you truly put it into practice, there is no reason it should not succeed; listen attentively.

In the Buddha-Dharma, teacher and disciple are bound together by the Way, which differs slightly from worldly ways. If one truly believes that one’s own mind is originally a true Buddha, hears it and deeply believes it, and puts forth effort to advance, then even without being enrolled as a disciple one is already a true son of the Tathagata. But if there are objects outside the mind — fortune and misfortune, prosperity and decline, fame and gain — that constantly entangle the mind, then though one cultivates contemplation and recites the Buddha and attends upon the teacher all day long, one has already betrayed the teacher and turned one’s back on the Buddha.

Since you, sir, wish to establish the relation of teacher and disciple, (your servant) should of course receive you. The conditions of prajñā are not to be compared with worldly power and profit. Even if we do not call one another teacher and disciple, whenever there is a question I would never dare not to tell you the truth; strive on, strive on. Now I will fulfill your wish and teach you with all my heart. That you have taken refuge with Master Yinguang is a very good thing. This master is the treasury of the true Dharma eye in our land today; whether Chan or Pure Land, school or doctrine, there is nothing he does not deeply understand. Yet by his vow he wishes to cover all capacities with the one dharma of the Pure Land, and so he urges the recitation of the Buddha exclusively. That he teaches you, worthy brother, to recite the Buddha with a single mind and not to weary your spirit studying sutras and treatises has a deep intent. You must strive to practice it; this master’s views are utterly right and he will never mislead anyone.

Your letter again requests the Pure Land contemplation, as though (your servant) were withholding something. This thought is mistaken. Not to teach the Dharma when the capacity is ripe is to lack the eye of wisdom; to teach it to one unsuited to it is to slander the Three Jewels. Having received your earnest insistence, (your servant) could never keep silent; what I feared was only that it might bring harm rather than benefit. Your aspiration is excellent; if you are willing to truly believe, then not only would rebirth in the West be as certain as holding the deed in one’s hand, but becoming a Buddha and a patriarch would be a matter within the proper portion of us who are (
chái

, people of the same generation) — by no means something beyond hope. Your letter mentioned that last year you joined the Tongshan Society; this is most harmful, and you must above all postpone the study of calm abiding and insight, or the harm will be deep. Reading your letter closely, you are urgently seeking knowledge and understanding, and this is very hard to answer. The Dharma-characteristics school analyzes most minutely; you say you dislike reading it, but it would still be best to read a little. You also say you like reading the books of the Tiantai school — could you read its three great treatises? If you could read them, that school strongly rejects spiritual powers, so why are you so shaken and amazed? I have now thought of a method: besides reciting the Buddha, read a few pages of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch every day. This book is most concise and essential, and its meaning is extremely deep and rich. Though you may not understand it, reading it will set your views straight, and the benefit is very great. Yang Renshan placed it among the four books of Buddhist study; its importance is clear. In learning the Dharma the ground of cultivation values what is true. To seek the end of birth and death and to seek rebirth in the West is the right cause. To seek worldly reward is a wrong cause. To seek efficacy in holding mantras is also a wrong cause. To seek spiritual powers is also a wrong cause. Guard against them, guard against them! Among my disciples there have been those who developed powers, and I rebuked them strongly; they no longer dare to dazzle people with spiritual powers. You ask how the daily recitation should be set. Simply recite the Buddha with all your strength — that is enough. Four-character or six-character [form] are both fine, and sitting cross-legged in full lotus is best. In leisure hours, add the Chapter on the Conduct and Vows of Samantabhadra.
There are still matters in your letter to which I must reply:

1. In studying the Mahayana, take the understanding of the one mind as the root, and reciting the Buddha for rebirth as your chief occupation. Your livelihood is not ample, and it is by no means impossible for you to engage in other work. As it is said, the works of livelihood do not obstruct the perfect teaching — only do not commit the ten evil deeds.

2. The meaning of understanding the one mind is the general outline of the Mahayana, the highest of vehicles; it stands higher than vowing to be born in the West by more than ten thousand times. Your holding mantras and reciting sutras falls, among the four siddhantas, still within the scope of the worldly siddhanta; the instructions in these two letters of mine belong entirely to the scope of the siddhanta of ultimate meaning. Treasure them and do not neglect them.

[The four siddhantas] Si means four methods; xi means universal; tan is the abbreviation of the Sanskrit dana, which is also the meaning of giving. The Buddha universally bestows four dharmas upon sentient beings so that all sentient beings may complete the Buddha Way; this is called “the four siddhantas.” First, the worldly siddhanta: at the beginning, the Buddha first accords with the ordinary feelings of the world and proclaims shallow and simple matters and principles, so that those who hear may rejoice and believe and accept. Second, the siddhanta suited to each person: the Buddha examines the faculties of sentient beings and the depth or shallowness of their capacity, and speaks the dharma each one needs, causing sentient beings to arouse right faith and increase their good roots. Third, the siddhanta of counteraction: to those with much anger he teaches the contemplation of compassion; to those with much delusion he teaches the contemplation of causes and conditions; to those with many hindrances he teaches the contemplation of the Buddha; thus he universally bestows all kinds of medicine for the dharma, to remove the evil illnesses of sentient beings. Fourth, the siddhanta of ultimate meaning: when the Buddha sees that the conditions of sentient beings are ripe, he speaks for them of the true mark of all dharmas, so that sentient beings may all at once awaken and enter the way of the sages.

3. The vinaya pitaka, in a thousand words and ten thousand phrases, has only two meanings: first, to be free of evil conduct; second, to be free of the conduct of desire. Being free of the conduct of desire has two further parts: first, not to commit sexual misconduct; second, to cut off lawful sexual union. Sexual misconduct is a cause of hell, and the Buddha does not permit it. Lawful union is for the sake of offspring, and for a layman it is no obstacle. Apart from the precept of desire, all the rest is being free of evil conduct. Have you received the five precepts?

4. Cultivating contemplation and holding the name — the two methods are equal. One who cultivates contemplation sees clearly; one who holds the name understands only when he reaches one mind undisturbed.

5. The three insights and the six spiritual powers differ between the Two Vehicles and the Great Vehicle. That they come without being sought is what is meant by “gain the mother, and the child comes of itself.”
6. Learning the Dharma has nothing to do with letters. One who cannot read becomes a Buddha just the same — how much more so is rebirth in the West?

7. You ask whether the ordinary daily recitation has any efficacy. Every single recitation of the Buddha’s name has merit — how could it be without efficacy? What the sutras say is a thousand times true and ten thousand times certain; the Buddha does not speak falsely. Never give rise to doubt. Again: that the lotus opens as soon as the vow is made is a true statement, wholly without deception.
The fifteenth day of the second month, spring of the twenty-fourth year.

Yesterday I received your letter; your questioning of the Dharma is earnest and commands respect. It is a pity that the meanings you set forth are all wrong knowledge and wrong views. This is because when you formerly inquired into the Buddha-Dharma you did not meet a single clear-headed person, and so the harm has been done. Now, on the several points you ask about, I shall refute and correct them one by one. Your former views must be swept away utterly. Books of the outside paths that attach themselves to Buddhism — put them far away, or consign them to bingding (that is, to fire). Recite the Buddha with a single mind, and do not seek to understand by reasoning. Carry on thus over the months and years, and perhaps you will find an entrance into the Pure Land school. I hope you will heed what I say and ponder it well.

You ask how it is that understanding the one mind surpasses vowing to be born in the West by ten thousand times. This meaning is the highest teaching of the Pure Land school, and it is also common talk in the Pure Land school; it is plainly present in the sutras. The Larger Amitābha Sutra speaks of rebirth in three grades, all of them grounded in arousing the bodhi mind. It also says that one who does not understand the four wisdoms is born only in the borderland city of doubt. The Contemplation Sutra says, “All Buddhas, the Tathagatas, are the dharmakāya, and enter into the minds and thoughts of all sentient beings,” and further, “This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha” — how could it not take the understanding of the one mind as its root? Cultivated in this way, one may hope within this life to attain the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas. The three words of the ordinary path — faith, vow, and practice — are of course not to be rejected, yet if no weight is given to the bodhi mind, then even if one is born in the West, one can hardly hope for the highest of the highest grade. Why? Because the one mind has not been understood. The one mind is hard to believe in, and to understand it is harder still. If one can understand it, one enters the stage of no further learning. Yet the meaning of the Mahayana should begin from this point, and only then is it arousing the mind. You need only believe that all dharmas are within the mind, that all Buddhas and sentient beings are also within the mind, and that the Pure Land and the defiled land are also within the mind; then recite the Buddha’s name with all your strength, and after a year or half a year of effort, ask again — do not rely on talk. In ordinary Buddha-recitation, if this matter is not understood, then even though one attains rebirth, it is still the lowest grade. I am teaching you the ultimate truth, beginning from the understanding of mind; naturally it is ten thousand times higher, for I am urging one of rather good faculties with the teaching of definitive meaning, grounded in arousing the bodhi mind.

The books of the scholastic tradition on arousing the mind are broad in text and wide in meaning, and hard to grasp at once. I instruct you with a simple method: understand the one mind alone, and all meanings are included; that is truly arousing the mind. If the one mind is not understood, then even though one vows to be reborn in the West, one still lingers in the borderland city of doubt. This is of course better than worldly dharmas, but in the end it is not the original intent with which our Buddha draws in sentient beings. This is why I urge you to read the Platform Sutra: that book never speaks of arousing the mind, yet every sentence points straight at the human mind, and every word is ultimate definitive meaning. You may calmly take it up and understand it; this book discloses everything without remainder. Why ask further about the ultimate truth? To understand the one mind is the true ultimate truth. The ultimate truth is the one mind. Called the Buddha-nature, called true suchness, called the dharmakāya, called the Dharma-realm — all are different names for the true mind, and all are one’s own mind. Buddhas and sentient beings are equal, without two. If you still do not understand, then recite the Buddha honestly, and a day of understanding will come. But if you merely chase after words, there is no hope.

The reason I urge you to read the Platform Sutra often is simply that this book may open your bodhi mind — who ever said I wished you to practice Chan meditation? The great Dharma banner of Chan meditation — can it be raised in these turbid times? As soon as you heard of the Platform Sutra, you pointed to a certain commentary, and to the Record of the Lamp of the Mind. Alas! Such books as cut off people’s good roots — how can they be set before the eyes? On the whole, the books of the Chan school need no commentary at all; every commentary is utterly absurd, an outside path attached to Buddhism. Why? The Chan school points directly at the original mind and has people awaken themselves; once one enters into explanation of meaning, the gate of awakening is blocked and the good roots are cut off forever. Hence Master Zhongfeng wrote works refuting the explanation of meaning with respect to the Faith Mind Inscription and the Song of Enlightenment, and so Zhongfeng is the treasury of the true Dharma eye. What need has the Platform Sutra of footnotes? If you want footnotes, then let me tell you: the Compendium of the Five Lamps, the Recorded Sayings of the Venerable Adepts, and the Record of Pointing at the Moon are all exquisite commentaries on the Platform Sutra. The former commentaries should be abandoned at once. Reading the Platform Sutra every day, one should let the straightforward mind awaken itself; what one does not understand, leave aside. The hundred and eight thousand words may be preserved without discussion; by no means force an interpretation in order to seek understanding by reasoning.

You further ask about “letting go being the hardest thing.” You should know that when you cannot let go, recite the Buddha’s name with a single mind, and you will be able to let go. The Pure Land school’s parable of the pearl clearing muddy water is exactly this. If the mind scatters and runs, oppose it with the Buddha’s name, and in time it will of itself grow still. In learning any dharma, who does not use bitter effort? If one could let go without effort, why would there be any need to learn? As for your schedule of Buddha-recitation, you may set it yourself. In my view, whenever one takes up a task, one should give it one’s whole strength — as in Buddha-recitation: then one keeps the thought fixed on it all day long, without pause. If you set fixed hours, your rest periods will be many indeed, and how could the day of success ever come? Recite with effort, recite without interval — press on, press on. Besides Buddha-recitation, the various mantras you uphold, since you have already studied them, need not be abandoned. Only know that the mind is the root, and every dharma-gate enters the ultimate truth.

You have two daughters but no son. You should know that the Universal Gateway chapter on Guanyin says: “If one wishes for a son, one will bear a son of merit and wisdom.” Why do you and your wife not constantly recite that sutra and hold the name of Guanyin? It benefits your Pure Land practice and also supplies what you desire — why not do it? The Buddha-Dharma is the speech of one family: if one simply penetrates the mind school and recites the Buddha’s name diligently, the merit is inconceivable. As for those who gain no result, it is that they are unwilling to practice long, they hold that there are dharmas outside the mind, and they practice by fits and starts. (Following this teaching, he afterward had four sons. — Note by Hongshu.)

Since you cultivate the Pure Land, you should receive the five precepts. Anyone who does not commit the ten evil deeds may receive the five precepts. Why? Because the five precepts are included within the ten good deeds. And the Yogacara bodhisattva precepts are fully included in the Six Perfections and the four means of gathering. If you truly arouse the bodhi mind, then not only should you receive the five precepts, you should also receive the bodhisattva precepts. You should know that the bodhisattva precepts have two kinds, for householders and for monastics, and the Yogacara precepts are the precepts common to both householders and monastics. If you can receive them, the benefit to your Pure Land practice is very great; do not be afraid, do not be afraid. You should know that one who can arouse the great mind should receive the bodhisattva precepts. These precepts take the bodhi mind as their root, and so they are no obstacle whatever to works of livelihood or to bearing sons and daughters. Only, at the time of receiving the precepts, on your own side there is simply the arousing of the mind and the understanding of what is to be observed and transgressed, what is permitted and what is prohibited; as for outer conditions, one must obtain an acarya of lofty conduct to perform the karma for one, otherwise one cannot obtain the highest, highest grade of precepts.

[The four means of gathering] These are the four methods of gathering: gathering by giving, by kind speech, by beneficial conduct, and by shared activity. Gathering by giving means that toward those whose hearts are set on wealth one practices the giving of goods, and toward those whose hearts are set on knowledge one practices the giving of Dharma, so that the affection of both sides deepens by degrees and one attains the goal of transforming the other. Gathering by kind speech means that, according to the faculties of sentient beings, one speaks to them with gentle and loving words, causing them to rejoice, to feel that one is kindly and approachable, and so to draw near, thus attaining the goal of transforming the other. Gathering by beneficial conduct means that one who practices the bodhisattva path must make all his actions of body, speech, and mind beneficial to others, and by conduct that harms himself and benefits others moves sentient beings to cultivate the Buddha Way together, thus attaining the goal of saving others. Gathering by shared activity means that one who practices the bodhisattva path must go deep into every level of society, come into contact with people of every trade, be their friend, share their work, and so transform them when the opportunity and conditions fit. In saving sentient beings, a bodhisattva must first practice these four means of gathering, so that sentient beings love, respect, and trust him; only then will they listen to his exhortation and cultivate the Buddha Way. [Acarya] That is acharya, rendered into Chinese as “personal teacher” or “model teacher.” [Karma] Rendered into Chinese as “action,” that is, a ceremony of proclamation by which the acts of conferring precepts, repentance, and so forth are carried out; by the words of proclamation in this ceremony the action undertaken is accomplished.
The twenty-fourth day of the sixth month, summer of the twenty-fifth year.

You have the mind to benefit others; as the Buddha said, “to save others before oneself is saved” — how could that be wrong? Yet you may not realize that the sutras say again and again: “If one is oneself in bonds and wishes to loose the bonds of another, that is impossible.” And again: “If one does not practice oneself and wishes another to practice, that is in the end impossible.” If you truly wish to benefit others, you should be diligent without weariness until you have some attainment. To be father and mother to the six realms and a teacher to gods and humans is a matter within your own portion. What benefit is there in publishing in newspapers or passing things from mouth to ear?

In learning any dharma, what matters is a resolute mind (not wavering until success), a long-enduring mind (doing it always, without interruption), and an uninterrupted mind (as when a hen broods on her eggs — once the warmth breaks off, there is no life in them). With these three minds, nothing fails. Now, the Buddha has all manner of dharmas to cure all manner of minds among sentient beings. Therefore the sutra says: the expedient means are many. Must one try every gate before one can succeed? What matters is to trust one gate and enter its depths — there lies the matter. The vow in the four universal vows, “the dharma-gates are immeasurable, I vow to learn them,” is spoken vertically, not horizontally; do not mistake it. Vertically means: master one dharma, then learn another kind, and afterward there will be immeasurable dharma-gates. It does not mean advancing on all at once. If you advance on all at once, not one dharma can be accomplished — what benefit is there in that? Remember this, remember this.
The seventh day of the seventh month, autumn of the twenty-sixth year.

I have heard it said that although the dharma-gates are immeasurable, one must penetrate deeply through one gate; there lies the matter. Therefore the great masters of old, in teaching people, always said: you must have a point of entry. Now what is called a point of entry differs from teaching to teaching. The Chan school takes knowing that there is [the Buddha-nature] as its point of entry; the gradual methods of Chan take the accomplishment of the first contemplation as their point of entry. Applying this to the esoteric dharma, one serves a single yidam, and it should be understood in the same way. In my humble view, once there is a point of entry, the wisdom of emptiness shines bright, and through all the ten thousand transformations you take this as your base. Otherwise you remain an outsider at the gate your whole life. You are a fine vessel; I hope you will set your mind on one dharma alone, spend your months and years on it, and bring it through to openness. Do not run after many at once, and do not change your mind at every new sight. To count grains of sand in the sea, to speak of food that does not fill you — these you should firmly renounce.

The world is in chaos, and people’s minds have nothing to rely on, so they seek it in the Buddha-Dharma. Now the Buddha-Dharma has become a fashionable commodity, dragons and snakes mixed together, the false confounding the true; for the most part what is sought is fame, gain, and profit. We must not join that company — then we are true sons of the Buddha.
The ninth day of the tenth month, winter of the twenty-sixth year.

I have just received your kind letter, earnestly requesting the Pure Land contemplation, as though you feared (your servant) were keeping something back. The Dharma values circulation; to be stingy and not give it is to break the precepts. But I feared the distance is too great and that there are things no pen can exhaust, and I feared also that you might hear and not practice; that is why I kept silent. Now three years have passed and your request has been made more than three times. I will therefore speak to you of this expedient means of entry; listen well, listen well:

One who studies this contemplation must, before the Buddha, silently recite the Three Refuges and the five precepts and keep the ten good paths. Then one arouses three kinds of mind: first, the vast and great mind (vowing to save all sentient beings); second, the resolute mind (not changing with every new sight if the contemplation does not yet succeed); third, the long-enduring mind.

Then one enters sitting (either full lotus or half lotus) and contemplates the six great elements as empty (earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness). The most important is the four great elements, for they break the view of self and the view of the body. First, the earth element disperses and returns to the west. (Whatever is hard from head to foot belongs to earth.) Second, the water element disperses and returns to the north. (Blood, sweat, and fluids all belong to water.) Third, the fire element disperses and returns to the south. (Warmth belongs to fire.) Fourth, the wind element disperses and returns to the east. (The breath of the nose belongs to wind.) When these four great elements are empty, only the great element of space remains (the fifth great element). That which knows space is then only consciousness (the sixth great element). These two great elements need not be dwelt on long. With this very mind of consciousness, one then contemplates the sun attentively (that is, the sun contemplation of the Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations). The first four great elements must be contemplated with the mind gathered. When sitting for the first time, each great element is pushed out and dispersed in its own direction, for at least ten minutes at the shortest, and longer is still better. This method is based on the Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra in Four Fascicles, fascicle three, page three. Examine it carefully. Whenever one sits, one must face west, and the mind must be calm and the breath quiet. At the beginning of the sitting one must gather the mind and not let it scatter; do not seek quick results; if there are results, do not be startled and delighted; in time it will come of itself. (This is an excellent expedient means before cultivating the sun contemplation; with this expedient means the sun contemplation is easily accomplished. — Note by Hongshu.)
You study the esoteric dharma, and with the four great elements and the six great elements you are long since (
yù

, meaning to have eaten one’s fill) familiar — nothing extraordinary in it; what matters is that one can enter it. (Your servant) returned home six years ago, and living apart from my disciples in seclusion, I do not know what their attainments are. Those who understand the Pure Land contemplation seem to be not a few. Of those with other wondrous contemplations there are about ten or more, and more than half have died — they are not worth mentioning.

On the whole, in these latter days women surpass men in learning the Dharma. (They surpass in knowing suffering.) Among men, the old surpass the young and strong. It is by knowing suffering that one enters the Buddha-Dharma; the young and strong mostly do not know suffering, and so it is hard for them to enter. One who learns the Dharma must have few desires and be content, not admire what is outside, not seek fame, gain, and profit — then he is a son of the Buddha. That the world is in such chaos is all because sentient beings cannot have few desires and be content, but commit the ten evil deeds, brewing this great calamity. We who have taken refuge in the Teacher of the Ten Powers — how can we not be vigilant ourselves!
In the thirty-fifth year (AD
), winter, the third day of the eleventh month

To my worthy younger brother Danyuan: I have just received your letter of the first day of the tenth month (the first). Such warmth and earnestness — how could it be less than that of flesh and blood? In these nine years the world has changed again and again; thorns of heaven and brambles of earth, the misery is too cruel to speak of. Your province lies in occupied territory, and the grief there is the deeper. When the war first broke out, news was cut off; gazing east at the clouds of Zhejiang, my thoughts of you were never forgotten. With last year’s victory I hoped you would send a letter, and unexpectedly your honored letter has now fallen from the sky. Truly I know that your good roots are deep, and that a further cause for rejoicing is that your whole household is at peace and your descendants flourish like the pepper plant (a simile for many descendants) — the law of cause and effect is not blind. Though I met with the national calamity, the wartime capital in Sichuan was reckoned the safest place, and so I have been blessed. Such is the lot of a mediocre man — my shame is extreme. In the course of several years I often traveled among Deyang, Guanghan, and Jintang, never ceasing to lecture. But a candle guttering in the wind, old and ill and broken down — it is truly pitiable.

Your letter speaks of the Mahayana method of calm abiding and insight, of cultivating the practice of no-thought. This is truly the wondrous truth of the Dharma-nature school, equal to the supreme yoga among the four yogas of the esoteric school, and it is the secret of the Chan school. The method of contemplation you describe — that ‘when a single thought arises, one immediately observes it; at the very moment of observing, the previous thought has ceased and the following thought has not yet arisen, and the present is without thought’ — this method, you say, is contemplating no-thought; it differs somewhat from my own view. What I rely on is the verse of the sutra: ‘You should observe this mind: thought after thought it ever arises and ceases. Like an illusion, it has nothing at all, and yet one obtains the great reward.’ This is truly arousing the bodhi mind; this is the practice of no-thought, no-abiding, and the markless. If you can grasp it, we may speak of it again later.
The third day of the first month, spring of the thirty-sixth year.

I received your letter yesterday, again asking about the cultivation of the no-thought practice. Now the one dharma of no-thought is the right cause of becoming a Buddha; the sutras state it plainly and repeatedly, and it is not only in the Treatise on the Awakening of Faith. In that treatise the gate of calm abiding and insight speaks of the samādhi of thusness, which is precisely the method of cultivating the no-thought practice. Not to apply yourself to this, but only to explain a few phrases at the beginning of the text — how could that be right? If you would apply effort, please read more of Xianshou’s Commentary on the Meaning of the Awakening of Faith; among the sutras, read the Mahayana Sutra of Mind Ground Contemplation of the Original Birth, and recite it long and thoroughly, and you should come to an understanding. In learning the Dharma one must first possess two conditions: first, not to busy oneself with outward things; second, the mind must be still and quiet. Contrary to this, a hundred kalpas bring no accomplishment.

Worthy brother, since you sincerely study the Dharma, I have three cautions: first, the Buddha-Dharma takes the mind ground as its root; do not abandon the root and chase the branches. Second, expedient means are the gate of practice; do not forget the substance and cling to the procedure. Third, worldly affairs are false; do not take them seriously. If you take them as real, how can you accord with the emptiness of dharmas? How can you enter the principle? Beyond this, it is essential to arouse the bodhi mind constantly.

Your letter also asks for lecture manuscripts. I send you the Guanghan lecture record; it gives a rough outline — you need not show it to others. I am a candle guttering in the wind, and how much life remains? I hope that you worthy brothers (elder and younger) may rival Yuan Zhonglang; then my wish is fulfilled. To your elder brother Oucun, simply say: ‘Recite the Buddha with a sincere mind, and Amitābha will constantly bless you.’ The contemplation is not yet accomplished, and so he does not know it of himself.
[Yuan Zhonglang] Yuan Hongdao (

), courtesy name Zhonglang, style name Shigong, a native of Chang’an village, Gong’an county, Hubei, in the Ming dynasty, a well-known man of letters. He and his elder brother Yuan Zongdao and his younger brother Yuan Zhongdao were all famed for talent, and people called them “the three Yuans”; one after another they all passed the presented-scholar examination, and all were fond of Chan. The world regards Hongdao as the most outstanding in literary achievement among the three Yuans, and his Complete Works of Yuan Zhonglang has come down to us. According to the Record of the Pure Land Sages: in the Wanli era Hongdao was magistrate of Wujiang, and later secretary of the Ministry of Rites. He pleaded illness and returned home; at first he studied Chan under Li Zhuowu, his understanding was keen and fluent, and he loved debate. Afterward he tested himself and said: “This is empty talk, not the real thing.” Thereupon he turned toward the Pure Land, bowed and recited morning and evening, and also kept the precepts. Because he widely gathered the sutras and teachings, he wrote the Comprehensive Treatise on the Western [Pure Land], which harmonized nature and characteristics and entered the gate of non-duality. Its discussion of the five kinds of practice (the practice of faith, the practice of calm abiding and insight, the practice of the Six Perfections, the practice of compassionate vows, and the practice of according with the Dharma) is especially essential. When the book was finished, Zongdao and Zhongdao at the same time aroused the mind and turned toward the Pure Land. Afterward Hongdao was restored to his former office and rose again to be director of the Bureau of Meritorious Records. He again asked for sick leave and returned home; a few days after reaching home he entered the city of Jingzhou and lodged in a monastery, where he died without illness.

His younger brother Zhongdao was a secretary of the Ministry of Rites at Nanjing. He asked to retire and grew old at home, where he was diligent in bowing and reciting. On the full-moon evening of the forty-second year of Wanli, when his recitation was done he sat cross-legged, his body and spirit calm and clear. Suddenly he entered samādhi, and his spirit went out above the roof, floating on the clouds, with two youths leading him westward; in a moment he came down to the ground.

He came to a building, and a man came down to welcome him whose face was like jade and whose robes were like clouds and mist, more than a fathom tall. Seeing Zhongdao, he said joyfully: “My brother has come.” Looking closely, it was Hongdao.

Zhongdao asked: “Where has my brother been born?” Hongdao said: “My vow for the Pure Land was deep, but the stains of affection were not yet removed; at first I was born here for a short while, and now I dwell in the Pure Land.

You and I have been brothers in life after life since the kalpa of the Empty King, and so it has been through all the six realms without exception. Fortunately I have obtained a good place; fearing that you might fall, by the power of expedient spiritual might I have drawn you here. Pure and defiled are kept apart, and you cannot stay long.” At that time Zongdao had already died, and so he asked where he had been born. Hongdao said: “His birthplace is good too; you will know later.” Then suddenly he rose into the air and was gone. Zhongdao stepped out upon the pond, and suddenly it was as if he had fallen into water; he started awake, and made this record himself.
The first day of the intercalary second month, spring of the thirty-sixth year.

You have heard me speak of the samādhi of thusness, yet you do not know that it is one and the same thing as contemplating no-thought; from this one may know that although the school of Asvaghosa has been on people’s lips since the Yuan and Ming, its learning has fallen into neglect. The Awakening of Faith takes Paramartha’s version as standard. Why? Because Xianshou based his commentary on it, and because Nagarjuna composed his treatise on its basis. The Tang translation may serve only for reference, and the Commentary That Rends the Net is not good. One who is skilled in expounding the Dharma-nature brings the Dharma-characteristics back into the Dharma-nature. That commentary is much plastered over with names and marks; it will just do for teaching beginners, but it obstructs the penetration of the Dharma-nature. In the Awakening of Faith, Xianshou is the orthodox line. Do not set it aside because it is hard to understand (the Commercial Press has the Commentary on the Meaning and the Lecture Notes). This treatise is the foremost guide of the Buddha-Dharma in our land; it must not be neglected.

[The Awakening of Faith] The abbreviated title of the Treatise on the Awakening of Faith in the Mahayana. It was composed by the bodhisattva Asvaghosa and has two translations: first, the Liang, translated by Paramartha, in one fascicle; second, the Tang, translated by Siksananda, in two fascicles. It sets forth the highest principle of the Mahayana in order to arouse right faith.

Your letter describes the no-thought contemplation you have learned; it is entirely wrong. You should know that learning contemplation is planting good roots. I now ask you: what is the seed? Where is it planted? How is it sown? Let me now teach you: it is planted on the mind of the Dharma-realm. (The mind of the Dharma-realm is your mind of ignorance, whose substance is true suchness.) The mind of the Dharma-realm is like a field; believing that one’s own mind has the Buddha-nature (that is, your nature of awareness) is the seed,
and contemplating the mind with prajñā is the sowing

. (To contemplate the essence of the mind without discrimination is to understand of itself.) Long contemplation brings forth concentration and wisdom — that is the good root arising. Further contemplation is the good root growing. Great thorough awakening is the good root ripening. You cultivate no-thought, yet your discriminating mind is much — how can you accord with prajñā?
I think of how earnestly you seek the Dharma; now I should teach you to arouse the ultimate bodhi mind:
An exhortation to arouse the true mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi
A. Four matters to examine beforehand. (Not for use while in sitting meditation; one should know them beforehand.)
1. For what purpose? (If it is for the sake of gaining benefit, the cause is not upright; one should seek to see the mind and realize the nature.)
2. Wash away old views. (One should wash away old views and old hearing until thoroughly clean.)
3. With what mind? (One should be free of the mind of perception, that is, free of mind, thought, and consciousness, and not employ the mind.)
4. What practice? (Not mixing in the marks of dharmas, solely the one method of contemplating the mind and guarding the mind unmoving.)
B. The method of proper practice. (This method is based on the four lines transmitted by Master Bodhidharma. Those with true faith may all study it; those without faith should not.)
1. Cut off all outward conditions. (Cast away the affairs of faculties and objects until thoroughly clean.)
2. Within, the mind has no panting. (“Panting” means movement; it says the mind does not move.)
3. The mind is like a wall. (It says discrimination does not arise, and one is free of subject and object.)
4. Then one may enter the Way. (This line is the fruit; the effort is only in the three lines above.)

Every day seated in full lotus, contemplate the mind according to the three lines. If a mind-thought arises, neither suppress it nor follow it; one should contemplate that delusive thoughts have no self-nature, and that their substance is empty, and the mind will naturally become still. When delusive thoughts cease, the spring of the mind is empty and still, prajñā accords, and the true nature first manifests. This method is the practice of no-thought, the practice of no-abiding, the practice of not-moving, which is the samādhi of thusness; it breathes through the same nostril as the Treatise on the Awakening of Faith, and instantly realizes in a single thought. (During contemplation one should not let states appear; this is most important. The number of sittings and their length may be as one pleases.)

C. The ceremony of receiving the Dharma. One must bathe, then bow to the Buddha and say: ‘Disciple So-and-so, today from such-and-such a worthy one, I study arousing the bodhi mind; I believe and rejoice, and will practice it my whole life, vowing never to forget.’ Saying this three times, do three prostrations. Afterwards, simply practice, and no further declaration is needed. From then on, one may not be negligent for a single day.

Recitation may be reduced; the Diamond Sutra may be recited — who says all sutras must be recited every day? Now, merely by arousing bodhicitta one directly enters the realm of the sages; why be greedy for more?

Your letter asks again: the Awakening of Faith says, ‘If one contemplates the Buddha’s Dharma-body of true suchness and constantly and diligently cultivates, one will in the end be born there, because one dwells in right concentration’ — is that Buddha Amitābha? And how is the Dharma-body of true suchness to be contemplated? Answer: That Buddha is Amitābha, and is also one’s own mind. Why? Because mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are three without difference, and because self and other are not two. To contemplate the Dharma-body of true suchness is to contemplate one’s own mind. Why? Because the true nature of ignorance is the Buddha-nature (the Buddha-nature is true suchness), and because the illusory, empty body is the Dharma-body. (The Dharma-body is the true mind.)
[The true nature of ignorance is the Buddha-nature; the illusory, empty body is the Dharma-body] This is quoted from Master Yongjia’s Song of Enlightenment.
Appendix: From the Record of Pointing at the Moon, the Record of the First Patriarch’s Teaching

The separate record says: The Patriarch first dwelt at Shaolin Monastery for nine years, and in teaching the Second Patriarch he taught only: ‘Cut off all outward conditions, within have no panting, let the mind be like a wall; then one may enter the Way.’ Huike spoke of mind and nature in various ways, but never yet hit the principle; the Patriarch only blocked what was wrong in it, and did not speak to him of
the essence of the no-thought mind

. Huike suddenly said: ‘I have already put all conditions to rest.’ The Patriarch said: ‘Is it not that you have become annihilation?’ Huike said: ‘It is not annihilation.’ The Patriarch said: ‘This is the essence of mind transmitted by all the Buddhas; doubt it no more.’ (Respectfully recorded by Hongshu for the reference of fellow practitioners.)
The first day of the third month, spring of the thirty-sixth year.

Your letter is received and understood. What pleases me most is that your grasp is very clear, that you hear the Dharma without abandoning sentient beings, and that your compassionate mind overflows — you truly have the line, and are fit to study the great dharma. Though you have only lately taken up the work and errors come out in layers, I cannot but clear them away for you. Listen well, listen well!

1. You do not distinguish the high from the low among dharma-gates. Your five-step program of contemplation (taking refuge and reverence, seeking blessing; reciting mantras and regulating the breath; dispersing the four great elements; attentively contemplating no-thought; and dedicating the merit and making vows), together with the passage you copied from the Record of Calm Abiding and Insight, are the wondrous dharma of the Three Vehicles, spoken for those of middling and lower faculties, a path to Buddhahood requiring three asamkhya kalpas. Bodhidharma’s dharma is the perfect and sudden dharma, spoken for those of the highest, highest faculties, a path to Buddhahood in a single thought. How can you mix them into one, without distinguishing high from low?

2. You do not rely on the oral transmission of the sages who went before. The sages of old had only two lines: ‘Point directly at the human mind; see the nature and become a Buddha.’ Bodhidharma added two more to make four — already an addition to the words; how can you add more?

3. You destroy the mind dharma. The five-step program replaces, for people of the world who chase the five desires and six sense-objects, those with five kinds of pure conditions; it is truly excellent. But now, when we speak of clarifying the mind and seeing the nature, both defiled conditions and pure conditions must come to rest — only that is the cutting off of all outward conditions. If you only still the defiled conditions and do not still the pure conditions, then the first line (cut off all outward conditions) is destroyed. (Defiled and pure are both conditions; to grasp defiled conditions as existent certainly prevents seeing the nature, and to grasp pure conditions as real also prevents seeing the nature; therefore only when all conditions are stilled can one see the nature. This division between the Three Vehicles and the One Vehicle is also the Buddhas’ painstaking labor of setting up the expedient for the sake of the real.) Having a program, one gives rise to movements of mind and thoughts, and the second line (within, the mind has no panting) is destroyed. Not knowing that the Three Jewels are in the mind, but making vows and dedicating the merit toward a Buddha outside as an outer object, one’s discrimination blazes and subject and object stand plainly apart, and the third line (the mind is like a wall) is destroyed. To wish to learn the dharma and instead destroy it — is that admissible? If it were as you intend, it would be to walk backwards and pull against the current; how could one enter the Way?

4. You go against the Awakening of Faith. Whoever speaks of the no-thought practice without understanding the samādhi of thusness is an outsider at the gate. Why is the five-step program utterly inadmissible? The Awakening of Faith has already discarded it. Does that treatise not say: ‘Not relying on the breath, not relying on earth, water, fire, and wind,’ and so forth? Have you not seen it?

The dharma of the First Patriarch is wholly identical with the Awakening of Faith. I think of how our letters have gone back and forth over more than ten years; though you have good roots, you have not found the gate, and so I have specially taught you to arouse the bodhi mind — it is not that I insist you study the Chan school. (In the perfect and sudden teaching the arousing of the mind is the same; if one can arouse this mind, one may study any other school. If one would study the Chan school, one must possess great merit; you may choose for yourself.)
Whoever learns the Dharma yet drifts along with objects, not taking mind contemplation as the root, is an outsider

Those of the three vehicles contemplate the mind, but not deeply and not thoroughly; only one of the one vehicle suddenly sees the original nature and suddenly becomes a Tathagata. The Lotus Sutra says: ‘Uprightly setting aside the expedient, he speaks only of the supreme Way.’ (The upright is opposed to the crooked, the direct to the devious; not to set aside the expedient is itself crooked. Not to understand the mind-nature is likewise crooked.) If you, sir, are bound (
niǔ

, to cling obstinately) to the expedient, how can you practice the deep prajñā-paramita? You take the arousal of the mind to mean the mind of the Way; that is far too vague and loose. Let me give you a definition: to arouse the bodhi mind is to arouse the mind that sees the nature. These words pierce bone and marrow; this is the truly certain explanation. Only when there is no object to be taken as a condition can one see the nature — what is called the gateless gate as the Dharma-gate. You cultivate no-thought and do not know this: is it not to drive south while your cart faces north? The ancient worthies said: ‘If one does not contemplate the mind, the Dharma has no place from which to come.’ That is to say, a pure condition cannot arise. Therefore know that to contemplate the mind or not is truly the crossroads of life and death in learning the Dharma. One who studies the Buddha and does not arouse the mind gains only human and heavenly karma. If one can arouse this mind of supreme meaning, then one receives the Buddhas’ prediction and can enter the kalpas and transcend the kalpas. There are many other wondrous meanings besides, which I cannot set out one by one.

You ask about the seeds. The seeds of defiled dharmas are formed by the perfuming of the faculties and their objects. The seeds of pure dharmas are originally possessed on the dharma-body (that is, on the dharma-nature). When one sees the nature the pure seeds appear; on the dharma-body the seeds of the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unshared dharmas are all complete, and seeing the nature is to obtain them. Therefore, after seeing the nature, one is an old Buddha newly accomplished.

The arousal of the bodhi mind must not be printed and published; those with the affinity will of themselves hear of it.
