This is the ancient method; those who know it are very many, yet in all the world few practice it. The reason I do not permit it to be spread abroad is this: the Platform Sutra says: ‘In other dharmas it must not be transmitted, for it would injure those who came before, and in the end bring no benefit. I fear that foolish people will not understand and will slander this Dharma-gate, and for a hundred kalpas and a thousand lives cut off the Buddha-nature.’ For of the one-vehicle Dharma, if one hears it and believes, age after age it profits one; if one hears it and gives rise to doubt, one is plunged into hell. Thus fearful is the speaking of Dharma — must one not be careful? I know that you have had more than ten years of faith, and even so it is this hard to teach you. Others have no faith in me and do not respect the Dharma; how can it be spoken of to them?
The thirteenth day of the fourth month, summer of the thirty-sixth year.

Both your letters are noted. Your earnest sincerity shines throughout; for the Dharma and for others you labor, and I cannot praise you enough, while my shame is truly deep. Since you are so attentive, I can only permit you to print it. The lecture records were taken down by a disciple and contain many errors and omissions; I shall correct them one by one. There is as yet no record of the arousal of the bodhi mind; I have now asked Mr. Liao to write out a copy for you, and although it is in two hands, it may be printed together. If you write a postscript at the end of the volume, you must by no means use words of excessive praise or exaggeration. All my life, in drawing people in, I have mostly used the Pure Land contemplation, and only when they had succeeded did I grant them the one vehicle.

In learning the profound contemplation there are two conditions: first, to rely on a teacher for several years, so that the faculties are clearly ascertained; second, to succeed in the Pure Land contemplation and understand dependent origination. Only when these two are present may it be taught. Why, when the arousal of the mind has barely been discussed, would you wish to empty the whole basket and tip out the whole chest? The Dharma of Bodhidharma and the Tiantai and Xianshou teachings have one and the same destination, though their points of entry differ. Do try to practice what I have granted you, and do not give rise to doubt. Now that you have found the path and asked the way, you should apply your mind single-mindedly and not waste the hours; this is of the utmost importance, of the utmost importance!
Here I record
verses from the Ratnakuta Sutra
to encourage you:
Though one should build jewelled stupas, as many as the sands of the Ganges;
Though to the end of future time one should wander through all Buddha-lands;
[To ponder this matter] ‘To ponder’ means to observe; ‘this matter’ means the mind-nature.
The following are verses from the Avatamsaka Sutra:
Whenever you grow weary of sitting, recite these verses; interest will well up and you will be able to advance diligently again. Strive on, strive on!
The eleventh day of the fifth month, summer of the thirty-sixth year.

I have read your letter carefully; its earnestness is beyond compare, a frank disclosure of the truth such as I have never before received. (Fuli) is old and sick, his fingers stiff and his hand trembling, with no strength to write; questions gush forth like a spring — how shall I answer them all? (In recent years, in replying to people, I stop at a few dozen words on a small note; never have I answered anyone at such length as you.) Yet a question from ten thousand li away — how can I turn it aside? I shall choose the essentials and answer them. To benefit others one must first benefit oneself; only when one has perfected oneself can one perfect others. (Printing the book is entirely unnecessary; in years of disorder and chaos one should especially spare the expense.) I hope you will be silent and contemplate the mind, and not let words and letters become an obstruction. The manuscript you copied I have checked through one by one. The questions you raised are answered separately on another sheet. You should know that this manuscript is throughout a brief exposition, meant to awaken right faith. If you wish to practice in earnest, there are more detailed instructions besides. (One may contemplate the mind without forming the mudra, and so the method of sitting was not set out in detail.) Every sutra has its implications, awaiting someone to draw them out; why should this one alone be different? Therefore I urge you to put your strength into contemplating the mind, and you will of yourself gain much learning.

I am now writing out my answers to your letter, correcting and striking out as I please, which is hardly respectful. But I know that you, worthy sir, seek the Dharma with a true heart, and in your postscript you have understood my meaning fairly well. The Sutra of the Contemplation of the Mind of the Great Vehicle says: ‘If there be a good man or good woman who hears this wondrous Dharma and it but once passes the ear, then in a single moment, gathering in the thoughts and contemplating the mind, he perfumes it into the supreme seed of great bodhi.’ It also says: ‘If one can cultivate the profound and wondrous contemplation, the fruits of delusion, karma, and suffering have no way to arise; only by contemplating the true mark, the real nature of suchness, do both subject and object perish, and one is free of all views.’ I hope you will constantly review and cultivate the sutra verses above, and then my wish will be fulfilled. Your discriminating mind is far too fierce; you should know that discrimination is deluded thought, is delusion and karma, and is directly opposed to arousing the mind and cultivating the practice of no-thought. As for the complete lecture record, every word of its sutras and treatises has a source; were I to note each one, the text would double in size — by no means necessary.
The five answers to your questions are listed below:
1. Question: How do the arousal of the mind, the Dharma of Bodhidharma, and the other perfect and sudden dharmas differ and agree?

Answer: The names differ but the substance is the same; only the three-vehicle dharmas are slightly different, and the progress of the Chan gate is somewhat different, yet all take seeing the nature as their destination. Guifeng says: the one lineage of Bodhidharma is the common road of the Buddha-Dharma (the same as ‘way’), on which Chan and the teachings alike rely, though their points of entry and the paths they take differ.
2. Question: Why must the Chan gate be furnished with great merit and blessing?
Answer: To hollow out (
kū

, to scoop out) the mind and see the nature — in this there is no realm whatsoever in between, and it differs from the contemplative practice; one must possess true faith before one can begin to walk it. The gate of contemplation has realms that can be taken as conditions, and so is easier. Great faith is great merit and blessing, and is not within the power of those of weak faculties.
3. Question: When the contemplation of the mind is finished, to what should one dedicate it?
4. In the text on arousing the mind, it would seem that passages on guarding against demons, removing obstructions, and the marks of realization should be added; what do you think?

Answer: It is not necessary. This is a hastily taken down manuscript, not a written work. (If there is need, one may read the Awakening of Faith.) If there is true practice, it must be received from a teacher; the various states will become clear of themselves, and no single word can exhaust them.
5. The three Pure Land sutras and the Vaipulya sutras speak differently; I wish to hear the reason.
[Vaipulya sutras] The general name for the Mahayana sutras.

Answer: The teaching of the Pure Land takes the larger and smaller Amitābha sutras and the Contemplation Sutra as its basis. The smaller Amitābha Sutra governs the holding of the name, the larger Amitābha Sutra governs the arousal of the mind, and the Contemplation Sutra governs cultivating contemplation and arousing the mind; these are the Buddha’s words. In the Vaipulya sutras it is said that Amitābha is self-nature and the Pure Land is mind-only; though this seems to go a step further, in truth the two dharmas are one and the same meaning. Yet for the universal covering of the many capacities, the three sutras are the essential thing, and one should not propound the lofty Vaipulya theme alone, to the confusion of middling and lesser capacities. Therefore the earlier letter said: too profound a mystery turns against the sutras.
The twenty-first day of the fifth month, summer of the thirty-sixth year.

I have just received the corrected manuscript of the arousal of the mind and have checked and settled it; it may go forward. You propose first to publish it in Awakened Sentient Beings — excellent, excellent! Those with the affinity will of themselves obtain it; those without the affinity will not believe even if compelled. The lecture record, through your repeated examination, has gradually reached completeness. On reflection, the chapter on what practice to cultivate seems out of keeping, and I shall rewrite it. You love the Dharma and take joy in it, and your sincerity is wholly revealed; I look forward with expectant eyes to its speedy completion. Strive on, strive on! Your questions are answered as follows:

1. The mind-contemplation Dharma-gate is Tathagata Chan; one need only practice it diligently and transcend and realize directly, without having to read the teachings. If one wishes to read the teachings, the Lankavatara Sutra and the Sutra of the Meaning of Intention are the best. Your study of doctrine is shallow, and these two sutras are not suitable for you; only the Sutra of the Contemplation of the Mind of the Great Vehicle is most suitable, and even that may be too long, so I first set out its essentials as a gift. As the Sutra of the Contemplation of the Mind of the Great Vehicle says: ‘You ordinary beings do not contemplate your own minds, and therefore drift about in the sea of birth and death. The Buddhas and bodhisattvas, because they can contemplate the mind, cross the sea of birth and death and reach the other shore.’ It also says: ‘Hard is it to see, hard is it to hear, this Dharma-gate of the mind-ground of the right way of bodhi. If there be a good man or good woman who hears this wondrous Dharma and it but once passes the ear, then in a single moment, gathering in the thoughts and contemplating the mind, he perfumes it into the supreme seed of great bodhi, and before long will sit on the diamond jewelled throne at the king of bodhi trees and attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.’ It also says in verse: ‘If one can cultivate the profound and wondrous contemplation, the fruits of delusion, karma, and suffering have no way to arise; only by contemplating the true mark, the real nature of suchness, do both subject and object perish, and one is free of all views.’ It also says: ‘Contemplate one’s own body and mind as no different from a withered tree, a wall, or broken tiles, and have no discrimination regarding any dharma. I contemplate body and mind as a dream or an illusion, with nothing real within; thought after thought they age, and when the breath has gone out it does not enter again.’ It also says that this Dharma is called the supreme secret mind-ground Dharma-gate of the Tathagatas of the ten directions; that this Dharma is called the Dharma-gate of sudden enlightenment by which all ordinary beings enter the Tathagata’s ground; and that this Dharma is called the true and right road by which all bodhisattvas proceed to the great bodhi of great bodhisattvas. Twenty-six phrases in all (Sutra of the Contemplation of the Mind of the Great Vehicle, juan 8, page 2); from this one may know the importance of the Dharma of the mind. This time, in printing the book, you even wished to cut into your own property, and I strongly stopped you. Please look at juan 2, page 14 of this sutra, where the Buddha speaks of three kinds of ten paramitas: first, the ten kinds of the paramita of giving; second, the ten kinds of the paramita of drawing near; third, the ten kinds of the true paramita. The first two, giving, are not yet called repaying the kindness; the third kind, arousing the supreme bodhi mind, dwelling in nothing obtainable, and urging all sentient beings to arouse this same mind, is alone called truly able to repay the four kindnesses. You must put your strength into contemplating the mind; this is true giving, this is true repayment of kindness, and the Buddhas approve it.

[Doctrinal study] The study of the meanings of terms and names, the study of theory, also called the study of understanding. Such as the studies of the Treasury of Abhidharma and of Consciousness-Only, which analyze the categories and numbers of the dharma-marks and set out in detail the organization of the stages and fruits of practice and the explanation of the words and phrases of the texts; that is, learning concerned with the theory of the teachings.

2. As for your question about dealing with demons, you bring up the sequential dhyana as an example — how strange, how extreme is this wrong clinging! The gates of Chan are measureless, but in broad division there are only two: first, the dhyana of calm abiding and insight, to which the sequential dharmas and the like belong; second, Tathagata Chan, which speaks only of seeing the nature and does not discuss dhyana or liberation — what realm of demons could there be in it? Let me ask: in the whole of the Five Lamps Meeting at the Source, what chapter discusses the matter of demons? Why do you doubt the one vehicle by means of the three vehicles? But then, is there absolutely no demon in learning Tathagata Chan? It is answered: there is. First, when the causal ground is not true; second, when the discriminating mind is strong; third, when one acts recklessly without a teacher. How could there be no demon? Conversely, there is absolutely no demon — why add feet to a drawing of a snake? That you take pleasure in the easy and simple and cultivate this Dharma — this is your causal ground not being true. You should know that this Dharma is the sudden-enlightenment Dharma-gate by which ordinary beings enter the Tathagata’s ground. It points directly at the human mind, and one sees the nature and becomes a Buddha. You must have a keen sense of birth and death, seek to see the original nature, and take joy in practicing it — only then is it a true cause; all else is not true. Bury your head and practice in fine detail; do not give rise to discrimination; take enlightenment as the term. If you have doubts, ask freely, but do not act recklessly — then the causes of demons are utterly cut off.

3. You ask about the states and marks after enlightenment. This was already explained in the text on arousing the mind: all samādhis, supernormal powers, and the rest appear from the mind. Why is it that you know only the words and not the meaning? That you devote yourself to the outside and not to the inside! That you ask about names, marks, and textual research, and do not diligently contemplate the mind! These three are your own flesh-and-blood illnesses, and you should strive to change them. (When I wrote that letter I did not know that you were in the midst of editing, and so raised this sort of question — my fault, my fault. Yet what is said here is most correct and most essential, and so I still send it for your reading.)

4. The subduing of demons and the marks of realization need not be included in the book. This belongs to the gate of sudden enlightenment; practicing in reliance on a teacher, with the Buddhas’ added blessing, there is decidedly no demon. Enlightenment itself is the patient endurance of the non-arising of dharmas — what marks of realization are there to discuss? The three-vehicle dharmas cannot in a single burst attain the patient endurance of the non-arising of dharmas, and so there are various marks of realization by which to test their falsity. Your letter says that the eyes grow cool and the belly warm: this is the dharma of the four dhyanas and eight concentrations, that is, the dhyana of calm abiding and insight, not Tathagata Chan, and it should be abandoned at once. This is markless contemplation, and one should not grasp at realms. When sitting, one need not be limited to the hours of mao and you. (Zi, wu, mao, and you are the words of the externalists.) In the Buddha-Dharma, throughout the six periods of the day and night and within the four dignified postures, the contemplation of the mind does not stop, save only at mealtimes. Therefore the earlier letter said: one may contemplate the mind without forming the mudra or sitting.
The twentieth day of the seventh month, autumn of the thirty-sixth year.

I have received two letters in succession; your heart and soul lie open before me. Why should you be so anxious all at once? The fault is mine! Yet this polishing is by no means to be dispensed with. You should know that my bond with you is a prajñā affinity, and has nothing to do with fame or profit; you should strive after purity. The least touch of suspicion and you enter the net of demons. Hereafter, question and answer as much as you like; I only hope that you may quickly awaken. The title of the book is settled as The Essentials of the Buddha-Dharma, to avoid duplication. Someone says that the two sections explaining the Lankavatara this time might be appended and printed at the end of the volume; I do not know what you think of it. Quickly arouse the mind and practice, and you will receive the Buddha’s prediction. Strive on, strive on! The answers to your questions are listed below:

Question: On what sutra is this mind-contemplation method based? My teacher often cites the Sutra of the Contemplation of the Mind; is it perhaps based on this sutra? Yet what this sutra teaches is the moon-disc contemplation; why does he not have one contemplate the moon, but has one contemplate the mind? This doubt is not yet cleared; I beg you to teach me.
Answer:

1. The sutra relied upon. Every contemplative practice must rest on the meaning of a sutra. The method I have granted you rests on the Lankavatara Sutra, not on the Sutra of the Contemplation of the Mind. The Sutra of the Contemplation of the Mind explains the mind-contemplation method in the greatest detail, and I cite it as evidence. In truth this Tathagata Chan takes the Lankavatara as its root, and it was for this reason that Bodhidharma transmitted the mind by means of it. The Tang translation of the Lankavatara Sutra, juan 3, says: “Mahamati the bodhisattva-mahasattva again said to the Buddha: ‘World-Honored One, may it please you to speak of the marks of the practice of the realization of sagely wisdom, and of the marks of the practice of the one vehicle, so that I and the bodhisattva-mahasattvas, having gained this skill in means, may in the Buddha-Dharma be enlightened without depending on another.’ The Buddha said: ‘Listen well; I shall speak for you.’ Mahamati said: ‘So be it.’ The Buddha said: ‘Mahamati, the bodhisattva-mahasattva, relying on the sagely teachings, is without discrimination. Dwelling alone in quiet retreat, he observes self-awakening, is enlightened without depending on another, is free of the view of discrimination, and advancing upward step by step, enters the ground of the Tathagata. Such cultivation is called the mark of the practice of self-realized sagely wisdom. What is called the mark of the practice of the one vehicle? It is the certifying knowledge of the one-vehicle path. What is called knowing the one-vehicle path? It is dwelling as it really is, free from the discrimination of the grasping subject and the grasped object. Mahamati, this one-vehicle path, save for the Tathagata alone, cannot be attained by the externalists, the two vehicles, Brahma the heaven king, or others.’” This sutra is the master key, and no doubt may be raised about it. If one cites the Lankavatara, the evidence is very plentiful; but its phrases are profound and expansive, and not easy to understand. Therefore I take the Contemplation of the Mind chapter as the evidence, since this is the common meaning of the Vaipulya teaching.
Question: Are the samādhis certified by Buddha-recitation and by cultivating contemplation the same or different? Are there shallow and deep ones? I respectfully beg you to explain.

Answer: The smaller Amitābha Sutra speaks of holding the name to the point of single-mindedness and non-disturbance; the Contemplation Sutra speaks of the Buddha-recitation samādhi. I say that the two sutras have different points of entry, yet the samādhi is not different. Why? The Amitābha (Sutra) takes the holding of the name as its main point, while the Contemplation Sutra contemplates the marks of the dependent and the direct retributions. Contemplating marks employs the mind more finely, while holding the name seems shallow. Yet if one can hold the name with samādhi, it is by no means not fine. Single-mindedness and non-disturbance: non-disturbance is concentration, and concentration is samādhi; since it comes from reciting the Buddha, it is called the Buddha-recitation samādhi. What is meant by the samādhi of the two sutras being equal? The treatise says: samādhi is the one-pointedness of mind upon a single object. Yet though the samādhi is equal, at this stage there is shallow and there is deep. The shallow one has mind and object undistracted, and the two retributions, dependent and direct, appear in their surpassing wonder, but he cannot bring forth the true unconditioned. The deep one, on attaining samādhi, at once brings forth the true unconditioned. These two capacities, shallow and deep, must be examined as the occasion arises, and taught according to the capacity. These two kinds of people will certainly be reborn in the Pure Land. The shallow one is not necessarily of the upper grade; the deep one is certainly reborn in the uppermost grade of the upper birth. I urge you to arouse the bodhi mind; this is the preparation for bringing forth the true later on. Again, the Buddha-recitation samādhi differs among the sutras and is not of a single kind. Earlier you asked about one-vehicle Buddha-recitation (that is, reciting the Dharma-body Buddha); this samādhi is the most supreme, and its source opens forth from the bodhi mind. Let me give one mark to make this clear: the Buddha-recitation samādhi of the Pure Land has a lotus flower as large as a cartwheel, or at most some yojanas in size. It is not so with the one-vehicle Buddha-recitation samādhi. On attaining that samādhi, the lotus throne is equal in measure to a trichiliocosm. How then can they be called the same? Why is there such a difference? The one-vehicle Buddha-recitation comes from the contemplation of the bodhi mind, and so attains the dharma-body. The Pure Land contemplation comes from the transformation-body and does not know the dharma-body; hence the difference.

Question: Should the two gates of Chan and Pure Land be cultivated exclusively, or should both be cultivated? Among my friends in the Pure Land, all who have seen my teacher’s lecture record are filled with joy and praise, and call it rare. Someone says: if the essential sayings of Chan Master Chewu were appended and printed at the end of the book, so that Chan and Pure Land were spread abroad together, that would be excellent. I do not know what your honored opinion is.

Answer: Your letter is full of contention (repeated calculation) over whether Chan and Pure Land should be cultivated together and spread abroad together. I say that this clings to the name and does not know the substance. Why? The two gates of Chan and Pure Land were originally one dharma. To arouse the bodhi mind is Tathagata Chan; it is to recite the Dharma-body Buddha, and thus already includes both — why speak again of including? To recite the Dharma-body Buddha is to recite the Buddha by means of reality, which is the most supreme vehicle of the Pure Land school, and it is already spread abroad — why speak again of spreading abroad? You should know that to recite the transformation-body alone, without knowing the dharma-body, brings a very low grade of rebirth. The crucial point is whether, on attaining samādhi, the true unconditioned is brought forth or not. If it is brought forth, one awakens and enters the first meaning; if not, one remains stuck in the transformation-land. Therefore the one dharma of contemplating the mind is, whether in Chan or in Pure Land, the most essential meaning — why debate whether they are combined or not? If you must cling to names, then taking the arousal of the mind as the primary and the holding of the name as the auxiliary is also acceptable. There is no need to drag in the recorded sayings of Chewu and the other Dharma-gates.
Question: What is called factual concentration? What is called concentration in principle? I beg you to explain.

Answer: The externalists too have dhyana concentration; the reason they are not the equal of the Buddha-Dharma and in the end fall back is this: the Buddha-Dharma’s dhyana concentrations are measureless, but in broad division they are factual concentration and concentration in principle. Factual concentration contemplates marks alone; concentration in principle must enter the principle of true emptiness. Let me give an example to make this clear: the four immeasurables — loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity — the externalists cultivate them too, yet they cannot share them with the Buddha-Dharma. Why? These four dharmas have three levels of meaning: first, the condition of sentient beings; second, the condition of dharmas; third, the unconditioned. The externalists who cultivate these four dharmas know only the condition of sentient beings and do not know the latter two. The condition of sentient beings is mark, is fact; the latter two are principle. The externalists do not know mind-only — how could they enter the principle? It is not so with the Buddha-Dharma: where there is a conditioned mark, one must enter the principle, and so the latter two are the weightiest. The Pure Land Dharma is likewise. When one attains samādhi and sees only a surpassing and wondrous realm, that is purely factual concentration; only when one attains the true unconditioned can one enter the principle. The sutra says: ‘To be able to contemplate the mind-nature is called supreme concentration.’ This is the contemplative practice that enters the principle. Further, when one attains the Buddha-recitation samādhi, as was said above, the true unconditioned may or may not be brought forth. There are two causes for its being brought forth: first, having perfumed it in a former life; second, arousing the bodhi mind in this life. For its not being brought forth the causes are the reverse: the perfuming of a former life cannot be made up for, (whereas) arousing the mind in this life brings great aid. Therefore ask only whether the mind is aroused or not, and do not ask whether the two are cultivated together. Moreover, the arousal of the mind requires the wisdom of non-discrimination; the wisdom of non-discrimination is the great prajñā — what need is there to debate combining? Do not cling to names and so lose the true meaning.
The nineteenth day of the ninth month, autumn of the thirty-sixth year.

I have just received your two letters; besides answering your questions, I shall briefly reply to the main points. In my late years I have gained you, a brother by nature fond of the Way — it is wholly a matter of former affinity. You should take it seriously to heart and not let it pass by. As for your illness, you should care for it well. Judged by karmic retribution, I fear long life will be hard to attain. Judged by the Buddha-Dharma, one who can truly arouse the mind (cannot) fail to attain long life. (The Record of the Mirror of the Teaching says: ‘The seed is the root of life.’ To arouse the mind can transform the seed, and so it is a dharma of long life. It also says: the root of life is posited in dependence on the mind; life is what depends, the mind is that on which it depends, and life’s dependence on the mind is like the passions’ dependence on the mind.)

I shall dedicate the merit for you (this is the condition), and you should truly arouse the bodhi mind and practice according to my method, sitting two or three times each day (this is the cause). This is the first dharma. Second, you must be free of desire. All lung disease, wheezing and coughing, comes from youthful indulgence in desire, and so the Buddha-Treasury Sutra has the instruction to be free of desire and free of views. Third, regulate food and sleep. Fourth, let medicine assist.

You fear that your years will not be long and that this life will hardly suffice. If you can truly arouse the mind, then even if this life does not accomplish it, the next life will surely bring it to completion. What Yongming said — “once one puts forth one’s head, at a single hearing one awakens to a thousand” — is in the end no empty word, for one perfumes it constantly. You may learn to practice the food offering and not let it be interrupted, for this is a cause of long life. Or hold the name of Guanyin, who responds to every prayer. You ask me to write a preface; this is a small matter of affinity — why write one? And there is no need to ask another to write one either. My brief explanation of the Lankavatara this time came about because you and Mr. Li Shaoyuan asked me why I do not grant the moon-disc contemplation but have people contemplate the mind; and so I set it out to show its basis.

[Brief explanation of the Lankavatara] Mr. Zhuyuan’s book The Essentials of the Buddha-Dharma has three parts: the upper part, the essential meaning in four lines; the middle part, the arousal of the bodhi mind; the lower part, a brief explanation of the Lankavatara.

It took me only one hour (that is, one hour by the clock) to give this teaching. Liao Jihui recorded it in a little over an hour; it was not composed beforehand. Liao Jihui is a celibate woman. She graduated from the Women’s Normal College and taught for more than twenty years. She has taken refuge with me for more than twenty years as well. For the past two years, all the answers to your questions have come from Liao’s hand, because my hand trembles and I cannot write much. Lately she has lived in my house for two years, cultivating contemplation and studying the teachings, and is about to return home. Hereafter I shall be hard put to it to find someone to take her place. The answers to your questions are listed below:

1. Question: How should one work when in motion? Answer: Just as when still. Before the contemplation of the mind is ripe, there is a distinction between motion and stillness; once it is ripe, motion and stillness are no different. The Chan gate says: ‘Among a thousand and ten thousand people, be as though there were not one; amid the myriad affairs in turmoil, be as though there were not one affair.’ From this one may know that motion and stillness are one. Beginners have not yet attained concentration, and so the patriarchs taught people to ‘keep and carry it along,’ meaning that in meeting affairs and dealing with people one should always keep and carry along this method of contemplating the mind. You need not worry; with long practice you will understand of yourself. I shall cite a passage of the Lankavatara Sutra for your use. The sutra says: ‘Contemplate all dharmas as without self-nature, like clouds in the sky, like a fire-wheel spun in the dark, like a city of the gandharvas, like an illusion, like a flame, like the moon in the water, like things seen in a dream, not apart from one’s own mind. Because of beginningless false views, one takes them as external. Having made this contemplation, one cuts off the conditions of discrimination and is also free of the names and meanings grasped by the deluded mind. Know that body and things, together with the place where one dwells, are all the realm of the storehouse consciousness, without grasping subject or grasped object, and without arising, dwelling, or ceasing. Thus pondering, one dwells in it without letting go.’ If you savor this passage of sutra in your mind, deep faith will arise. That you are unable to do so has two causes: first, the doctrine is not familiar; second, the power of concentration is not yet achieved. In short, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, you must never be apart from the contemplation of the mind.

2. Question: That the arousal of the bodhi mind is Tathagata Chan and is the recitation of the Dharma-body Buddha, so that Chan and Pure Land are not two — I have already received your instruction. But then, are the so-called one-vehicle Buddha-recitation and Buddha-recitation by means of reality both other names for the arousal of the mind? Answer: They are. (Question:) Are the contemplation of the mind and the contemplation of the dharma-realm the same or different? Are there shallow and deep? Answer: The contemplation of the mind is the contemplation of the dharma-realm; there is no same or different, no shallow or deep, and one must not follow the name and be blind to the substance. (Question:) As for the three levels of meaning of the four immeasurable minds, please teach me again. Answer: The condition of sentient beings means seeing all the sentient beings of the trichiliocosm in the sea of suffering, and drawing each one out of suffering and giving each one joy. This meaning is shared by the externalists and the Buddha-Dharma. The condition of dharmas means that all sentient beings are marks of the aggregates, realms, and fields (the five aggregates, the eighteen realms, and the twelve fields), and that within them there is no person at all. The unconditioned means that the aggregates, realms, and fields are without nature and are empty, that there is no dharma at all, only the nature. In the condition of sentient beings, person and dharma are both present. In the condition of dharmas, there is dharma but no person. In the unconditioned, there is nature but no dharma. (Question:) What is meant by the one-pointedness of mind upon a single object? Answer: Concentration has seven names, and this is one of them. The old translation renders the factor of dhyana as the factor of one mind; the Tang Tripitaka master translated it as the one-pointedness of mind upon a single object. It means that when one attains dhyana concentration, the mind is single and undistracted, dwelling exclusively on one kind of object; this is called the nature of the mind dwelling on a single object. This explains the mark of concentration, and it is divided into the defiled and the undefiled. The defiled is consciousness, and is attained by the externalists and the three vehicles alike; the undefiled is suchness, and is attained by the one vehicle alone.

3. Question: In the scriptures, what is the meaning of 'thus' and of 'suchness'? It is answered: 'Thus' is emptiness. Prajñā says: 'Dharmas being thus, this is the Buddha.' And it says: 'The Tathagata is none other than the meaning of dharmas being thus.' The mind being thus means the mind is empty; the realm being thus means the realm is empty. Maitreya too is thus; these words come from the Vimalakirti [Sutra], and they discuss the substance, and so Maitreya is classed together with living beings. (Question:) What is meant by the mind and the realm not reaching one another? It is answered: That the mind and realm reach one another belongs to the realm of the karmic consciousness. For instance, in putting on clothes and eating a meal, the clothing reaches the body and the food reaches the mouth. As for the realm of right wisdom and Dharma-nature, it is neither a faculty, nor an object, nor a consciousness; it is empty and without boundary, and only by self-realization does one know it. (Question:) What is meant by 'not reaching'? And what is meant by 'the mind not being different'? It is answered: When sundry thoughts arise, that is difference; when there are no sundry thoughts, that is 'thus.'

4. What the Lankavatara Concordance says, 'contemplate that false thoughts are originally without self-nature,' is one with what I have said. Why? False thoughts are ignorance; to contemplate false thoughts as without nature is to contemplate the ignorant mind. In the Buddha Dharma all dharmas are without self-nature; how could this ignorance alone have a nature? The one thing is that it instructs people to investigate exhaustively the place from which false thoughts arise, and this statement is greatly mistaken! For exhaustive investigation requires the use of the intellect. But this method of contemplating the mind is apart from mind, intention, and consciousness; how could there be any principle of using the intellect? Simply gaze on it directly and that is all; there is no need for exhaustive investigation. The ancients said: 'When the light of the mind shines through, the remaining blemishes exhaust themselves.' How concise and essential! What need is there to deliberate and inquire into it?

5. Of the Lankavatara, the Tang translation is the best. The ancients took the three translations as one sutra, the same text rendered differently; but I say the three translations are three sutras, which may be used for mutual reference. The Song translation came first; when the ancients raised and expounded it, they mostly cited the Song text, yet in the end it is not as fine as the Tang translation. As for the commentaries, the works of the Six Dynasties and Tang men have all perished; only Xianshou's two juan, the Profound Meaning of the Lankavatara, still survive (published by the Jinling Sutra Engraving Office), and they are the most subtle. Nagarjuna commented on this sutra in a thousand juan, but it was never translated into this land. Ming monks commented on it in more than ten kinds, and only Hanshan and Ouyi are somewhat acceptable; none of them can carry on Xianshou.
The first day of the eleventh month, winter of the thirty-sixth year.

In the autumn I was at Chengdu, Guanghan, and Deyang, lingering to give lectures, and there I often met fine people. On my return I received your letter, with a letter from Mr. He Huizhao enclosed. You asked me to appraise and answer it, which I dare not presume to do. Interpreting Mr. He's intent, there are about three doubts, which I briefly answer here:

1. He doubts that the method of arousing the bodhi mind is too elevated, suited to those of superior faculties and not to those of middling or lower. It is answered: it is not too high. Without arousing the mind, nothing is genuine. The Avatamsaka says: 'As when taking medicine, if the medicine does not suit the illness one may change it again and again; only the water, the single flavor, may not be changed.' The water is a simile for the bodhi mind. Later teachers speak of the Buddha-name recitation and not of arousing the bodhi mind, first because the ignorant do not know of it, and second because their method is incomplete. Now the three Pure Land sutras, the Larger Amitābha [Sutra] and the Contemplation [Sutra], both contain passages on arousing the bodhi mind. To say that the Smaller Amitābha [Sutra] has none is wrong. This sutra contains the phrase 'non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-sambodhi'; if one had not already aroused the mind beforehand, of what then would it speak of not retreating? This meaning has never been pointed out by anyone; think on it and it becomes clear of itself.

2. He doubts that one who recites the Buddha-name should also practice arousing the bodhi mind, fearing it to be a mixing of practices. It is answered: it is not mixed. In reciting the Buddha-name, is one not seeking one mind undisturbed? (One who has never contemplated the mind, from where would he know one mind undisturbed?) The method of arousing the bodhi mind enters directly into the realm of the one mind; how could it be called mixed? Moreover, in our recitation of the Buddha-name from morning till night, can the threefold karma of body, speech, and mind be, thought after thought, never apart from the Buddha? In dealing with affairs and meeting people, can we be, even for an instant, never apart from the Buddha? If you say, 'Not so, we are apart from the Buddha more often than not,' then as to this falling away you do not regard it as a defect of mixing; that a single arousing of the bodhi mind alone you condemn as mixed, is that admissible? For one who studies the Dharma to reject the arousing of the bodhi mind, I fear there is no justification in it.

3. He doubts that those of superior faculties are few. It is answered: they are very many. I say that of ten thousand people, nine thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine are of superior faculties; there is only one of the lowest, lowest faculties. He says: How is it then that none of them succeeds? It is answered: They lack faith; it is not that their faculties are defective. Consider the six kinds of people set forth in the Bhadrakalpa Sutra: before they arouse the mind, who could determine that they were of superior faculties? The Diamond Sutra says: 'Living beings, living beings, the Tathagata says they are not living beings, and so they are called living beings.' The Neo-Confucian scholars of the Confucian school do not allow it to be said that there are no good people in the world; the perfect and sudden masters of the Buddhist school do not allow it to be said that living beings have inferior faculties. (Because they have not yet been carved; once carved, they become vessels.) Someone may say: Why do the Chan school always speak of needing the highest, highest faculties? It is answered: This is a word of warning, a meaning of urging upward. Whatever the Chan school says is a living phrase. If one clings to it as real, that is one-sided discrimination and it becomes a dead sentence; how could that be called understanding words!
Kindly convey these three meanings tactfully.
The twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month, winter of the thirty-sixth year.

All my life I have had no teacher and yet I first studied the learning of the scriptures, which honors the teacher's method and does not muddle. I used that method to read the books of the nature and appearance schools, and to govern the studies of the Tiantai and Xianshou schools. Later I entered the Chan school, the rules of its gate unconfused, and so amid having no teacher I found a teacher. Looking back at the ancients, none of them were otherwise; how different from your own lack of order and plan! Your fondness for the Dharma is earnest indeed, yet you resemble a general merchandise stall, and this is why it is hard for you to succeed, because you have no teacher. Do not make yourself a field over which the water merely flows, and only then will you get somewhere.

Your illness is due to reading too many books and to exerting effort while seated. Reading can be moderated; in sitting meditation one must let everything go, so why exert effort? To exert effort is to cling, and with clinging how can one contemplate the mind? You should correct this firmly, and then the illness will easily heal and the contemplation will easily succeed. (The Verse on the Faith Mind says: 'Keep nothing, hold nothing to remember; the empty brightness reflects itself, and does not weary the mind and thought.' The Essentials of the Mind-Dharma Transmission says: 'Still thought and forget deliberation, and the Buddha appears of itself before you.'
'Straight away become without mind, and the original substance appears of itself.' Both make clear the method of letting go and contemplating the mind, appended by Hongshu.)

You ask whether there is any further method. This is a remark showing you have not yet grasped the flavor of the Dharma. The three phrases of Bodhidharma encompass everything. The Sixth Patriarch's 'not thinking of good, not thinking of evil' is precisely 'externally, still all conditions.' 'At just this such moment' is precisely 'internally, the mind has no panting.' The sentences differ, but how could there be two? When one reaches 'at just this such moment,' it is only a single unmoving flavor, carried on as a single thought for ten thousand years; what further method could there be? 'What, Reverend Ming, is your original face?' is a question, and is called 'setting off the trigger.' (The doctrinal school calls it the constant mechanism. Buddhism takes the mind as the mechanism, and so it says: in a single thought the wheel turns back, and one is the same as one's original possession.) The Chan school says: the mysterious gate of the ordinary man is tightly shut, and the lock of consciousness is hard to open. The mechanism is precisely the mysterious gate; one of superior faculties casts a single word into it, striking and setting off its trigger, and he thereupon awakens at once. Yet the most important thing in this gongan is the three words 'at such a moment' (that is, the moment of not thinking good or evil); this is the secret of the Chan school. If one who has aroused the mind can thus dwell the mind, then awakening is not far off. The patriarchs said: 'At such a moment is called the time before the Buddha is born.' It is also called dwelling at the summit, of incomparable dignity and worth. If in a single day one can dwell the mind thus for several hours, only then is it in accord with the Dharma. There will of itself be the occasion that sets off the trigger; one need not await another's direction. The patriarchs said: 'If only you can be at such a moment, do not worry that you will not fully awaken.' This belongs to the secret essentials of the mind-method, and may be practiced with all one's strength.

Someone does not know that the mind itself is the Buddha, and says that in contemplating the mind one does not rely on the Buddha's power, and so fears one may not be reborn in the West; let him go ahead and recite the name as he pleases. The ancients said: 'The moment the bodhisattva first arouses the bodhi mind (that is, contemplates the mind), the Buddhas at once draw him into the Pure Land.' (Bear this sentence firmly in mind.) The people of the world value the recitation of the name and slight the contemplation of the mind, or make them into two separate matters; how laughable! Editing and collating should be done little, while contemplation of the mind should be done diligently (one may contemplate anywhere, and is not limited to sitting meditation; just contemplate on and on, and there is no need to read many books), taking awakening as the appointed time, and this will never cheat you.
Excerpts from several letters of the thirty-seventh year.

You seek only a great deal of hearing without earnestly contemplating the mind, and are very far from the Buddha Dharma. Turn back quickly, and it is not yet too late! The most laughable thing is that you ask what it is like after seeing the nature; this is reciting the words without knowing their meaning. Now, seeing the nature and becoming a Buddha is an everyday saying, and you do not understand it at all. Why? When it is said 'seeing the nature,' one has become a Buddha. A Buddha is wisdom, is bodhi. The words of Yongjia are the marks of the accomplishment of wisdom. To gain the accomplishment of wisdom one must contemplate the mind; that you do not contemplate the mind but merely recite its words, is that not laughable? In studying the Dharma one should have a great aim and a firm conduct; why must you ask others about seeing the nature, showing only stubbornness and weakness? Your illness: first, self-will. Second, you want to open a general merchandise stall. (You wish to gather the Buddha Dharma into a new compilation of proved prescriptions; if that could be done, the ancients would have done it long ago.) Third, you do not apply effort. I now advise you to contemplate the mind calmly for two or three months, and see whether there is any improvement; otherwise it is hard to cure. When applying effort, you must let go of all things; only by letting go can you contemplate the mind. There is no need to read books, for they only confuse the mind.
Day by day do the work of taming and subduing, and the thoughts of the mind become clear and still, and wisdom is then born

; this is an expedient means for entering the principle, and you must not neglect it because it is small. As for one who contemplates the mind, the mind is the Pure Land; to contemplate it is precisely faith, vow, and practice, and one is at once reborn in the Pure Land. The mind is the Buddha-nature of suchness, and that is the Land. Therefore the arousing of the bodhi mind is the Buddha-name recitation of the highest meaning. There is an invitation from Chengdu, and I shall shortly be on the road again for a few months more of traveling. (Spring, the twentieth day of the second month.)

You should apply your whole mind to cultivating the method of arousing the bodhi mind. Unless this pass is penetrated, it is hard to enter the gate all at once. This method is simply contemplating the mind, letting go of the myriad affairs and myriad conditions in a single stroke; in time one naturally finds the entry. Do not greet it, do not chase it, do not demand results. '
With a mind emptied, return home having passed the examination.'

Think on it, think on it. You are fond of investigating on the level of words and phrases and do not observe on the level of the thought of the mind, so entering the principle is a little harder. But if only in a single thought the wheel turns back, what difficulty is there? In late spring there is much rain; take good care of yourself.

I arrived in the provincial capital (that is, the Sichuan provincial capital Chengdu) on the twenty-fourth, and began lecturing on the Shurangama, using the Correct Lineage commentary. The Tang commentaries on this sutra have all perished; only in the Record of the Mirror of the Teaching can one catch a glimpse of them; the rest were all made by Song and Yuan masters. The Ming monks wavered between the two, and none of them was good. Only Master Jiaoguang, in his Correct Lineage commentary, refuted the old explanations wholesale; not only are the Ming men unable to match him, but the Song and Yuan masters cannot so much as see the dust of his heels. Because this master was a student of the Avatamsaka, and explained this sutra as an expedient entrance into the Avatamsaka, and so he stands transcendent. You ask whether there are any records [of these lectures]; if there are, I will send them; if not, do not await them in expectation. You ask also what book it is best to read; the Essentials of the Mind of Yuanwu is best, and I will later send you a copy. This printing of books (referring to the publication of the book The Essentials of the Buddha Dharma) has burdened you far too much. Once the printing is done, my vow to spread the Dharma is fulfilled; from now on I look only to cultivate the Dharma calmly, without interval and without break. Contemplating the mind and nurturing the body are one meaning; when one has fully awakened, the many illnesses heal of themselves. (Spring, the fifth day of the fourth month.)
